topic_text: Topic 9: What are Carve Outs/Ins in Ind AS?
question_html: What do you mean by Carve outs/ins in Ind AS? Explain.
answer_html: Certain changes have been made in Ind AS considering the economic environment of the country, which is different as compared to the economic environment presumed to be in existence by IFRS. These differences are due to differences in economic conditions prevailing in India. These differences which are in deviation to the accounting principles and practices stated in IFRS, are commonly known as 'Carve-outs'. Additional guidance given in Ind AS over and above what is given in IFRS, is termed as 'Carve in'.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating every difference between Ind AS and IFRS as a "carve-out", without recognising that removal of an option available under IFRS is explicitly not treated as a carve-out under the Ind AS framework.

topic_text: Topic 1: Introduction
question_html: "Accounting Standards standardize diverse accounting policies with a view to eliminate the non-comparability of financial statements and improve the reliability of financial statements." Discuss and explain the benefits of Accounting Standards.
answer_html:
Accounting Standards standardize diverse accounting policies with a view to eliminate the non-comparability of financial statements and improve the reliability of financial statements. Accounting Standards provide a set of standard accounting policies, valuation norms and disclosure requirements. Accounting standards aim at improving the quality of financial reporting by promoting comparability, consistency and transparency, in the interests of users of financial statements.

The following are the benefits of Accounting Standards:

(i) Standardization of alternative accounting treatments: Accounting Standards reduce to a reasonable extent confusing variations in the accounting treatment followed for the purpose of preparation of financial statements.

(ii) Requirements for additional disclosures: There are certain areas where important information is not statutorily required to be disclosed. Standards may call for disclosure beyond that required by law.

(iii) Comparability of financial statements: The application of accounting standards would facilitate comparison of financial statements of different companies situated in India and facilitate comparison, to a limited extent, of financial statements of companies situated in different parts of the world. However, it should be noted in this respect that differences in the institutions, traditions and legal systems from one country to another give rise to differences in Accounting Standards adopted in different countries.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is listing the benefits of Accounting Standards as a generic definition of what AS is, rather than specifically explaining how they reduce comparability problems, mandate additional disclosure, and aid cross-company/cross-border comparison.

topic_text: Topic 1: Introduction
question_html: What are the issues, with which Accounting Standards deal?
answer_html: Accounting Standards deal with the issues of (i) Recognition of events and transactions in the financial statements, (ii) Measurement of these transactions and events, (iii) Presentation of these transactions and events in the financial statements in a manner that is meaningful and understandable to the reader, and (iv) Disclosure requirements.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is listing only two or three of the four issues (recognition, measurement, presentation, disclosure), or substituting a generic description of "what Accounting Standards are" for this specific four-part enumeration the question asks for.

topic_text: Topic 1: Introduction
question_html: “Accounting Standards standardize diverse accounting policies with a view to eliminate the non-comparability of financial statements and improve the reliability of financial statements.” Discuss and explain the benefits of Accounting Standards.
answer_html:
Accounting Standards standardize diverse accounting policies with a view to eliminating non-comparability of financial statements and improving the reliability of financial statements. They provide a set of standard accounting policies, valuation norms, and disclosure requirements, aiming at improving the quality of financial reporting by promoting comparability, consistency, and transparency in the interests of users of financial statements.

Benefits of Accounting Standards:

(i) Standardization of alternative accounting treatments: Accounting Standards reduce, to a reasonable extent, confusing variations in the accounting treatment used to prepare financial statements.

(ii) Requirements for additional disclosures: there are certain areas where important information is not statutorily required to be disclosed; Standards may call for disclosure beyond that required by law.

(iii) Comparability of financial statements: applying accounting standards facilitates comparison of financial statements of different companies situated in India, and to a limited extent, of companies situated in different parts of the world — though differences in institutions, traditions, and legal systems from one country to another still give rise to differences in the Accounting Standards adopted in different countries.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is listing only one or two benefits instead of covering the full range (standardisation, additional disclosure, comparability), or omitting the caveat that cross-country comparability remains limited by differing legal/institutional environments.

topic_text: Topic 1: Introduction
question_html: What are Accounting Standards? Explain the objectives of "Accounting Standards" in brief, also state the advantages of setting Accounting Standards. (4 Marks)
answer_html:
Accounting Standards are the written policy documents issued by Government relating to various aspects of measurement, treatment, presentation and disclosure of accounting transactions and events.

Objectives of Accounting Standards: (a) Accounting Standards harmonize the diverse accounting policies and practices followed by different companies in India. (b) Accounting Standards facilitate the preparation of financial statements and make them comparable. (c) Accounting Standards give a sense of faith and reliability to the users.

Advantages of setting Accounting Standards: (a) Accounting Standards make the financial statements of different companies comparable, which helps investors in decision making. (b) Accounting Standards prevent any misleading accounting treatment. (c) Accounting Standards prevent manipulation of data by the management.
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: A few examinees could not clearly explain objectives of "Accounting Standards" and advantages of setting the Accounting Standards.

topic_text: Topic 5: Need Conv. towa. Global Stds
question_html: Explain the key aspects which required the need for convergence towards global standards of financial reporting. (4 Marks)
answer_html:
A few key aspects which required the need for convergence are as under:

1. Raising funds from international markets: Each country has its own set of rules and regulations for accounting and financial reporting. Therefore, when an enterprise decides to raise capital from markets other than the country in which it is located, the rules and regulations of that other country will apply, requiring the enterprise to understand the differences between the rules governing financial reporting in the foreign country as compared to its own.

2. Comparability of Financial Statements: International analysts and investors would like to compare financial statements based on similar ASs, leading to a growing need for an internationally accepted set of ASs for cross-border filings, raising investor confidence generally.

3. Uniformity, Comparability, Transparency etc.: A strong need was felt to bring about uniformity, rationalisation, comparability, transparency and adaptability in financial statements. A multiplicity of AS systems worldwide produces different reported numbers for the same events, creating confusion and encouraging error or fraud. The cure is a single set of global standards, of the highest quality, set in the public interest.

4. Global Investment: Convergence contributes to the free flow of global investment, improves investors' ability to compare investments globally (lowering risk of errors of judgment), facilitates accounting/reporting for companies with global operations, eliminates costly requirements like reinstatement of financial statements, creates a new standard of accountability and transparency, and reduces operational challenges for accounting firms.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Several examinees listed only one or two convergence drivers instead of the full range (fund-raising, comparability, uniformity, global investment), losing marks for an incomplete answer to a theory question that explicitly asks for "key aspects" in the plural.

topic_text: Topic 6: International Acct Std Board
question_html: Write a short note on International Accounting Standard Board (IASB).
answer_html:
With a view of achieving the objective of setting global standards, the London based group namely the International Accounting Standards Committee (IASC), responsible for developing International Accounting Standards (IAS), was established in June, 1973.

  • It is presently known as International Accounting Standards Board (IASB).
  • Between 1973 and 2001, the IASC released IASs. Between 1997 and 1999, the IASC restructured their organisation, which resulted in formation of IASB. These changes came into effect on 1st April, 2001. Subsequently, IASB issued statements about current and future standards.
  • IASB publishes its Standards in a series of pronouncements called International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS).
  • The standards issued by IASC till 31.03.2001 are known as IASs and the standards issued by IASB since 01.04.2001 are known as IFRSs.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees conflated the IASC and IASB timelines, or reversed which body issued IASs versus IFRSs, resulting in imprecise historical sequencing in their responses.

topic_text: Topic 1: Status of Accounting Standards
question_html:
Based upon criteria for rating of non-corporate entity, categorize the following as Level I, Level II, Level III and Level IV entities for the purpose of compliance of Accounting Standards in India.

  1. Rama Textiles whose turnover (excluding other income) exceeds ten crore but does not exceed rupees fifty crore in the immediately preceding accounting year.
  2. Star Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees two crore but not in excess of rupees ten crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  3. Newman Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) less than rupees fifty lakh at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  4. SS Finance is a financial institution carrying its business in India since last 10 years.
  5. DD Finance, holding company of SS Finance. (Entity mentioned at Point (v) above)
  6. Reliable Co-op Bank, a co-operative bank, carrying banking operations since last 15 years.
answer_html:
1. Level III Entity – Rama textiles, whose turnover (excluding other income) exceeds rupees ten crore but does not exceed rupees fifty crore in the immediately preceding accounting year.
  2. Level III Entity – Star industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees two crore but not in excess of rupees ten crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  3. Level IV Entity – Newman Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) of less than rupees fifty lakhs at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  4. Level I Entity – SS is a financial institution carrying its business in India since last 10 years.
  5. Level I Entity – DD finance, holding company of SS finance (Entity mentioned in point (d) above).
  6. Level I Entity – Reliable co-operative banks carrying on banking business for the last 15 years.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is missing that a holding company of a Level I entity is itself automatically Level I regardless of its own size, and that banks/financial institutions/co-operative banks are Level I entities by their nature, not by a turnover or borrowings threshold.

topic_text: Topic 2.1: Revised MSME classification criteria - turnover/borrowings thresholds
question_html: Virat Traders, an unlisted partnership firm, had a turnover of ₹249.99 crore and borrowings of ₹25.01 crore during the financial year 2023-24. It is not a bank, financial institution, or insurance company, and also not a subsidiary of any other entity. The firm wishes to avail MSME exemptions for FY 2024-25. Is it eligible?
answer_html:
Company qualifies as an MSME if following conditions are satisfied:

  1. whose equity or debt securities are not listed or are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange, whether in India or outside India;
  2. which is not a bank, financial institution or an insurance company;
  3. whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed 250 crore rupees in the immediately preceding accounting year;
  4. which does not have borrowings in excess of 50 crore rupees at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and
  5. which is not a holding or subsidiary of an entity which is not a MSME entity.

Yes, Virat Traders qualifies as an MSME since it meets all five criteria.

Further, it has been assumed that Virat Traders is not newly qualifying as an MSME in FY 2024-25 because a non-company entity that newly qualifies as an MSME can avail exemptions only after it remains as MSME for two consecutive years.

Until then, full AS compliance is required.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees applied the five MSME tests mechanically and concluded eligibility without addressing the two-consecutive-year assumption for newly-qualifying entities, missing part of what the question was testing.

topic_text: Topic 1: Status of Accounting Standards
question_html: As per the revised scheme effective from accounting periods commencing on or after 1st April, 2024, classify non-company entities for the purpose of applicability of Accounting Standards. Briefly explain the criteria for each category.
answer_html:
Non-company entities are classified into two categories: Micro, Small and Medium Sized Entities (MSMEs) and Large entities.

A non-company entity qualifies as an MSME if it satisfies all of: (i) its equity/debt securities are not listed or in the process of listing on any stock exchange (in India or abroad); (ii) it is not a bank, financial institution, or insurance company; (iii) turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed ₹250 crore in the immediately preceding accounting year; (iv) it does not have borrowings exceeding ₹50 crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and (v) it is not a holding or subsidiary of an entity that is not itself an MSME. These conditions are assessed as at the end of the relevant accounting period. A Large entity is any non-company entity that does not meet the MSME definition, and must comply in full with all Accounting Standards; MSMEs receive certain exemptions/relaxations.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A direct recall question from the announcement text; common gaps include omitting one of the five MSME conditions, especially the holding/subsidiary condition.

topic_text: Topic 9: Elements of Financial Statements
question_html: Briefly explain the elements of financial statements.
answer_html:
ElementDefinition
AssetResource controlled by the enterprise as a result of past events from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise.
LiabilityPresent obligation of the enterprise arising from past events, the settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow of a resource embodying economic benefits.
EquityResidual interest in the assets of an enterprise after deducting all its liabilities.
Income/gainIncrease in economic benefits during the accounting period in the form of inflows or enhancement of assets or decreases in liabilities that result in increase in equity other than those relating to contributions from equity participants.
Expense/lossDecrease in economic benefits during the accounting period in the form of outflows or depletions of assets or incurrence of liabilities that result in decrease in equity other than those relating to distributions to equity participants.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common gap is omitting income and expense from the list of financial statement elements, discussing only assets, liabilities and equity.
chapter_label: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements

topic_text: Topic 7: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts
question_html: "One of the characteristics of financial statements is neutrality"— Do you agree with this statement?
answer_html: Yes, one of the characteristics of financial statements is neutrality. To be reliable, the information contained in financial statement must be neutral, that is free from bias. Financial Statements are not neutral if by the selection or presentation of information, the focus of analysis could shift from one area of business to another thereby arriving at a totally different conclusion on the business results.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is confusing neutrality with conservatism/prudence, treating a deliberately cautious understatement of results as still "neutral" when it is in fact a form of bias in the opposite direction.
chapter_label: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements

topic_text: Topic 5: Objectives & Users of Fin Stmts   +   Topic 6: Fundamental Accounting Assumptions   +   Topic 7: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts   +   Topic 9: Elements of Financial Statements
question_html:
(i) With regard to financial statements name any four: (1) Users; (2) Qualitative characteristics; (3) Elements.
(ii) What are fundamental accounting assumptions? (5 Marks)
answer_html:
(i) (1) Users of financial statements: Investors, Employees, Lenders, Suppliers/Creditors, Customers, Government & Public.
(2) Qualitative Characteristics of Financial Statements: Understandability, Relevance, Comparability, Reliability & Faithful Representation.
(3) Elements of Financial Statements: Asset, Liability, Equity, Income/Gain and Expense/Loss.

(ii) Fundamental Accounting Assumptions: Accrual, Going Concern and Consistency.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is confusing the four qualitative characteristics (Understandability, Relevance, Reliability, Comparability) with the three fundamental accounting assumptions (Going Concern, Accrual, Consistency), or listing "Materiality"/"Prudence" as standalone qualitative characteristics rather than as components nested within Relevance and Reliability respectively.
chapter_label: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements

topic_text: Topic 7: Qual. Char. Fin Stmts
question_html: What are the qualitative characteristics of the financial statements which improve the usefulness of the information furnished therein?
answer_html:
The qualitative characteristics are attributes that improve the usefulness of information provided in financial statements. Understandability; Relevance; Reliability; Comparability are the qualitative characteristics of financial statements.

Understandability – Information presented in financial statements should be readily understandable by the users with reasonable knowledge of business and economic activities.

Relevance – Financial statements should contain relevant information only. Information, which is likely to influence the economic decisions of the users is called relevant.

Reliability – Information must be reliable; that is to say, they must be free from material error and bias.

Comparability – Financial statements should provide both inter-firm and intra-firm comparison.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is naming only two or three of the four characteristics, or confusing "Reliability" (freedom from material error/bias) with "Relevance" (capacity to influence economic decisions) – the two are frequently swapped in a rushed answer.
chapter_label: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements

(3) Rent of the premises is outstanding ₹20,000. (4) Mr. A withdrew ₹18,000 for his personal use. You are required to show the effect of above transactions on Balance Sheet in the form of Assets – Liabilities = Equity after each transaction.

Effect of each transaction on the Balance Sheet:

TransactionsAssets (₹ lakh)Liabilities (₹ lakh)Equity (₹ lakh)
Opening16.00−6.00=10.00
(1) Dividend earned16.40−6.00=10.80
(2) Settlement of Creditors15.40−4.60=10.80

topic_text: Topic 11: Capital Maintenance
question_html: A trader commenced business on April 1, 2022 with ₹1,20,000 represented by 6,000 units of a certain product at ₹20 per unit. During the year 2022-23 he sold these units at ₹30/- per unit and had withdrawn ₹60,000. The price of the product at the end of financial year was ₹25/- per unit. Compute retained profit of the trader under the concept of physical capital maintenance at current cost. Also state, whether answer would be different if the trader had not withdrawn any amount.
answer_html:
In the given case, the specific price index applicable to the product is 125 (25/20 × 100).

Current cost of opening stock = (₹1,20,000/100) × 125 Or 6,000 units × ₹25 = ₹1,50,000

Current cost of closing cash = ₹1,20,000 (₹1,80,000 − ₹60,000)

Opening equity at closing current costs = ₹1,50,000

Closing equity at closing current costs = ₹1,20,000

Retained Profit = ₹1,20,000 − ₹1,50,000 = (−) ₹30,000

The negative retained profit indicates that the trader has failed to maintain his capital. The available fund of ₹1,20,000 is not sufficient to buy 6,000 units again at increased price of ₹25 per unit. The drawings should have been restricted to ₹30,000 (₹60,000 − ₹30,000).

If the trader had not withdrawn any amount, then the answer would have been as below:

Current cost of opening stock = ₹1,80,000

Opening equity at closing current costs = ₹1,50,000

Retained Profit = ₹1,80,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹30,000

If the trader had not withdrawn any amount, then the retained profit would have been ₹30,000.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is computing retained profit as historical sale proceeds less historical cost of goods sold (a financial-capital-maintenance answer) instead of restating the opening stock to its current replacement cost and comparing that against the closing cash balance, which is what the physical-capital-maintenance concept specifically requires.
chapter_label: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements

topic_text: Topic 10: Meas of Elements of Fin Stmts
question_html: Explain in brief, the alternative measurement bases, for determining the value at which an element can be recognized in the Balance Sheet or Statement of Profit and Loss.
answer_html:
The Framework for Recognition and Presentation of Financial statements recognizes four alternative measurement bases for the purpose of determining the value at which an element can be recognized in the balance sheet or statement of profit and loss. These bases are: (i) Historical Cost; (ii) Current cost (iii) Realizable (Settlement) Value and (iv) Present Value.

A brief explanation of each measurement basis is as follows:

  1. Historical Cost: Historical cost means acquisition price. According to this, assets are recorded at an amount of cash or cash equivalent paid or the fair value of the asset at the time of acquisition. Liabilities are generally recorded at the amount of proceeds received in exchange for the obligation.
  2. Current Cost: Current cost gives an alternative measurement basis. Assets are carried out at the amount of cash or cash equivalent that would have to be paid if the same or an equivalent asset was acquired currently. Liabilities are carried at the undiscounted amount of cash or cash equivalents that would be required to settle the obligation currently.
  3. Realisable (Settlement) Value: As per realizable value, assets are carried at the amount of cash or cash equivalents that could currently be obtained by selling the assets in an orderly disposal. Liabilities are carried at their settlement values; i.e. the undiscounted amount of cash or cash equivalents paid to satisfy the liabilities in the normal course of business.
  4. Present Value: Under present value convention, assets are carried at present value of future net cash flows generated by the concerned assets in the normal course of business. Liabilities under this convention are carried at present value of future net cash flows that are expected to be required to settle the liability in the normal course of business.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is confusing Current Cost with Realisable Value – both involve a “current” amount, but Current Cost is the cost to acquire an equivalent asset today while Realisable Value is the amount obtainable by selling the existing asset today, a distinction the Framework treats as two genuinely separate bases.
chapter_label: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements

topic_text: Topic 1.2: The five key elements - assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses
question_html: What are the key elements of financial statements? Explain.
answer_html:
1. Assets: a resource controlled by the enterprise from past events, expected to bring future economic benefits (e.g. plant, patents, receivables).
  2. Liabilities: a present obligation arising from past events, settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow of economic benefits (e.g. borrowings, provisions).
  3. Equity: the residual interest in assets after deducting all liabilities — owners' claim (capital, reserves), distinct from liabilities (claims of parties other than owners); changes through contributions/distributions or income/expenses.
  4. Income/Gain: increases in economic benefits through inflow of assets or reduction of liabilities, increasing equity (includes revenue and gains).
  5. Expenses/Loss: decreases in economic benefits through outflows/depletion of assets or incurrence of liabilities, decreasing equity (other than distributions to owners) — expenses arise in the ordinary course (e.g. wages); losses may or may not (e.g. loss on PPE disposal), and are shown separately to aid performance assessment.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A direct theory recall question; common gaps include omitting the equity definition's distinction from liabilities, or failing to note that losses (unlike ordinary expenses) may fall outside the enterprise's normal activities.
chapter_label: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements

topic_text: Topic 9: Elements of Financial Statements
question_html:
Giant Ltd. has entered into a binding agreement with Tiny Ltd. to buy a custom-made machine of ₹1,00,000 at the end of 2024-25, before delivery of the machine, Giant Ltd. had to change its method of production. The new method will not require the machine ordered and it will be scrapped after delivery. The expected scrap value is nil.

You are required to advise the accounting treatment and give necessary journal entry in the year 2024-25.
answer_html:
A liability is recognized when outflow of economic resources in settlement of a present obligation can be anticipated and the value of outflow can be reliably measured.

When flow of economic benefit to the enterprise beyond the current accounting period is considered improbable, the expenditure incurred is recognised as an expense rather than as an asset.

In the given case, Giant Ltd. should recognise a liability of ₹1,00,000 to Tiny Ltd.

Also, the flow of future economic benefit from the machine to the enterprise is improbable.

Thus, the entire amount of purchase price of the machine should be recognised as an expense.

topic_text: Topic 1.9: Costs excluded from inventory cost - abnormal waste, storage, non-attributable admin overheads, selling/distribution
question_html: "In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred." Provide examples of such costs as per AS 2 (Revised) 'Valuation of Inventories'.
answer_html: Examples of costs excluded from inventory cost and expensed as incurred: (a) abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs; (b) storage costs, unless required by the production process itself; (c) administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition; (d) selling and distribution costs.

topic_text: Topic 1.9: Abnormal waste excluded from inventory cost and expensed to P&L; normal waste absorbed into remaining good units' cost
question_html: In a production process, normal waste is 5% of input. 5,000 MT of input were put in process resulting in wastage of 300 MT. Cost per MT of input is ₹1,000. The entire quantity of waste and finished output is in stock at the year end. State with reference to Accounting Standard, how will you value the inventories in this case? What will be treatment for normal and abnormal waste?
answer_html:
As per para 13 of AS 2 (Revised), abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognized as expenses in the period in which they are incurred.

In this case, normal waste is 250 MT and abnormal waste is 50 MT. The cost of 250 MT will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end. The cost of abnormal waste (50 MT × 1,052.6315 = ₹52,632) will be charged to the profit and loss statement.

Cost per MT (Normal Quantity of 4,750 MT) = 50,00,000 / 4,750 = ₹1,052.6315

Total value of inventory = 4,700 MT × ₹1,052.6315 = ₹49,47,368.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is spreading the abnormal loss quantity into the cost-per-unit computation along with the normal loss, understating the abnormal loss charged to the profit and loss statement and correspondingly overstating closing inventory.

topic_text: Topic 1.9: Abnormal waste excluded from inventory cost and expensed; normal loss absorbed into remaining good units' cost
question_html: Wooden Plywood Limited has a normal wastage of 5% in the production process. During the year 2023-24, the Company used 16,000 MT of Raw material costing ₹190 per MT. At the end of the year, 950 MT of wastage was in stock. The accountant wants to know how this wastage is to be treated in the books. You are required to: (1) Calculate the amount of abnormal loss. (2) Explain the treatment of normal loss and abnormal loss in the context of AS-2.
answer_html:
(i) As per AS 2 'Valuation of Inventories', abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognised as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. The normal loss will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end.

(ii) Material used 16,000 MT @ ₹190 = ₹30,40,000. Normal Loss (5% of 16,000 MT) = 800 MT (included in calculation of cost of inventories). Net quantity of material = 15,200 MT.

(iii) Abnormal Loss in quantity (950 − 800) = 150 MT. Abnormal Loss = ₹30,000 [150 units @ ₹200 (₹30,40,000/15,200)]. The amount of ₹30,000 (Abnormal loss) will be charged to the Profit and Loss statement.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is computing the abnormal loss quantity against the gross 16,000 MT used rather than against the 800 MT normal-loss benchmark, or valuing the abnormal loss at the original ₹190/MT purchase rate instead of the higher ₹200/MT rate that results once the normal loss is absorbed into the remaining good units.

topic_text: Topic 1.9: Normal loss absorbed into the cost of remaining good units, abnormal loss quantified separately and expensed
question_html:
Wooden Plywood Limited has a normal wastage of 5% in the production process. During the year 2024-25, the Company used 16,000 MT of Raw material costing ₹190 per MT. At the end of the year, 950 MT of wastage was in stock. The accountant wants to know how this wastage is to be treated in the books.

You are required to: (1) Calculate the amount of abnormal loss. (2) Explain the treatment of normal loss and abnormal loss [In the context of AS-2].
answer_html:
As per AS 2 (Revised) 'Valuation of Inventories', abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognised as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. The normal loss will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end.

Material used: 16,000 MT @ ₹190 = ₹30,40,000.

Normal Loss (5% of 16,000 MT) = 800 MT (included in calculation of cost of inventories).

Net quantity of material = 15,200 MT.

Abnormal Loss in quantity = (950 − 800) = 150 MT.

Abnormal Loss = ₹30,000 [150 units @ ₹200 (₹30,40,000/15,200)].

The amount of ₹30,000 (Abnormal loss) will be charged to the Profit and Loss statement.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A frequent mistake here is computing the cost per MT by dividing total material cost by the full 16,000 MT used (or by the 15,050 MT actually remaining after all wastage), instead of by the 15,200 MT net quantity remaining after only the normal loss is absorbed, which is the figure AS 2 requires for costing the abnormal loss.

topic_text: Topic 1.13/1.14: Item-by-item comparison of cost and NRV; materials held for use written down to replacement cost only when the finished product they convert into will sell below cost
question_html:
Mr. Jatin gives the following information relating to the items forming part of the inventory as on 31.03.2023. His enterprise produces product P using Raw Material X.

  1. 900 units of Raw Material X (purchased @ ₹100 per unit). Replacement cost of Raw Material X as on 31.03.2023 is ₹80 per unit.
  2. 400 units of partly finished goods in the process of producing P. Cost incurred till date is ₹245 per unit. These units can be finished next year by incurring additional cost of ₹50 per unit.
  3. 800 units of Finished goods P and total cost incurred is ₹295 per unit.

Expected selling price of product P is ₹280 per unit, subject to a payment of 5% brokerage on selling price.

Determine how each item of inventory will be valued as on 31.03.2023. Also calculate the value of total Inventory as on 31.03.2023.
answer_html:
As per AS 2 (Revised) “Valuation of Inventories”, materials and other supplies held for use in the production of inventories are not written down below cost if the finished products in which they will be incorporated are expected to be sold at cost or above cost. However, when there has been a decline in the price of materials and it is estimated that the cost of the finished products will exceed net realizable value, the materials are written down to net realizable value. In such circumstances, the replacement cost of the materials may be the best available measure of their net realizable value. In the given case, selling price of product P is ₹266 and total cost per unit for production is ₹295.

Hence the valuation will be done as under:

  1. 900 units of raw material X will be written down to replacement cost as market value of finished product is less than its cost, hence valued at ₹80 per unit.
  2. 400 units of partly finished goods will be valued at ₹216 per unit i.e., lower of cost (₹245) or Net realizable value ₹216 (Estimated selling price ₹266 per unit less additional cost of ₹50).
  3. 800 units of finished product P will be valued at NRV of ₹266 per unit since it is lower than cost ₹295.

Valuation of Total Inventory as on 31.03.2023:

ParticularsUnitsCost (₹)NRV / Replacement cost (₹)Value = units × cost or NRV whichever is less (₹)
Raw material X9001008072,000
Partly finished goods40024521686,400
Finished goods P8002952662,12,800
Value of Inventory3,71,200
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is comparing raw material's own cost against its own replacement cost in isolation, instead of first checking whether the finished product it converts into (Product P) will sell below its own total cost – AS 2 only permits marking raw material down to replacement cost when that downstream test fails. It is also easy to compute net selling price by forgetting the 5% brokerage deduction, which changes both the partly-finished-goods NRV and the finished-goods valuation.

topic_text: Topic 1.3/1.9: Costs excluded from cost of inventories and expensed as incurred (abnormal waste, unnecessary storage, non-contributing admin overheads, selling/distribution costs); lower-of-cost-and-NRV valuation with the agent's selling commission deducted from expected sale value
question_html:
(i) “In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognize them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred”. Provide examples of such costs as per AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’.

(ii) X Limited purchased goods at the cost of ₹40 lakhs in October, 2022. Till March, 2023, 75% of the stocks were sold. The company wants to disclose closing stock at ₹10 lakhs. The expected sale value is ₹11 lakhs and a commission at 10% on sale is payable to the agent. Advise, what is the correct value of closing stock to be disclosed as at 31.3.2023.
answer_html:
(i) As per AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’, certain costs are excluded from the cost of the inventories and are recognized as expenses in the period in which incurred. Examples of such costs are:

  1. abnormal amount of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs;
  2. storage costs, unless those costs are necessary in the production process prior to a further production stage;
  3. administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition; and
  4. selling and distribution costs.

(ii) As per AS 2 “Valuation of Inventories”, the inventories are to be valued at lower of cost or net realizable value. In this case, the cost of inventory is ₹10 lakhs. The net realizable value is ₹11,00,000 × 90% = ₹9,90,000. So, the stock should be valued at ₹9,90,000.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating storage costs as always excludable rather than only when unnecessary to a further production stage in part (i); and in part (ii), comparing the disclosed cost of ₹10 lakhs against the gross expected sale value of ₹11 lakhs instead of first deducting the 10% agent's commission, which changes the net realizable value from ₹11,00,000 to ₹9,90,000 and hence which figure actually governs.

topic_text: Topic 1.9: Costs excluded from inventory valuation and expensed as incurred - abnormal waste, avoidable storage, non-contributing admin overheads, selling/distribution costs
question_html: "In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred." Provide examples of such costs as per AS 2 (Revised) 'Valuation of Inventories'.
answer_html:
In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. Examples of such costs are:

(a) Abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs;

(b) Storage costs, unless the production process requires such storage.

(c) Administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition.

(d) Selling and distribution costs.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees who selected this theory alternative listed only one or two of the four categories of cost excluded from inventory valuation under AS 2, most often omitting the distinction between avoidable and production-necessary storage costs.

topic_text: Topic 1.14: Finished goods at lower of cost and NRV; feeding raw material written down to replacement cost once FG NRV falls below cost
question_html: SR Limited manufactures finished goods 'MP' from raw material 'RP'. Year ended 31st March 2025: Opening Inventory MP 4,000 units ₹1,20,000; RP 4,400 units ₹52,800. Purchase of RP 40,000 units ₹4,80,000. Labour ₹3,23,200. Fixed Overheads ₹3,15,000. Sales 40,200 units ₹11,20,000. Closing Inventory: MP 4,200 units; RP 4,000 units. Expected production 45,000 units of MP. Due to fall in market demand, sales price of MP fell to ₹22/unit; replacement cost of RP ₹11.50/unit on closing day. Calculate the value of Closing Stock of 'MP' and 'RP' as on 31st March 2025.
answer_html:
W.N.1 Actual production: Sales 40,200 + Closing FG 4,200 − Opening FG 4,000 = 40,400 units.

W.N.2 RP consumed: Opening RP 4,400 + Purchases 40,000 = 44,400 available; less Closing RP 4,000 = 40,400 units consumed (1 unit RP per unit MP produced).

W.N.3 Cost per unit RP (weighted average): (Opening value 52,800 + Purchases 4,80,000) / 44,400 units = 5,32,800/44,400 = ₹12.00/unit.

Cost of Material Consumed (40,400 × ₹12)4,84,800
Direct Labour3,23,200
Fixed Overhead (3,15,000 × 40,400/45,000 — based on normal/expected production, not actual)2,82,800
Cost of Production10,90,800
Cost per unit (10,90,800/40,400)₹27
Net Realisable Value per unit (selling price)₹22

Since NRV (₹22) is less than cost (₹27), the closing MP inventory is valued at NRV. Since finished goods NRV is below cost, the raw material RP feeding it is valued at replacement cost (₹11.50), per AS 2's write-down rule.

Value of closing inventory: MP (4,200 × ₹22) = ₹92,400. RP (4,000 × ₹11.50) = ₹46,000.
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: The performance of examinees in this part was not satisfactory. A majority of them were unable to determine the value of closing inventory of finished goods (MP) and raw materials (RP) in accordance with AS 2 "Valuation of Inventories". Several examinees failed to compute the cost of production correctly, particularly where certain items required proportionate allocation. Many could ascertain only the labour cost of ₹3,23,200, while the remaining elements of cost were incorrectly computed. Further, a large number of examinees valued the closing stock of finished goods (on NRV basis) and raw materials (on replacement cost basis) incorrectly.

topic_text: Topic 1.3: Lower of cost and NRV - the NRV-only exception is limited to specific industries, not general manufacturing
question_html: A private limited company manufacturing fancy terry towels had valued its closing inventory of finished goods at realisable value, inclusive of profit and export cash incentives. Firm contracts had been received and goods were packed for export, but ownership had not been transferred to the foreign buyers. Comment on the valuation of the inventories by the company.
answer_html:
AS 2 requires inventories to be valued at the lower of historical cost and net realisable value. AS 9 permits valuing goods at net realisable value only in specific industries where performance is substantially complete prior to the transaction generating revenue — e.g. harvested agricultural crops or extracted mineral ores, where a sale is assured under forward contract/government guarantee or a ready market exists with negligible risk of failure to sell.

Fancy terry towels do not fall into the agricultural-crop or mineral-ore category. Since ownership had not transferred to the foreign buyers, the sale was not yet complete. The closing inventory should therefore have been valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, not at net realisable value. Further, export cash incentives are recognised only in the year the export sale actually takes place, not accrued into inventory valuation ahead of the sale. The company's valuation policy is therefore not correct.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees accepted the NRV-inclusive-of-profit valuation on the basis of firm export contracts alone, not recognising that the AS 9 exception is limited to specific industries (agricultural/mineral) and does not extend to manufactured goods merely because a sale contract exists.

topic_text: Topic 1.6: Fixed production overheads absorbed on normal capacity, excluding interest, for standard-cost/closing-stock valuation
question_html:
Kirti Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing computers. During the year ended 31st March, 2024, the company manufactured 550 computers. It has the policy of valuing finished stock of goods at a standard cost of ₹1.8 lakh per computer. The details of the costs are as under:

(₹ in lakh)
Raw material consumed400
Direct Labour250
Variable production overheads150
Fixed production overheads (including interest of ₹100 lakh)290

Compute the value cost per computer for the purpose of closing stock.
answer_html:
As per para 9 of AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’, for inclusion in the cost of inventory, allocation of fixed production overheads is based on the normal capacity of the production facilities.

In this case, finished stock has been valued at a standard cost of ₹1.8 lakh per computer which incidentally synchronizes with the value computed on the basis of absorption costing as under:

(₹ in lakh)
Materials400
Direct Labour250
Variable production overheads150
Fixed production overheads290
Less: Interest(100)190
Total cost990

Number of computers produced = 550 computers (Assumed to be normal production).

Cost per computer ₹990 lakh / 550 computers = ₹1.80 lakh.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is including the ₹100 lakh interest component within fixed production overheads when arriving at the cost of inventory, instead of excluding financing costs that are not part of bringing the inventory to its present location and condition.

topic_text: Topic 1.10: Joint products and by-products - by-product/scrap NRV deducted from joint cost; raw material stays at cost when finished goods sell above cost
question_html: Zing Ltd., 2024-25: Raw Material closing stock 700 units, cost ₹35/unit, replacement cost ₹20/unit. Finished products FP1/FP2: Production 3,000/1,600 units; Closing stock 500/300 units. Material consumed ₹3,20,000; Direct labour ₹1,60,000; Direct expenses ₹78,000 (these three cost figures pertain to combined joint production). Fixed overhead ₹95,000, including ₹15,000 godown rent (for storing finished products, not a production cost). 1,000 units of by-product BY also emerged, sold @₹12/unit after ₹2,500 expense; ₹4,800 realized from scrap sale. Average market price: FP1 ₹160/unit, FP2 ₹100/unit. Calculate the value of closing stock per AS 2.
answer_html:
Per AS 2, most by-products/scrap are measured at NRV, deducted from the cost of the main product.

NRV of by-product BY: Selling price (1,000×₹12) 12,000, less separate processing charges 2,500 = ₹9,500.

Joint cost to allocate: Raw material 3,20,000 + Labour 1,60,000 + Direct expenses 78,000 + Fixed overhead (95,000−15,000 godown rent, excluded as unrelated to production) 80,000 = 6,38,000; less NRV of BY (9,500) and scrap sale value (4,800) = ₹6,23,700 to allocate between FP1 and FP2.

FP1FP2
Output (units)3,0001,600
Sales price/unit₹160₹100
Sales value4,80,0001,60,000
Allocation ratio31
Joint cost allocated (3:1)4,67,7751,55,925
Cost per unit₹155.93₹97.45

Since both FP1 (₹155.93 cost vs ₹160 selling price) and FP2 (₹97.45 vs ₹100) sell above cost, both finished goods are valued at cost, and the raw material feeding them is valued at its own cost (₹35/unit, not written down to the ₹20 replacement cost).

Closing inventory: FP1 (500×₹155.93) = ₹77,965. FP2 (300×₹97.45) = ₹29,235. Raw material (700×₹35) = ₹24,500. Total closing inventory = ₹77,965 + ₹29,235 + ₹24,500 = ₹1,31,700.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees included the godown rent (storage cost unrelated to production, per AS 2's general exclusion of storage costs) in the joint cost pool, or wrote raw material down to replacement cost despite both finished goods selling above their allocated cost.

topic_text: Topic 2.6-2.7: Initial measurement of PPE at cost - directly attributable costs and decommissioning/restoration estimate included, initial operating losses excluded
question_html:
Preet Ltd. is installing a new plant at its production facility. It has incurred these costs:

Particulars₹
Cost of the plant (cost per supplier's invoice plus taxes)10,00,000
Initial delivery and handling costs80,000
Cost of site preparation2,40,000
Consultants used for advice on the acquisition of the plant2,80,000
Estimated dismantling costs to be incurred after 7 years1,20,000
Operating losses before commercial production1,60,000

Please advise Preet Ltd. on the costs that can be capitalised in accordance with AS 10 (Revised). (5 Marks)
answer_html:
According to AS 10 (Revised), these costs can be capitalised:

#Particulars₹
1.Cost of the plant10,00,000
2.Initial delivery and handling costs80,000
3.Cost of site preparation2,40,000
4.Consultants' fees2,80,000
5.Estimated dismantling costs to be incurred after 7 years1,20,000
Total17,20,000

Note: Operating losses before commercial production amounting to ₹1,60,000 are not regarded as directly attributable costs and thus cannot be capitalized. They should be written off to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the period they are incurred.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is including the pre-commercial-production operating losses in the capitalised cost of the plant, on the mistaken reasoning that they were incurred before the asset was ready for use – AS 10 specifically excludes initial operating losses as a directly attributable cost, regardless of timing.

topic_text: Topic 2.5/2.6/2.9: Nil depreciation when residual value equals cost; freehold land not depreciated; depreciation on a self-constructed asset begins when ready for use, not when actually used; revised useful-life estimate spread prospectively over the remaining life
question_html:
A Ltd. had following assets. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2023 for each asset as per AS 10 (Revised):

  1. Machinery purchased for ₹10 lakhs on 1st April, 2018 and residual value after useful life of 5 years, based on 2018 prices is ₹10 lakhs.
  2. Land for ₹50 lakhs.
  3. A Machinery is constructed for ₹5,00,000 for its own use (useful life is 10 years). Construction is completed on 1st April, 2022, but the company does not begin using the machine until 31st March, 2023.
  4. Machinery purchased on 1st April, 2020 for ₹50,000 with useful life of 5 years and residual value is NIL. On 1st April, 2022, management decided to use this asset for further 2 years only. (4 Parts × 5 Marks = 20 Marks)
answer_html:
Computation of amount of depreciation as per AS 10

AssetDepreciation (₹)
(i) Machinery purchased on 1/4/18 for ₹10 lakhs (having residual value of ₹10 lakhs).
Reason: The company considers that the residual value, based on prices prevailing at the balance sheet date, will equal the cost. Therefore, there is no depreciable amount and depreciation is correctly zero.		Nil
(ii) Land (₹50 lakhs) (considered freehold).
Reason: Land has an unlimited useful life and therefore, it is not depreciated.		Nil
(iii) Machinery constructed for own use (₹5,00,000/10).
Reason: The entity should begin charging depreciation from the date the machine is ready for use i.e. 1st April, 2022. The fact that the machine was not used for a period after it was ready to be used is not relevant in considering when to begin charging depreciation.		50,000
(iv) Machinery having revised useful life.
Reason: The entity has charged depreciation using the straight-line method at ₹10,000 per annum i.e. (50,000/5 years). On 1st April, 2022 the asset’s net book value is [50,000 − (10,000 × 2)] i.e. ₹30,000. The remaining useful life is 2 years as per revised estimate. The company should amend the annual provision for depreciation to charge the unamortized cost over the revised remaining life of 2 years. Consequently, it should charge depreciation for the next 2 years at ₹15,000 per annum i.e. (30,000/2 years).		15,000
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error on part (iii) is deferring the start of depreciation to the date the machine is actually put into use rather than the date it becomes ready for use, and on part (iv) treating the revised remaining life as a fresh 5-year period instead of amending the existing straight-line rate to spread the asset's already-reduced net book value over only the 2 years actually remaining.

topic_text: Topic 2.6-2.7: Costs excluded from PPE cost even though incidental to acquiring/renovating the asset - pre-opening staff costs and reorganisation-type expenditure not directly attributable to bringing the asset to its intended working condition are expensed, not capitalised
question_html:
Neon Enterprise operates a major chain of restaurants located in different cities. The company has acquired a new restaurant located at Chandigarh. The new-restaurant requires significant renovation expenditure. Management expects that the renovations will last for 3 months during which the restaurant will be closed.

Management has prepared the following budget for this period –

ParticularsAmount (₹)
Salaries of the staff engaged in preparation of restaurant before its opening7,50,000
Construction and remodelling cost of restaurant30,00,000

Explain the treatment of these expenditures as per the provisions of AS 10 "Property, Plant and Equipment".
answer_html: Constructing or acquiring a new asset may result in incremental costs that would have been avoided if the asset had not been constructed or acquired. These costs are not to be included in the cost of the asset if they are not directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management. The costs to be incurred by the company are in the nature of costs of reducing or reorganizing the operations of the company. These costs do not meet that requirement of AS 10 “Property, Plant and Equipment” and cannot, therefore, be capitalized.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating the pre-opening staff salaries and the construction/remodelling cost identically merely because both fall within the same closure period, without separately testing each item against AS 10's directly-attributable-cost condition.

topic_text: Topic 2.6-2.7: Costs of relocating/reorganising operations excluded from the cost of an asset; computing the directly attributable acquisition cost of land net of recoverable GST on salvage proceeds
question_html:
Hardy Ltd. intends to extend the factory set up on the adjacent plot with disintegrated old premises. It acquired the land having an area of 250 hectares at a cost of ₹25,000 per hectare.

Hardy Ltd. incurred Stamp duty and registration charges of 5% of land value. Legal fees were paid ₹4,75,000 for land acquisition.

Hardy Ltd. incurred ₹37,85,000 for demolishing old premises thereon. A sum of ₹12,60,000 (including 5% GST thereon) was realized from the sale of material salvaged from the site.

Till the new site with extended factory premises is ready, the company needs to move the present production facilities to another (temporary) site. The following incremental costs will be incurred.

(1) Set up costs of ₹7,50,000 to install machinery in the new location. (2) Rent of ₹12,00,000. (3) Removal costs of ₹2,50,000 to transport the machinery from the old location to the temporary location.

(i) Management is of the opinion that the cost of moving the production facilities to another temporary location can be capitalised. You are required to advise. (ii) You are also required to compute the cost of land acquired. (7 Marks)
answer_html:
(i) Constructing or acquiring a new asset may result in incremental costs that would have been avoided if the asset had not been constructed or acquired. These costs are not to be included in the cost of the asset if they are not directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition necessary for it to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management. The costs to be incurred by the company are in the nature of costs of relocating or reorganising operations of the company and do not meet the requirement of AS 10 (Revised). Therefore, these costs cannot be capitalized.

(ii) Computation of cost of land:

Particulars₹
Purchase Price250 hectares × ₹25,000 per hectare62,50,000
Stamp Duty and Registration Charges5% of ₹62,50,0003,12,500
Legal and Consultancy Fees4,75,000
Demolition Expenses (Net of Salvage Income)₹37,85,000 − ₹12,60,000 × (100/105) [i.e. ₹37,85,000 − ₹12,00,000]25,85,000
Cost of Land96,22,500
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: A significant number of examinees displayed a lack of understanding of the provisions of AS 10 "Property, Plant and Equipment." Instead of applying the correct provisions, many examinees incorrectly based their responses on AS 16 — Borrowing Costs, especially while commenting on the capitalisation of expenses related to the relocation of production facilities. Additionally, several examinees were unable to accurately compute the cost of land.

topic_text: Topic 2.10: Replacement of a significant component: capitalise the new part's cost and derecognise the estimated carrying amount of the part replaced
question_html:
MS Ltd. has acquired a heavy machinery at a cost of ₹1,00,00,000 (with no breakdown of the component parts). The estimated useful life is 10 years. At the end of the sixth year, one of the major components, the turbine requires replacement, as further maintenance is uneconomical. The remainder of the machine is perfect and is expected to last for the next four years. The cost of a new turbine is ₹45,00,000. The discount rate assumed is 5%.

Can the cost of the new turbine be recognised as an asset, and, if so, what treatment should be used?
answer_html:
The new turbine will produce economic benefits to MS Ltd., and the cost is measurable. Hence, the item should be recognised as an asset. The original invoice for the machine did not specify the cost of the turbine; however, the cost of the replacement ₹45,00,000 can be used as an indication (usually by discounting) of the likely cost, six years previously.

topic_text: Topic 2.5: Nil depreciable amount when residual value equals cost
question_html: Machinery purchased 1st April, 2020 for ₹10 lakhs, useful life 5 years, residual value (at 2020 prices) ₹10 lakhs. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025 per AS 10 (Revised).
answer_html: Nil. Since the residual value (₹10 lakhs) equals the cost (₹10 lakhs), the depreciable amount is nil; depreciation is correctly zero throughout the asset's life.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees computed depreciation on the full cost, ignoring the stated residual value entirely.

topic_text: Topic 2.5: Freehold land is not depreciated - unlimited useful life
question_html: The company owns a piece of land acquired for ₹50 lakhs, held for use in its factory operations. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
answer_html: Nil. Land has an unlimited useful life (unless it is a wasting asset such as a quarry) and is therefore not depreciated.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A basic but recurring error is depreciating land alongside buildings without separating the two components.

topic_text: Topic 2.6: Depreciation begins when the asset is ready for use, not when actual use commences
question_html: Zenith Ltd. constructed a machine for its own use, total cost ₹5,00,000, completed 1st April, 2024, useful life 10 years; the company did not commence using the machine until 31st March, 2025. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
answer_html: ₹50,000 (₹5,00,000/10 years). Depreciation begins from the date the machine is ready for use (1st April, 2024), regardless of when actual use commenced — the fact that it sat idle for a period after being ready is not relevant to when depreciation begins.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees charged no depreciation at all, reasoning the machine was never actually used during the year, missing that "ready for use" (not actual use) triggers depreciation.

topic_text: Topic 2.9: Revised useful-life estimate - unamortised cost spread prospectively over the revised remaining life
question_html: Another machine was purchased 1st April, 2022, for ₹50,000, useful life 5 years, nil residual value. On 1st April, 2024, management decided the machine would now be used for only two more years. Calculate depreciation for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
answer_html: Original SLM depreciation = ₹50,000/5 = ₹10,000/year. Net book value on 1st April, 2024 (after 2 years) = 50,000−20,000 = ₹30,000. With the revised remaining useful life of 2 years, the unamortised cost is spread over the revised remaining life: 30,000/2 = ₹15,000/year for the next 2 years.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees continued the original ₹10,000/year rate, not recognising that a revised useful-life estimate requires recomputing the annual charge over the remaining life going forward.

topic_text: Topic 2.6-2.7: Cost of a PPE item as purchase price plus directly attributable costs, at actual cost with internal profit eliminated
question_html:
Shrishti Ltd. contracted with a supplier to purchase machinery which is to be installed in its Department A in three months' time. Special foundations were required for the machinery which were to be prepared within this supply lead time. The cost of the site preparation and laying foundations were ₹1,41,870. These activities were supervised by a technician during the entire period, who is employed for this purpose at ₹45,000 per month. The technician's services were given by Department B to Department A, which billed the services at ₹49,500 per month after adding 10% profit margin.

The machine was purchased at ₹1,58,34,000 inclusive of IGST @ 12% for which input credit is available to Shrishti Ltd. ₹55,770 transportation charges were incurred to bring the machine to the factory site. An Architect was appointed at a fee of ₹30,000 to supervise machinery installation at the factory site.

Ascertain the amount at which the Machinery should be capitalized under AS 10, considering that IGST credit is availed by Shrishti Limited. Internally booked profits should be eliminated in arriving at the cost of machine.

ParticularsBasis₹
Purchase PriceGiven (₹1,58,34,000 × 100/112, IGST credit removed)1,41,37,500
Add: Site Preparation CostGiven1,41,870
Add: Technician's SalarySpecific/attributable overhead for 3 months, at cost, no internal profit (45,000 × 3)1,35,000
Add: Transportation ChargesInitial delivery cost, given55,770
Add: Architect's FeesProfessional fees for installation, given30,000

The technician's cost is included at its actual salary cost of ₹45,000/month (attributable overhead directly related to bringing the asset to its working condition), not the ₹49,500/month inter-departmental billing rate, since the 10% mark-up billed by Department B to Department A is an internally booked profit that must be eliminated when arriving at the cost of the machine for external financial reporting.

topic_text: Topic 2.4: Directly attributable costs capitalised, including net trial-run/testing cost after deducting any proceeds from test output
question_html: Precision Tools Ltd. purchased a machine for ₹12,00,000 on 1st October 2024. Additional expenses: Freight and insurance ₹60,000; Erection charges ₹40,000; Testing cost — raw materials used ₹25,000, wages ₹10,000, sale of finished goods from testing production ₹8,000. Calculate the amount to be capitalized for this machine per AS 10.
answer_html:
Purchase Price12,00,000

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Component replacement - derecognise the replaced component's carrying amount, capitalise the new component's cost
question_html: On 1st December 2024, Precision Tools Ltd. replaced the motor of an old machine with a new one costing ₹1,20,000, improving output capacity by 15%. The old motor had cost ₹50,000 and accumulated depreciation ₹35,000. Calculate the amount to be capitalized.
answer_html: Carrying amount of the old motor = 50,000−35,000 = ₹15,000, which is derecognised (written off) since it is being replaced. The new motor's acquisition cost of ₹1,20,000 is capitalised as a separate component (component accounting under AS 10). Net effect: ₹1,20,000 capitalised, ₹15,000 carrying amount of the old motor removed/expensed.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees simply added the new motor's cost to the machine's carrying value without also derecognising the replaced motor's remaining carrying amount.

topic_text: Topic 2.4: Relocation/reorganisation costs are never capitalised, regardless of connection to a specific asset
question_html: On 15th March 2025, Precision Tools Ltd. shifted a machine from one factory to another, incurring: Dismantling cost ₹12,000; Transport and installation ₹18,000; Loss due to damage in transit ₹6,000. Calculate the amount to be capitalized.
answer_html: Nil is capitalised — costs of relocating or reorganising part or all of an enterprise's operations are not included in the carrying amount of PPE under AS 10. The entire ₹36,000 (12,000+18,000+6,000) is charged off to the Profit and Loss Account.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees capitalised the transport and installation cost, reasoning it was directly attributable to the machine, missing AS 10's specific exclusion of relocation costs regardless of their connection to a particular asset.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Cost of installation - directly attributable labour/supervisor/testing costs; deferred-credit interest excluded   +   Topic 7.13/7.16: Impairment loss on a revalued asset - first set off against the revaluation reserve balance, remainder to P&L
question_html:
On 1 April, 2022, Sky Limited purchased a machinery for ₹7,35,000 (inclusive of GST @5%, input credit available for entire amount). Other installation expenses: Cost of preparation of site ₹16,500; Total Labour charges ₹75,000 (200 of 500 total men hours spent on installation); Total salary of supervisor ₹34,000 (25% of time spent on installation); Interest charges paid to supplier for deferred credit ₹8,000; Test run and experimental production expenses ₹28,200; Consultancy charges to architect for plant set up ₹18,800; Depreciation on assets used for installation ₹8,000. The machine was ready for use on October 1, 2022 but was put to use from February 1, 2023 (further expenses of ₹10,800 incurred due to this delay). Estimated useful life 10 years, SLM, no residual value.

On September 30, 2025, the company revalued the machine at ₹7 lakhs, surplus credited to revaluation reserve. For the year ended March 31, 2026, conditions indicating impairment existed and the recoverable amount was ascertained to be only ₹3 Lakhs.

You are required to: (i) Calculate the value at which the machine should be capitalized and the amount of depreciation to be charged for the year ending March 31, 2023 in the books of Sky Limited. (ii) Calculate the loss on impairment of the machine and show how this loss is to be treated in the books of Sky Limited. The company had followed the policy of writing down the revaluation surplus by the increased charge of depreciation resulting from the revaluation. (5 Marks)
answer_html:
(i) Calculation of Cost of Machinery:

Purchase Price7,35,000
Add: Site Preparation Cost16,500
Labour charges (75,000 × 200/500)30,000
Supervisor's Salary (25% of 34,000)8,500
Test run and experimental production charges28,200
Architect Fees for set up18,800
Depreciation on assets used for installation8,000
Total Cost of Asset8,45,000
Less: GST credit receivable(35,000)
Value to be capitalized8,10,000
Depreciation to be charged on 31.3.2023 (for 6 months, SLM 10 year)40,500

Note: (i) Further expenses of ₹10,800 from 1.10.2022 to 1.2.2023 are charged to profit and loss A/c, as the plant was ready for production on 1.10.2022 (already capitalised) – the delay in actual use does not extend capitalisation. (ii) Interest charges of ₹8,000 paid on deferred credit terms to the supplier of the plant (not a qualifying asset) are not directly attributable costs and are written off to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the period incurred.

(ii) Statement showing impairment loss and its treatment:

Carrying amount of the machine as on 01/10/20228,10,000
Less: Depreciation for 3 years (8,10,000 x 3/10)(2,43,000)
Carrying amount as on 30/09/20255,67,000
Add: Upward revaluation (credited to revaluation reserve)1,33,000
Carrying amount of the machine as on 30/09/2025 (post-revaluation)7,00,000
Less: Depreciation for 6 months up to 31/03/2026 (7,00,000 x 0.5/7)(50,000)
Carrying amount as on 31/03/20266,50,000
Less: Recoverable amount(3,00,000)
Impairment Loss3,50,000
Less: balance in revaluation reserve as on 31/03/2026 [1,33,000 − (50,000−40,500)](1,23,500)
Impairment Loss to be debited to Profit & Loss Account2,26,500

Depreciation for 01/10/2025 to 31/03/2026 (7,00,000 x 0.5/7) = ₹50,000. Depreciation set off against Revaluation Reserve = (1,33,000 x 0.5/7) = ₹9,500 (Impairment loss set off against revaluation reserve balance as per para 58 of AS 28 "Impairment of Assets").
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees debited the entire ₹3,50,000 impairment loss to the profit and loss account, not applying AS 28's requirement (para 58) to first set off an impairment loss on a revalued asset against the remaining balance in that asset's revaluation reserve before charging the balance to P&L. Several also capitalised the ₹10,800 delay-related expenses instead of expensing them, since the asset was already ready for use on 1st October, 2022.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Cost of a self-constructed asset - directly attributable costs only, excluding relocation/inauguration   +   Topic 4.4/4.9: Eligible borrowing cost net of temporary-investment income, capitalisation period
question_html:
On 1st April, 2024, Y Limited purchased an industrial plot of land for ₹50,00,000 for the purpose of constructing a new factory. This cost of ₹50,00,000 included legal cost of ₹2,50,000 incurred for the purpose of acquisition of this plot. The construction of the factory commenced on 1st May, 2024. Y Limited provides you with the following details of the costs incurred in relation to the above construction:

However, it was estimated that the roof would need to be replaced 20 years after the date of completion. The cost of replacing the roof at current prices would be 25% of the total cost of the building. The construction of the factory was partly financed by a loan of ₹56,00,000 raised from State Bank of India on 1st April, 2024 at an interest rate of 9% per annum. During the period when the loan proceeds had been fully utilized to finance the construction, Y Limited earned an income of ₹50,000 from the temporary investment of the proceeds. Assume that all of the net finance cost needs to be allocated to the cost of factory (excluding land) and interest cost to be capitalized based on eight months' period.

You are required to compute the carrying amount (i.e. value after charging depreciation) of the Factory in the books of Y Limited as at 31 March, 2025 as per the provisions of the relevant Accounting Standard.

Cost of construction of the factory

Cost of Industrial Plot50,00,000

Purchase of Raw materials for the construction42,48,000
Overhead costs incurred directly on the construction of the factory (₹50,000 per month) for 8 months4,00,000
Interest on ₹56,00,000 for 9 months @ 9% = ₹3,78,000 less ₹50,0003,28,000
Total Cost (A)1,06,00,000
Depreciation (B) (W.N.)43,750

On land of ₹50,00,000: Nil. On remaining cost of Building i.e. ₹1,06,00,000 − ₹50,00,000 = ₹56,00,000:

  • On Building: ₹56,00,000 × 75% / 40 yrs × 3/12 = ₹26,250
  • On roof: ₹56,00,000 × 25% / 20 yrs × 3/12 = ₹17,500
  • Total Depreciation charged = ₹43,750

Several also capitalised the gross interest of ₹3,78,000 without netting the ₹50,000 temporary-investment income against it, as AS 16 requires.

topic_text: Topic 6.17: Recognition-as-expense rule - once expensed in a prior period, a cost cannot later be capitalised even after approval/criteria are met
question_html: As per provisions of AS-26, how would you deal to the following situations: (1) ₹23,00,000 paid by a manufacturing company to the legal advisor for defending the patent of a product is treated as a capital expenditure. (2) During the year 2023-24, a company spent ₹7,00,000 for publicity and research expenses on one of its new consumer products which was marketed in the same accounting year but proved to be a failure. (3) A company spent ₹25,00,000 in the past three years to develop a product, these expenses were charged to profit and loss account since they did not meet AS-26 criteria for capitalization. In the current year approval of the concerned authority has been received. The company wishes to capitalize ₹25,00,000 by disclosing it as a prior period item. (4) A company with a turnover of ₹200 crores and an annual advertising budget of ₹50,00,000 had taken up for the marketing of a new product by a company. It was estimated that the company would have a turnover of ₹20 crore from the new product. The company had debited to its Profit & Loss Account the total expenditure of ₹50,00,000 incurred on extensive special initial advertisement campaign for the new product.
answer_html:
As per AS 26 "Intangible Assets", subsequent expenditure on an intangible asset after its purchase or its completion should be recognized as an expense when it is incurred unless (a) it is probable that the expenditure will enable the asset to generate future economic benefits in excess of its originally assessed standard of performance; and (b) expenditure can be measured and attributed to the asset reliably. If these conditions are met, the subsequent expenditure should be added to the cost of the intangible asset.

  1. In the given case, the legal expenses to defend the patent of a product amounting ₹23,00,000 should not be capitalized and be charged to Profit and Loss Statement.
  2. The company is required to expense the entire amount of ₹7,00,000 in the Profit and Loss account for the year ended 31st March, 2024 because no benefit will arise in the future.
  3. As per AS 26, expenditure on an intangible item that was initially recognized as an expense by a reporting enterprise in previous annual financial statements should not be recognized as part of the cost of an intangible asset at a later date. Thus, the company cannot capitalize the amount of ₹25,00,000 and it should be recognized as expense.
  4. Expenditure of ₹50,00,000 on advertising and promotional activities should always be charged to Profit and Loss Statement. Hence, the company has done the correct treatment by debiting the sum of ₹50 lakhs to Profit and Loss Account.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A frequent mistake is capitalising defence-of-patent legal costs or attempting to retrospectively capitalise previously expensed development costs once approval is later obtained; AS 26 bars reinstating costs already recognised as an expense in an earlier period.

topic_text: Topic 6.24-6.25: Carrying amount from the date recognition criteria first met, then tested for impairment against recoverable amount
