topic_text: Topic 6.5: Subsequent expenditure, previously-expensed items never later capitalized, advertising always expensed
question_html: As per provisions of AS-26, how would you deal with the following situations: (1) ₹23,00,000 paid by a manufacturing company to the legal advisor for defending the patent of a product, treated as capital expenditure. (2) During 2024-2025, a company spent ₹7,00,000 on publicity and research expenses on a new consumer product, marketed the same year but proved a failure. (3) A company spent ₹25,00,000 over three years to develop a product, charged to P&L since AS-26 capitalization criteria were not met; in the current year approval was received and the company wishes to capitalize ₹25,00,000 as a prior period item. (4) A company (turnover ₹200 crores, annual advertising budget ₹50,00,000) debited ₹50,00,000 to P&L for an extensive special initial advertisement campaign for a new product expected to generate ₹20 crore turnover.
answer_html:
(1) The legal expenses of ₹23,00,000 to defend the patent should not be capitalized — subsequent expenditure on an intangible asset is expensed unless it enables the asset to generate future economic benefits in excess of its originally assessed performance and can be reliably measured and attributed. Defending an existing right does not meet this test; charge to P&L.

(2) The full ₹7,00,000 must be expensed in the year ended 31st March, 2025, since the product failed and no future economic benefit will arise.

(3) AS 26 explicitly prohibits reinstating expenditure on an intangible item that was previously recognised as an expense — the company cannot capitalize the ₹25,00,000 even with the current-year approval; it remains an expense already recognised, not a prior period item to be restated.

(4) Advertising and promotional expenditure is always charged to the Profit and Loss Account as incurred, regardless of expected future revenue benefit — the company's treatment of debiting the full ₹50,00,000 is correct.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees allowed the ₹25,00,000 to be capitalized once approval was received, missing AS 26's explicit bar on reinstating expenditure once it has been recognised as an expense in an earlier period.

topic_text: Topic 6.7: Amortization in the ratio of estimated future cash flows, not straight-line
question_html: Record Journal Entries for amortization in the books of Huge Ltd. for the year ended 31st March, 2025 with reference to AS-26: Patent Rights acquired for ₹340 lakhs on 01.04.2023, estimated product life 4 years, amortization decided in the ratio of estimated future cash flows: Year 1 ₹140 lakhs, Year 2 ₹350 lakhs, Year 3 ₹280 lakhs, Year 4 ₹420 lakhs.
answer_html:
Amortization for the second year (2024-25, the year in question): ₹340 lakhs × 350/(140+350+280+420) = 340 × 350/1,190 = ₹100 lakhs.

Journal entry (31.3.2025): Amortization A/c Dr. 100 lakhs; To Patent Rights A/c 100 lakhs. P&L A/c Dr. 100 lakhs; To Amortization A/c 100 lakhs.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees amortized the patent on a straight-line basis (₹85 lakhs/year) instead of following the cash-flow-ratio method the question specifically directs.

topic_text: Topic 6.17: Expenditure that fails asset-recognition criteria must be expensed, never later deferred once no future benefit is expected
question_html: K Ltd. launched a project for producing product X in October, 2023. The Company incurred ₹40 lakhs towards Research and Development expenses upto 31st March, 2024. Due to prevailing market conditions, the Management came to conclusion that the product cannot be manufactured and sold in the market for the next 10 years. The Management hence wants to defer the expenditure write off to future years. Advise the Company as per the applicable Accounting Standard.
answer_html:
As per AS 26 "Intangible Assets", expenditure on research should be recognized as an expense when it is incurred. An intangible asset arising from development (or from the development phase of an internal project) should be recognized if, and only if, an enterprise can demonstrate all of the conditions specified in para 44 of the standard. An intangible asset (arising from development) should be derecognised when no future economic benefits are expected from its use according to para 87 of the standard. Thus, the manager cannot defer the expenditure write off to future years in the given case.

Hence, the expenses amounting ₹40 lakhs incurred on the research and development project has to be written off in the current year ending 31st March, 2024.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is advising deferral of the expenditure on the basis that the product might still become viable in future, rather than applying AS 26's rule that once no future economic benefit is expected, the amount cannot be carried forward or deferred, regardless of management's stated intention.

topic_text: Topic 6.15: Costs incurred before technological feasibility is established are expensed (research phase); costs from that point until product-master completion are capitalised (development phase); post-development duplication/packing costs are expensed
question_html:
During 2023-2024, an enterprise incurred costs to develop and produce a routine, low risk computer software product, as follows:

Completion of detailed programme and design (Phase 1)₹25,000
Coding and Testing for establishing technical feasibility (Phase 2)₹20,000
Other coding costs (Phase 3)₹42,000
Testing costs (Phase 4)₹12,000
Product masters for training materials (Phase 5)₹13,000
Duplication of computer software and training materials, from product masters (2,000 units) (Phase 6)₹40,000
Packing the product (1,000 units) (Phase 7)₹11,000

After completion of phase 2, it was established that the computer software is technically feasible for the market. What amount should be capitalized as software costs in the books of the company, on the Balance Sheet date?
answer_html:
As per para 44 of AS 26, costs incurred in creating a computer software product should be charged to research and development expense when incurred until technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria has been established for the product. Technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria have been established upon completion of detailed programme design or working model. In this case, ₹45,000 would be recorded as an expense (₹25,000 for completion of detailed programme design and ₹20,000 for coding and testing to establish technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria).

Cost incurred from the point of technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria until the time when product costs are incurred are capitalized as software cost (₹42,000 + ₹12,000 + ₹13,000) = ₹67,000. Duplication of computer software and training materials, from product masters and packing the products are costs incurred after the development phase. Hence, the same shall be expensed off during the year it is incurred.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is capitalising the cost of completing the detailed programme design and the coding/testing performed to establish technical feasibility, missing that AS 26 requires all costs incurred before technological feasibility is established to be expensed as research and development, with capitalisation beginning only from that point onward.

topic_text: Topic 6.7: Amortization ratio revised mid-life when future-cash-flow estimates and remaining useful life change
question_html: Swift Limited acquired patent rights to manufacture Solar Roof Top Panels for ₹600 lacs. Product life cycle estimated at 5 years; amortization decided in the ratio of future cash flows: Year 1–5: 300, 300, 300, 150, 150 (₹ lacs). After Year 3, estimated balance future life revised to 3 years, with expected cash flow after Year 5 of ₹75 lacs. Determine the amortization cost of the patent for each year per AS 26.
answer_html:
Years 1–3, amortized in the ratio of the originally estimated future cash flows 300:300:300:150:150 (total 1,200): each of Years 1, 2, 3 = ₹600 × 300/1,200 = ₹150 lacs/year.

Unamortized patent cost after Year 3 = 600−450 = ₹150 lacs, now amortized over the revised remaining life of 3 years (Years 4, 5, 6) in the ratio of the revised estimated future cash flows: 150:150:75 (i.e. 2:2:1). Year 4 = 150×2/5=₹60 lacs; Year 5 = ₹60 lacs; Year 6 = 150×1/5=₹30 lacs.

Total amortized over the patent's full (revised) life: 150+150+150+60+60+30 = ₹600 lacs, fully recovering the original cost.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees continued amortizing the remaining balance using the original 5-year cash-flow ratio, not re-basing the calculation on the revised 3-year remaining life and its own revised cash-flow estimates.

topic_text: Topic 6.7-6.11: Separately-acquired intangibles (franchise, patent, purchased-business goodwill) recognised at cost and amortised over their useful/contractual/economic life
question_html:
Naresh Ltd. had the following transactions during the financial year 2022-2023:

  1. Naresh Ltd. acquired the running business of Sunil Ltd. for ₹10,80,000 on 15th May, 2022. The fair value of Sunil Ltd.'s net assets was ₹5,16,000. Naresh Ltd. is of the view that due to popularity of Sunil Ltd.'s product in the market, its goodwill exists.
  2. Naresh Ltd. had taken a franchise on July 2022 to operate a restaurant from Sankalp Ltd. for ₹1,80,000 and at an annual fee of 10% of net revenues (after deducting expenditure). The franchise expires after 6 years. Net revenues were ₹60,000 during the financial year 2022-2023.
  3. On 20th August, 2022, Naresh Ltd, incurred costs of ₹2,40,000 to register the patent for its product. Naresh Ltd. expects the patent's economic life to be 8 years.

Naresh Ltd. follows an accounting policy to amortize all intangibles on straight line basis over the maximum period permitted by accounting standards taking a full year amortization in the year of acquisition. Goodwill on acquisition of business to be amortized over 5 years (SLM) as per AS 14. Prepare a schedule showing the intangible assets section in Naresh Ltd. Balance Sheet at 31st March, 2023.

topic_text: Topic 4.4/4.6: Borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation on a specific borrowing - actual interest incurred less income earned on temporary investment of the surplus, not the weighted-average general-borrowing rate
question_html: Vital Limited borrowed an amount of ₹150 crores on 1.4.2021 for construction of boiler plant @ 10% p.a. The plant is expected to be completed in 4 years. Since the weighted average cost of capital is 13% p.a., the accountant of Vital Ltd. capitalized ₹19.50 crores for the accounting period ending on 31.3.2022. Due to surplus fund out of ₹150 crores, an income of ₹1.50 crores was earned and credited to profit and loss account. Comment on the above treatment of accountant with reference to relevant accounting standard. (5 Marks)
answer_html:
Para 10 of AS 16 'Borrowing Costs' states that to the extent the funds are borrowed specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset, the amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization on that asset should be determined as the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing during the period less any income on the temporary investment of those borrowings. The capitalization rate should be the weighted average of the borrowing costs applicable to the borrowings of the enterprise that are outstanding during the period, other than borrowings made specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset. Hence, in the above case, treatment of accountant of Vital Ltd. is incorrect. The amount of borrowing costs capitalized for the financial year 2021-22 should be calculated as follows:

Particulars₹
Actual interest for 2021-22 (10% of ₹150 crores)15.00 crores
Less: Income on temporary investment from specific borrowings(1.50 crores)
Borrowing costs to be capitalized during year 2021-2213.50 crores
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is applying the enterprise's weighted average cost of capital (or the general-borrowings capitalisation rate) to a loan that was specifically raised for the qualifying asset, instead of using the actual interest rate on that specific borrowing net of any temporary-investment income earned on the surplus funds.

question_html: ABC Limited has started construction of an asset on 1st December, 2021, which continues till 31st March, 2022 (and is expected to go beyond a year). The entity has not taken any specific borrowings to finance the construction of the asset but has incurred finance costs on its general borrowings during the construction period. The directly attributable expenditure at the beginning of the month on this asset was ₹10 lakh in December 2021 and ₹4 lakh in each of the months of January to March 2022. At the beginning of the year, the entity had taken Inter Corporate Deposits of ₹20 lakh at 9% rate of interest and had an overdraft of ₹4 lakh, which increased to ₹8 lakh on 1st March, 2022. Interest was paid on the overdraft at 10% until 1st January, 2022 and then the rate was increased to 12%. You are required to calculate the annual capitalization rate for computation of borrowing cost in accordance with AS 16 'Borrowing Costs'.

Calculation of capitalization rate on borrowings other than specific borrowings

Nature of general borrowingsPeriod of outstanding balanceAmount of loan (₹)Rate of interest p.a.Weighted average amount of interest (₹)

topic_text: Topic 4.11: Cessation of capitalisation - substantially complete activities; part-by-part cessation for assets completed in stages
question_html: When capitalisation of borrowing cost should cease as per Accounting Standard 16? Explain in brief.
answer_html: Capitalization of borrowing costs should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are complete. An asset is normally ready for its intended use or sale when its physical construction or production is complete even though routine administrative work might still continue. If minor modifications such as the decoration of a property to the user's specification, are all that are outstanding, this indicates that substantially all the activities are complete. When the construction of a qualifying asset is completed in parts and a completed part is capable of being used while construction continues for the other parts, capitalization of borrowing costs in relation to a part should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare that part for its intended use or sale are complete.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is assuming capitalisation continues until the asset is actually put into use or sold, rather than ceasing once the asset is merely ready for its intended use, even if routine administrative work or minor finishing touches remain outstanding.

topic_text: Topic 4.4/4.6/4.7: Eligible borrowing cost - specific vs general borrowings, netting temporary investment income
question_html:
Glen Ltd. began construction of a new building on 1st January, 2025. On 1st April, 2025, following two loans were obtained to fund the construction cost:
(i) Loan of ₹60,00,000 from Data Bank Ltd. was taken at interest rate of 8% per annum. This loan was fully utilized for construction of the new building.
(ii) Loan of ₹20,00,000 from Satya Bank Ltd. Out of this, loan amount of ₹6,00,000 was utilized for working capital purpose. Total interest of ₹1,92,000 were paid to Satya Bank Ltd. for the financial year 2025-26.
Construction of the new building was completed on 31st January, 2026 and was ready for its intended use on the same date.
None of the loan was repaid during the year. The building is a qualifying asset for the purpose of AS-16.
Out of loan from Data Bank Ltd., surplus funds were temporarily invested for the short period of time. This temporary investment earned interest of ₹30,000.
You are required to calculate the amount of interest (a) to be capitalized, (b) to be charged to profit and loss account from the total interest incurred as borrowing cost during the year 2025-26 (as per AS-16). (5 Marks)
answer_html:
According to AS 16 “Borrowing Costs”, borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset. The amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization should be determined in accordance with this Standard. Other borrowing costs should be recognised as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

The standard also states that to the extent that funds are borrowed specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset, the amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization on that asset should be determined as the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing during the period less any income on the temporary investment of those borrowings.

Thus, eligible borrowing cost on Loan of data bank to be capitalized:
= ₹(60,00,000 x 8%) x 10/12 − ₹30,000
= ₹(4,80,000 x 10/12) = ₹4,00,000
= ₹4,00,000 − ₹30,000
= ₹3,70,000

topic_text: Topic 4.11: Cessation of capitalisation, including the part-completion case
question_html: When capitalisation of borrowing cost should cease as per Accounting Standard 16? Explain in brief. (4 Marks)
answer_html: Capitalization of borrowing costs should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are complete. An asset is normally ready for its intended use or sale when its physical construction or production is complete even though routine administrative work might still continue. If minor modifications such as the decoration of a property to the user's specification, are all that are outstanding, this indicates that substantially all the activities are complete. When the construction of a qualifying asset is completed in parts and a completed part is capable of being used while construction continues for the other parts, capitalization of borrowing costs in relation to a part should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare that part for its intended use or sale are complete.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Several examinees described only the overall-completion cessation rule and omitted the part-completion exception, despite this being the same principle tested numerically elsewhere in this paper's Case Scenario I.

topic_text: Topic 4.4: Borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation - apportionment of a composite loan's interest between one qualifying asset and several non-qualifying assets
question_html:
On 15th April, 2022 RBM Ltd. obtained a Term Loan from the Bank for ₹320 lakhs to be utilized as under:

Particulars₹ (in lakhs)
Construction for factory shed240
Purchase of Machinery30
Working capital24
Purchase of Vehicles12
Advance for tools/cranes etc.8
Purchase of technical know how6

In March, 2023 construction of shed was completed and machinery was installed. Total interest charged by the bank for the year ending 31st March, 2023 was ₹40 lakhs.

In the context of provisions of AS 16 ‘Borrowing Costs’, show the treatment of interest and also explain the nature of Assets.
answer_html:
As per AS 16 a qualifying asset is an asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale. Other investments and those inventories that are routinely manufactured or otherwise produced in large quantities on a repetitive basis over a short period of time, are not qualifying assets. Assets that are ready for their intended use or sale when acquired also are not qualifying assets. Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset. Other borrowing costs should be recognized as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

Construction of factory shed amounting ₹240 lakhs is a qualifying asset in the given case. The interest for this amount during the year will be added to the cost of factory shed. All others (purchase of machinery, vehicles and technical know how, working capital, advance for tools/cranes) are non-qualifying assets and related borrowing cost will be charged to Profit and Loss statement.

Qualifying Asset as per AS 16 (construction of a shed) = ₹240 lakhs
Borrowing cost to be capitalized = ₹40 lakhs × 240/320 = ₹30 lakhs
Interest to be debited to Profit or Loss account: ₹(40 − 30) = ₹10 lakhs.

Note: Assumed that construction of factory shed completed on 31st March, 2023.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is capitalising interest on the entire ₹320 lakh loan, or on the machinery/vehicle/technical-know-how portions as well, instead of identifying the factory shed as the only qualifying asset and apportioning the ₹40 lakh interest strictly in the ratio of that asset's own utilisation (240/320) to the total borrowing.

topic_text: Topic 4.5: 12-month substantial-period presumption is rebuttable when a shorter period is genuinely, technically justified
question_html: A company incorporated in June 2023, has setup a factory within a period of 8 months with borrowed funds. The construction period of the assets had reduced drastically due to usage of technical innovations by the company and the company is able to justify the reasons for the same. Whether interest on borrowings for the period prior to the date of setting up the factory should be capitalized although it has taken less than 12 months for the assets to get ready for use. You are required to comment on the necessary treatment with reference to AS 16.
answer_html:
As per AS 16 ‘Borrowing Costs’, a qualifying asset is one that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale. What constitutes a substantial period of time primarily depends on the facts and circumstances of each case; ordinarily a period of twelve months is considered substantial unless a shorter or longer period can be justified. In estimating the period, the time an asset takes, technologically and commercially, to get ready for its intended use or sale is considered — there is a rebuttable presumption that 12 months constitutes a substantial period.

Under circumstances where the construction period has reduced drastically due to technical innovation, the 12-month period should be looked at as a benchmark, not a conclusive yardstick. An enterprise that completes the asset in 8 months should not be penalised for its efficiency by being denied interest capitalisation. The substantial-period criterion exists to ensure enterprises do not spend disproportionate time and effort capturing immaterial interest cost for capitalisation purposes.

Conclusion: since the factory was constructed in 8 months (a genuinely justified, technically-innovation-driven reduction), it is still considered a qualifying asset, and the interest on borrowings for the same shall be capitalised, although it took less than 12 months for the asset to get ready for use.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is treating the 12-month benchmark as a rigid, non-rebuttable rule and denying capitalisation outright once construction takes under 12 months, without weighing the facts-and-circumstances test AS 16 actually applies.

topic_text: Topic 4.4: Amortised bond discount is a borrowing-cost component, capitalised only for the portion of the period during which the qualifying asset's acquisition/construction/production takes place
question_html: How will interest be capitalised when qualifying assets are funded by borrowings in the nature of bonds that are issued at a discount?
answer_html:
As per AS 16, "Borrowing costs are interest and other costs incurred by an enterprise in connection with the borrowing of funds." The Statement also contemplates "amortisation of discounts or premiums relating to borrowings" as a component of borrowing costs (paragraph 4(b)). Thus, borrowing costs comprise the periodic interest payable on the bonds in question and the amount of discount amortised during the period.

Paragraph 6 of the Statement states that "Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalised as part of the cost of that asset." Paragraph 19 further states that "Capitalisation of borrowing costs should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are complete." Thus, only that portion of the amortised discount should be capitalised as part of the cost of a qualifying asset which relates to the period during which acquisition, construction or production of the asset takes place.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is treating only the coupon interest as the borrowing cost and overlooking that the periodic amortisation of a bond's issue discount is itself an explicit component of borrowing cost under AS 16.

topic_text: Topic 4.6/4.7: Specific borrowings (Data Bank, fully attributable) and a single general borrowing (Satya Bank) apportioned between a qualifying asset and working capital, net of temporary-investment income
question_html:
Glen Ltd. began construction of a new building on 1st January, 2022. On 1st April, 2022, following two loans were obtained to fund the construction cost:

(i) Loan of ₹60,00,000 from Data Bank Ltd. was taken at interest rate of 8% per annum. This loan was fully utilized for construction of the new building.

(ii) Loan of ₹20,00,000 from Satya Bank Ltd. Out of this, loan amount of ₹6,00,000 was utilized for working capital purpose. Total interest of ₹1,92,000 were paid to Satya Bank Ltd. for the financial year 2022-23.

Construction of the new building was completed on 31st January, 2023 and was ready for its intended use on the same date.

None of the loan was repaid during the year. The building is a qualifying asset for the purpose of AS-16.

Out of loan from Data Bank Ltd., surplus funds were temporarily invested for the short period of time. This temporary investment earned interest of ₹30,000.

You are required to calculate the amount of interest (a) to be capitalized, (b) to be charged to profit and loss account from the total interest incurred as borrowing cost during the year 2022-23 (as per AS-16). (5 Marks)
answer_html:
According to AS 16 “Borrowing Costs”, borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset. The amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization should be determined in accordance with this Standard. Other borrowing costs should be recognised as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

The standard also states that to the extent that funds are borrowed specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset, the amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization on that asset should be determined as the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing during the period less any income on the temporary investment of those borrowings.

Thus, eligible borrowing cost on Loan of Data Bank to be capitalized:

= ₹(60,00,000 × 8%) × 10/12 − ₹30,000
= ₹4,00,000 − ₹30,000
= ₹3,70,000

topic_text: Topic 4.4: Amortisation of a bond discount is a component of borrowing cost eligible for capitalisation only up to the period during which the qualifying asset is under construction
question_html:
How will interest be capitalized when qualifying assets are funded by borrowings in the nature of bonds that are issued at a discount?

X Ltd. issued in year 1, a 3 year 10% p.a. (interest paid annually) bond with a face value of ₹1,00,000 at a price of ₹90,000 to finance a qualifying asset which is ready for intended use at the end of year 2. Compute the amount of borrowings costs to be capitalized if the company uses for amortization of discount straight line basis.
answer_html:
As per AS 16, "Borrowing costs are interest and other costs incurred by an enterprise in connection with the borrowing of funds". Further, as per para 4(b) of the standard, "amortization of discounts or premiums relating to borrowings" is a component of borrowing costs. Thus, the borrowing costs comprise the periodic interest payable on the bonds in question and the amount of discount amortised during the period.

Paragraph 6 of the Statement, inter-alia, states that "Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset". Further, paragraph 19 states that "Capitalisation of borrowing costs should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are complete". Thus, only that portion of the amortised discount should be capitalised as part of the cost of a qualifying asset which relates to the period during which acquisition, construction or production of the asset takes place.

Straight line basis (Amount in ₹)

YearsInterestAmortisation of discountTotal borrowing costs
Year 110,0003,33313,333
Year 210,0003,33313,333
Year 310,0003,33413,334

In the above case, the amount of borrowing costs capitalized would be ₹13,333 in Year 1 and Year 2. The borrowing costs of ₹13,334 incurred in Year 3 would be expensed since the asset is ready for its intended use at the end of Year 2.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is capitalising the entire annual bond discount amortisation for all three years as a borrowing cost, missing that AS 16 requires capitalisation to cease once the qualifying asset is ready for its intended use — here, at the end of Year 2 — so the Year 3 amortised discount and interest must be expensed, not capitalised.

topic_text: Topic 4.2: Interest capitalised into inventory cost only for the exceptional qualifying-asset case (substantial maturation period)
question_html: Can interest be included in the cost of inventories?
answer_html:
As a general rule, AS 2 (para 12) provides that interest and other borrowing costs are usually not related to bringing inventories to their present location and condition, and are therefore usually excluded from inventory cost.

However, AS 16 (para 6) requires borrowing costs directly attributable to acquisition/construction/production of a qualifying asset to be capitalised, and para 5 specifically includes "inventories that require a substantial period of time to bring them to a saleable condition" as an example of a qualifying asset (e.g. liquor requiring 12+ months of maturation, per ASI 1). It is only in such exceptional cases — where time is a major factor in changing the condition of the inventory — that borrowing costs are included in inventory valuation. Routinely/repetitively manufactured inventory over a short period is never a qualifying asset, so its borrowing costs are never capitalised.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees answered with a flat "no", missing the exceptional qualifying-asset case (e.g. maturing liquor) where AS 16 does require capitalisation into inventory cost.

topic_text: Topic 4.4: Apportionment of interest on a mixed-purpose loan between qualifying-asset capitalisation and expense, by proportion of funds actually used for each purpose
question_html:
U Limited has obtained a term loan of ₹620 lacs for a complete renovation and modernisation of its Factory on 1st April, 2023. Plant and Machinery was acquired under the modernisation scheme and installation was completed on 30th April, 2024. An expenditure of ₹510 lacs was incurred on installation of Plant and Machinery, ₹54 lacs has been advanced to suppliers for additional assets which were also received and installed before 30th April, 2024 (additional asset has taken substantial period of time in its installation), and the balance loan of ₹56 lacs has been used for working capital purposes.

The company has paid total interest of ₹68.20 lacs during financial year 2023-2024 on the above loan. The accountant seeks your advice how to account for the interest paid in the books of accounts.
answer_html:
As per AS 16 'Borrowing Costs', borrowing costs directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset; other borrowing costs should be recognized as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

Qualifying Asset: an asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time (ordinarily 12 months, unless a shorter or longer period is justified by the facts) to get ready for its intended use or sale.

Since construction of the asset completed only on 30th April, 2024 (after the year end), the treatment for the total borrowing cost of ₹68.20 lacs is:

PurposeNatureInterest to be capitalised (₹ lacs)Interest to be charged to P&L (₹ lacs)
Modernisation and renovation of plant and machineryQualifying asset68.20 × (510/620) = 56.10—
Advance to suppliers for additional assetsAssumed as qualifying asset (took substantial time to install)68.20 × (54/620) = 5.94—
Working CapitalNot a qualifying asset—68.20 × (56/620) = 6.16
Total62.046.16
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is capitalising interest on the entire ₹620 lacs loan without apportioning it by actual fund usage, missing that the ₹56 lacs used for working capital is not a qualifying asset and its share of interest must be expensed, not capitalised.

topic_text: Topic 4.3: Borrowing costs on an incidental, already-ready asset are still capitalised into the main qualifying asset when necessary for its construction
question_html: Is it permissible to capitalise borrowing costs incurred on assets necessary for the construction of qualifying assets? A company constructing a large manufacturing plant in a backward area also purchased a residential building (funded by a long-term loan) to house workers engaged in the plant's construction, intending to dispose of the building once construction completes. If the manufacturing plant is a qualifying asset, are the borrowing costs on the residential-building loan eligible for capitalisation?
answer_html:
Per AS 16 para 3, a qualifying asset "necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale"; para 5 clarifies that assets ready for use when acquired are not qualifying assets. Prima facie, the residential building appears ready for use on acquisition, suggesting no capitalisation.

However, since providing housing is necessary for the construction of the plant, the borrowing costs on the building loan are, in substance, directly attributable to the construction of the manufacturing plant. The company should therefore capitalise these borrowing costs as part of the cost of the manufacturing plant, up to the period the plant is ready for its intended use.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees stopped at the observation that the residential building is itself "ready for use" and concluded no capitalisation applies, missing the substance-over-form link to the main construction project's necessity.

topic_text: Topic 2.7: Directly attributable costs including regulatory-mandated modifications   +   Topic 4.10: Capitalised borrowing cost as computed in Q7 feeds into total plant cost
question_html:
Case Scenario:

It has commenced construction of the plant on April 1, 2023 and has incurred following expenses: acquired land for installing Plant for ₹50,00,000; incurred ₹35,00,000 for material and direct labour cost for developing the Plant; incurred ₹10,00,000 for head office expenses at New Delhi which included rent, employee cost and maintenance expenditure; borrowed ₹25,00,000 for construction work of Plant @12% per annum on April 1, 2023 (Director finance incurred travel and meeting expenses of ₹5,00,000 during the year for arranging this loan).

On November 1, 2023, the construction activities of the plant were interrupted as the local people alongwith activists raised issues relating to environmental impact of the plant being constructed; construction came to a standstill for 3 months. With the help of Government and NGOs, the agitation was over by February 28, 2024 and the work resumed. However, to balance the impact on environment, government ordered the company to install certain devices for which the Company had to incur ₹6,00,000 in March 2024. The rate of depreciation on Plant is 10%.

Based on the above information, answer Question Nos. 6–9.

The total cost of plant as on March 31, 2024 will be:

  1. ₹85,00,000
  2. ₹98,00,000
  3. ₹93,00,000
  4. ₹95,00,000
answer_html: Answer: (c) ₹93,00,000 = Land ₹50,00,000 + material/labour ₹35,00,000 + capitalised borrowing cost ₹2,00,000 + government-mandated environmental devices ₹6,00,000 (head office expenses and loan-arrangement travel costs excluded).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees excluded the government-mandated environmental device cost, not recognising it as a cost necessary to bring the plant to a condition of operating in compliance with regulatory requirements, and so directly attributable under AS 10.

topic_text: Topic 4.3: Exchange differences on a foreign-currency borrowing treated as a borrowing cost only to the extent they approximate the interest-rate differential against an equivalent local-currency loan   +   Topic 3.5: Exchange difference on restatement of a foreign-currency monetary borrowing at the closing rate, with the AS 16-eligible portion carved out of the total exchange loss and the remainder recognised under AS 11
question_html:
Omega Limited has borrowed a sum of US $10,00,000 at the beginning of Financial Year 2022-23 for its residential project at 4%. The interest is payable at the end of the Financial Year. At the time of availment of loan exchange rate was ₹56 per US $ and the rate as on 31st March, 2023 was ₹62 per US $. If Omega Limited had borrowed the loan in India in Indian Rupee equivalent, the pricing of loan would have been 10.50%.

You are required to compute Borrowing Cost and exchange difference for the year ending 31st March, 2023 as per applicable Accounting Standards.
answer_html:
1. Interest for the period 2022-23 = US $10 lakhs × 4% × ₹62 per US$ = ₹24.80 lakhs
  2. Increase in the liability towards the principal amount = US $10 lakhs × ₹(62 − 56) = ₹60 lakhs
  3. Interest that would have resulted if the loan was taken in Indian currency = US $10 lakhs × ₹56 × 10.5% = ₹58.80 lakhs
  4. Difference between interest on local currency borrowing and foreign currency borrowing = ₹58.80 lakhs − ₹24.80 lakhs = ₹34 lakhs.

Therefore, out of ₹60 lakhs increase in the liability towards principal amount, only ₹34 lakhs will be considered as the borrowing cost. Thus, total borrowing cost would be ₹58.80 lakhs being the aggregate of interest of ₹24.80 lakhs on foreign currency borrowings plus the exchange difference to the extent of difference between interest on local currency borrowing and interest on foreign currency borrowing of ₹34 lakhs.

Hence, ₹58.80 lakhs would be considered as the borrowing cost to be accounted for as per AS 16 and the remaining ₹26 lakhs (60 − 34) would be considered as the exchange difference to be accounted for as per AS 11.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating the entire ₹60 lakh increase in the rupee liability as either wholly a borrowing cost under AS 16 or wholly an exchange difference under AS 11, instead of splitting it at the interest-rate-differential figure of ₹34 lakhs.

topic_text: Topic 5.10: Sale and leaseback classified as an operating lease - profit/loss recognition split by sale price vs fair value vs carrying amount
question_html: A Ltd. sold JCB having WDV of ₹20 lakhs to B Ltd. for ₹24 lakhs and the same JCB was leased back by B Ltd. to A Ltd. The lease is operating lease. In context of Accounting Standard 19 "Leases" explain the accounting treatment of profit or loss in the books of A Ltd. if: (i) Sale price of ₹24 lakhs is equal to fair value. (ii) Fair value is ₹20 lakhs and sale price is ₹24 lakhs. (iii) Fair value is ₹22 lakhs and sale price is ₹25 lakhs. (iv) Fair value is ₹25 lakhs and sale price is ₹18 lakhs. (v) Fair value is ₹18 lakhs and sale price is ₹19 lakhs.
answer_html:
Following will be the treatment in the given cases (WDV of the JCB = ₹20 lakhs throughout):

  1. When sale price of ₹24 lakhs is equal to fair value, A Ltd. should immediately recognise the profit of ₹4 lakhs (i.e. 24 − 20) in its books.
  2. When fair value is ₹20 lakhs & sale price is ₹24 lakhs then profit of ₹4 lakhs is to be deferred and amortised over the lease period.
  3. When fair value is ₹22 lakhs & sale price is ₹25 lakhs, profit of ₹2 lakhs (22−20) to be immediately recognised in its books and balance profit of ₹3 lakhs (25−22) is to be amortised/deferred over lease period.
  4. When fair value of leased machinery is ₹25 lakhs & sale price is ₹18 lakhs, then loss of ₹2 lakhs (20−18) to be immediately recognised by A Ltd. in its books provided loss is not compensated by future lease payment.
  5. When fair value is ₹18 lakhs & sale price is ₹19 lakhs, then the loss of ₹2 lakhs (20−18) to be immediately recognised by A Ltd. in its books and profit of ₹1 lakh (19−18) should be amortised/deferred over lease period.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is recognising the entire profit on a sale-and-leaseback transaction immediately, without checking whether the sale price exceeds fair value and confirming that only the profit up to fair value qualifies for immediate recognition, with any excess deferred over the lease term.

topic_text: Topic 5.3: Finance lease classification test and lessor's unearned finance income computation
question_html: Colour Limited leased a Machine to Red Limited on 1st April, 2021: Cost of machine ₹18,00,000; Lease term 3 years; Fair market value ₹18,00,000; Unguaranteed residual value as on 31.3.2024 ₹2,00,000; Internal rate of return 12%. Expected useful life 5 years; machine reverts to Colour Limited on termination. Lease payments at the end of each year, in 3 equal parts. PV of ₹1 due at end of 3rd year at 12% = ₹0.7118. PV of annuity of ₹1 for 3 years at 12% = ₹2.4018. Analyze whether the lease constitutes a finance lease. Also calculate unearned finance income, if any.
answer_html:
Computation of Annual Lease Payment: PV of unguaranteed residual value = 2,00,000 × 0.7118 = 1,42,360. PV of Lease Payments to recover = 18,00,000 − 1,42,360 = 16,57,640. Annual Lease Payment = 16,57,640 / 2.4018 = ₹6,90,166 (approx).

Classification: PV of lease payments (₹16,57,640) is 92.09% of fair value (₹18,00,000) — substantially covers the fair value of the leased asset. Lease term (3 years) covers the major part of the asset's economic life (5 years). Both indicators point to a finance lease.

Unearned Finance Income: Total Lease Payments (6,90,166 × 3) 20,70,498 + Unguaranteed residual value 2,00,000 = 22,70,498; less Net investment (PV of payments + residual = 1,42,360+16,57,640 = 18,00,000) = Unearned Finance Income ₹4,70,498 (approx, matching source's ₹4,70,495 to rounding).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees computed unearned finance income using the guaranteed residual value formula, not adjusting for the fact that this residual value is unguaranteed (still included in the lessor's net investment, but the classification/income mechanics require care in distinguishing guaranteed vs unguaranteed treatment).

topic_text: Topic 5.8: Lessee's finance-lease recognition at the lower of fair value and PV of minimum lease payments, plus finance-charge amortisation table
question_html:
Lessee Ltd. took a machine on lease from Lessor Ltd., the fair value being ₹7,00,000. The economic life of machine as well as the lease term is 3 years. At the end of each year Lessee Ltd. pays ₹3,00,000. The Lessee has guaranteed a residual value of ₹22,000 on expiry of the lease to the Lessor. However, Lessor Ltd., estimates that the residual value of the machinery will be only ₹15,000. The implicit rate of return is 15% p.a. and present value factors at 15% are 0.869, 0.756 and 0.657 at the end of first, second and third years respectively.

answer_html:
As per AS 19 "Leases", the lessee should recognize the lease as an asset and a liability at the inception of a finance lease. Such recognition should be at an amount equal to the fair value of the leased asset at the inception of lease. However, if the fair value of the leased asset exceeds the present value of minimum lease payment from the standpoint of the lessee, the amount recorded as an asset and liability should be the present value of minimum lease payments from the standpoint of the lessee.

Computation of Value of machinery: Present value of minimum lease payment = ₹6,99,054 (see working note below). Fair value of leased asset = ₹7,00,000. Therefore, the recognition will be at the lower of the two, i.e. ₹6,99,054.

Working Note — Present value of minimum lease payments: Annual lease rental × PVIF + Present value of guaranteed residual value = ₹3,00,000 × (0.869 + 0.756 + 0.657) + ₹22,000 × 0.657 = ₹6,84,600 + ₹14,454 = ₹6,99,054.

topic_text: Topic 5.5-5.7/5.8: Deterministic indicators of a finance lease (PV of MLP vs. fair value; lease term vs. asset life) and computation of unearned finance income
question_html:

Both the cost and fair value of equipment are ₹12,50,000. (ii) The equipment reverts back to the lessor on termination of the lease. (iii) The unguaranteed residual value is estimated at ₹1,20,000 at the end of the financial year 2023-2024. (iv) The amount will be paid in 4 equal instalments at the end of each year. (v) Consider IRR = 8%. (vi) The present value of ₹1 at the end of 4th year at 8% of interest is ₹0.735. (vii) The present value of annuity of ₹1 due at the end of 4th year at 8% IRR is ₹3.312.

State whether this lease is operating lease or Finance lease (by applying two deterministic parameters). Also calculate unearned finance Income. (5 Marks)
answer_html:

Cost of equipment12,50,000.00
Unguaranteed residual value1,20,000.00

Present value of lease payments (₹12,50,000 − ₹88,200)11,61,800.00
Present value of annuity for four years is 3.312
Annual lease payment [11,61,800/3.312]3,50,785.02

Parameter 1: The present value of the lease payment i.e. ₹11,61,800 which equals 92.94% of the fair market value i.e. ₹12,50,000. The present value of minimum lease payments substantially covers the fair value of the leased asset.

Parameter 2: The lease term (i.e. 4 years) covers the major part of the life of asset (i.e. 6 years).

Therefore, it constitutes a finance lease.

topic_text: Topic 5.3: Unearned finance income = gross investment in the lease less the present value of minimum lease payments and unguaranteed residual value, discounted at the interest rate implicit in the lease
question_html:

Ascertain Unearned Finance Income.

(a) Gross investment = Minimum lease payments + Unguaranteed residual value = [Total lease rent + Guaranteed residual value (GRV)] + Unguaranteed residual value (URV) = [(₹4,00,000 × 5 years) + ₹80,000] + ₹70,000 = ₹21,50,000 (a)

topic_text: Topic 5.9: Sale-and-leaseback resulting in a finance lease - profit deferred and amortised in proportion to asset depreciation
question_html: On 1st April, 2024, Mansi Ltd. sold a plant for ₹8,52,800 (carrying amount ₹1,80,000) as part of a sale-and-leaseback package with Akash Ltd., leasing the asset back for an 8-year term. Economic life of the asset is 8 years. Minimum lease rents ₹1,60,000/year, payable annually from 31st March, 2025. Mansi Ltd.'s incremental borrowing rate is 10% p.a. Calculate the net effect on the Statement of Profit and Loss in Mansi Ltd.'s (the lessee's) books.
answer_html:
Lease classification: lease term (8 years) covers the entire economic life (8 years). PV of minimum lease payments = ₹1,60,000 × 5.335 (annuity factor @10% for 8 years) = ₹8,53,600, which substantially covers the fair value/sale price (₹8,52,800). This is therefore a finance lease.

Per AS 19 para 48, where a sale-and-leaseback results in a finance lease, the profit on sale (₹8,52,800−₹1,80,000 = ₹6,72,800) is not recognised immediately — it is deferred and amortised over the lease term in proportion to the depreciation of the leased asset.

Assuming straight-line depreciation: Depreciation = ₹8,52,800/8 = ₹1,06,600/year. Deferred profit amortised = ₹6,72,800/8 = ₹84,100/year. Net effect on Statement of P&L = ₹1,06,600 − ₹84,100 = ₹22,500 debit per annum, for each of the 8 years of the lease term.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees recognised the full sale profit immediately in the year of sale, not applying AS 19's specific deferral-and-amortisation rule for a sale-and-leaseback that results in a finance lease.

topic_text: Topic 5.5-5.7: Finance-vs-operating lease classification tested against both the PV-of-minimum-lease-payments test and the major-part-of-economic-life test
question_html: Sooraj Limited wishes to obtain a machine costing ₹30 lakhs by way of lease. The effective life of the machine is 14 years, but the company requires it only for the first 3 years. It enters into an agreement with Star Ltd., for a lease rental for ₹3 lakhs p.a. payable in arrears and the implicit rate of interest is 15%. The chief accountant of Sooraj Limited is not sure about the treatment of these lease rentals and seeks your advice. (Use annuity factor at @ 15% for 3 years as 2.28)
answer_html:
As per AS 19 'leases', a lease will be classified as finance lease if at the inception of the lease, the present value of minimum lease payment amounts to at least substantially all of the fair value of leased asset. In the given case, the implicit rate of interest is given at 15%. The present value of minimum lease payments at 15% using PV-Annuity Factor can be computed as:

Annuity Factor (Year 1 to Year 3)2.28
Present Value of minimum lease payments (₹3 lakhs each year)₹6.84 lakhs

Thus, the present value of minimum lease payments is ₹6.84 lakhs and the fair value of the machine is ₹30 lakhs. In a finance lease, the lease term should be for a major part of the economic life of the asset even if title is not transferred. However, in the given case, the effective useful life of the machine is 14 years while the lease is only for three years. Therefore, a lease agreement is an operating lease. Lease payments under an operating lease should be recognized as an expense in the statement of profit and loss on a straight-line basis over the lease term unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern of the user's benefit.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is classifying the lease as a finance lease purely because the present value of minimum lease payments is a large absolute number, without comparing it against the machine's fair value and separately checking whether the lease term covers a major part of the asset's economic life.

topic_text: Topic 5.5-5.7: Finance vs operating lease classification via the PV-of-minimum-lease-payments and lease-term-vs-economic-life indicators
question_html: Sun Limited wishes to obtain a machine costing ₹30 lakhs by way of lease. The effective life of the machine is 14 years, but the company requires it only for the first 3 years. It enters into an agreement with Star Ltd. for a lease rental of ₹3 lakhs p.a. payable in arrears, and the implicit rate of interest is 15%. The chief accountant of Sun Limited is not sure about the treatment of these lease rentals and seeks your advice. (Use annuity factor at 15% for 3 years as 3.36.)
answer_html:
As per AS 19 'Leases', a lease will be classified as a finance lease if, at the inception of the lease, the present value of minimum lease payments amounts to at least substantially all of the fair value of the leased asset (discounted at the interest rate implicit in the lease).

Amount
Annuity Factor (Year 1 to Year 3) @ 15%3.36
Present Value of minimum lease payments (₹3 lakhs each year)₹10.08 lakhs (approx.)

The present value of minimum lease payments (₹10.08 lakhs) is far below the fair value of the machine (₹30 lakhs). Additionally, in a finance lease the lease term should cover the major part of the economic life of the asset even where title does not transfer – here the effective useful life of the machine is 14 years while the lease is only for 3 years. Both indicators point away from a finance lease.

The lease agreement is therefore an operating lease. Lease payments under an operating lease should be recognized as an expense in the statement of profit and loss on a straight line basis over the lease term, unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern of the user's benefit – i.e. Sun Limited should expense ₹3 lakhs each year for the 3-year lease term.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is classifying this as a finance lease purely because a lease-rental agreement with an "implicit rate of interest" is quoted, without actually testing the present value of minimum lease payments against the machine's fair value, which here comes out at barely a third of fair value – a clear operating-lease signal.

topic_text: Topic 5.9: Accounting for operating leases - lessor's presentation, income recognition, depreciation, impairment
question_html: Explain, in brief, the accounting treatment for an asset given under Operating Lease in the books of the Lessor.
answer_html:
The accounting treatment for an asset given under Operating Lease in the books of the lessor is given as under:

  1. The Lessor should present an asset given under Operating Lease as PPE in its balance sheet.
  2. Lease income from operating leases should be recognized in the Statement of Profit and Loss on a straight-line basis over the lease term, unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern in which benefit derived from the use of the leased asset is diminished.
  3. Depreciation should be recognized in the books of the lessor. The depreciation of leased assets should be on a basis consistent with the normal accounting policy of the lessor for similar assets, and the depreciation charge should be calculated on the basis set out in AS 10.
  4. The impairment loss on assets given on operating leases are determined and treated as per AS 28.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees conflated lessor and lessee treatments, describing finance-lease-style derecognition of the asset instead of the lessor retaining the asset as PPE and depreciating it under AS 10, resulting in partial credit loss.

topic_text: Topic 5.9: Sale-and-leaseback resulting in a finance lease - profit deferred and amortised in proportion to asset depreciation
question_html: On 1st April, 2024, Mansi Ltd. sold a plant for ₹8,52,800 (carrying amount ₹1,80,000) as part of a sale-and-leaseback package with Akash Ltd., leasing the asset back for an 8-year term. Economic life 8 years. Minimum lease rents ₹1,60,000/year, payable annually from 31st March, 2025. Incremental borrowing rate 10% p.a. Calculate the net effect on the Statement of Profit and Loss in Mansi Ltd.'s (lessee's) books.
answer_html:
Lease classification: lease term (8 years) = entire economic life (8 years). PV of minimum lease payments = ₹1,60,000 × 5.335 (annuity factor @10% for 8 years) = ₹8,53,600, substantially covering the fair value/sale price (₹8,52,800). This is a finance lease.

Per AS 19 para 48, where a sale-and-leaseback results in a finance lease, the profit on sale (₹8,52,800−₹1,80,000 = ₹6,72,800) is not recognised immediately — deferred and amortised over the lease term in proportion to the leased asset's depreciation.

Assuming straight-line depreciation: Depreciation = ₹8,52,800/8 = ₹1,06,600/year. Amortised deferred profit = ₹6,72,800/8 = ₹84,100/year. Net effect on Statement of P&L = ₹1,06,600 − ₹84,100 = ₹22,500 debit per annum, for each of the 8 years of the lease term.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees recognised the full sale profit immediately in the year of sale, not applying AS 19's deferral-and-amortisation rule for a sale-and-leaseback resulting in a finance lease.

topic_text: Topic 7.7: Impairment loss = carrying amount less recoverable amount (higher of net selling price and value in use)
question_html: X Ltd. purchased a Property, Plant and Equipment four years ago for ₹150 lakhs and depreciates it at 10% p.a. on straight line method. At the end of the fourth year, it has revalued the asset at ₹75 lakhs and has written off the loss on revaluation to the profit and loss account. However, on the date of revaluation, the market price is ₹67.50 lakhs and expected disposal costs are ₹3 lakhs. What will be the treatment in respect of impairment loss on the basis that fair value for revaluation purpose is determined by market value and the value in use is estimated at ₹60 lakhs?
answer_html:
Treatment of Impairment Loss: As per AS 28 "Impairment of assets", if the recoverable amount (higher of net selling price and its value in use) of an asset is less than its carrying amount, the carrying amount of the asset should be reduced to its recoverable amount. In the given case, net selling price is ₹64.50 lakhs (₹67.50 lakhs − ₹3 lakhs) and value in use is ₹60 lakhs. Therefore, recoverable amount will be ₹64.50 lakhs. Impairment loss will be calculated as ₹10.50 lakhs [₹75 lakhs (Carrying Amount after revaluation – Refer Working Note) less ₹64.50 lakhs (Recoverable Amount)].

Thus impairment loss of ₹10.50 lakhs should be recognised as an expense in the Statement of Profit and Loss immediately since there was downward revaluation of asset which was already charged to Statement of Profit and Loss.

Working Note — Calculation of carrying amount of the Property, Plant and Equipment at the end of the fourth year on revaluation (₹ in lakhs):

Purchase price of a Property, Plant and Equipment150.00
Less: Depreciation for four years [(150 lakhs / 10 years) × 4 years](60.00)
Carrying value at the end of fourth year90.00
Less: Downward revaluation charged to profit and loss account(15.00)
Revalued carrying amount75.00
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is using net selling price or value in use alone instead of the HIGHER of the two as the recoverable amount, or crediting the impairment loss against a revaluation reserve balance that does not exist here (the earlier downward revaluation was already charged to profit and loss, leaving no reserve to absorb the fresh impairment loss).

topic_text: Topic 7.7: Impairment loss on a previously-revalued asset set off first against the remaining revaluation reserve balance, before charging any excess to profit and loss
question_html:
A machine was acquired by Zest Ltd. on 01/04/2019 for ₹60 lakhs. It had a useful life of 6 years. The machine is depreciated on straight line basis and does not carry any residual value. On 01/04/2022, the carrying value of the machine was reassessed at ₹36 lakhs. The surplus arising out of the revaluation being credited to revaluation reserve.

For the year ended March 2024, conditions indicating an impairment of the existed machine and the amount recoverable ascertained to be ₹9 lakhs.

You are required to calculate the loss on impairment of the machine and show how this loss is to be treated in the books of Zest Ltd. The company had followed the policy of writing down the revaluation surplus by the increased charge of depreciation resulting from the revaluation. (4 Marks)

Statement Showing Impairment Loss (₹ in lakhs):

Depreciation for 3 years i.e. 2019-2020 to 2021-2022 (60/6 × 3)(30)
Carrying amount as on 31.03.202230
Add: Upward Revaluation (credited to Revaluation Reserve account)6
Carrying amount of the machine as on 1st April, 2022 (revalued)36
Less: Depreciation for 2 years i.e. 2022-2023 & 2023-2024 (36/3 × 2)(24)
Carrying amount as on 31.03.202412

Impairment loss3

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Cost of installation - directly attributable labour/supervisor/testing costs; deferred-credit interest excluded   +   Topic 7.13/7.16: Impairment loss on a revalued asset - first set off against the revaluation reserve balance, remainder to P&L
question_html:
On 1 April, 2022, Sky Limited purchased a machinery for ₹7,35,000 (inclusive of GST @5%, input credit available for entire amount). Estimated useful life 10 years, SLM, no residual value.

On September 30, 2025, the company revalued the machine at ₹7 lakhs, surplus credited to revaluation reserve. For the year ended March 31, 2026, conditions indicating impairment existed and the recoverable amount was ascertained to be only ₹3 Lakhs.

You are required to: (i) Calculate the value at which the machine should be capitalized and the amount of depreciation to be charged for the year ending March 31, 2023 in the books of Sky Limited. (ii) Calculate the loss on impairment of the machine and show how this loss is to be treated in the books of Sky Limited. The company had followed the policy of writing down the revaluation surplus by the increased charge of depreciation resulting from the revaluation. (5 Marks)
answer_html:
(i) Calculation of Cost of Machinery:

(ii) Statement showing impairment loss and its treatment:

Less: Depreciation for 3 years (8,10,000 x 3/10)(2,43,000)

Several also capitalised the ₹10,800 delay-related expenses instead of expensing them, since the asset was already ready for use on 1st October, 2022.

topic_text: Topic 7.6: CGU impairment loss allocated first to goodwill, then pro-rata to other assets
question_html: Grace Limited acquired the business (a cash-generating unit) of Venus Limited on 31st March 2023 for ₹8,000 lakhs: Fair value of identifiable assets ₹6,000 lakhs, Goodwill (amortised over 5 years) ₹2,000 lakhs. Anticipated useful life of acquired assets: 8 years, nil residual value, straight-line. On 31st March 2025, significant decline in production estimated due to government policy changes; net selling price of identifiable assets ₹3,000 lakhs. Cash flow forecast for next 6 years (₹ lakhs): 1,000/800/700/800/600/500. Discount rate 10% (PV factors: 0.909, 0.826, 0.751, 0.683, 0.621, 0.564). Calculate: (i) Value in use at 31 March 2025; (ii) Impairment loss for year ended 31 March 2025; (iii) Revised carrying amount of asset.
answer_html:
(i) Value in Use: 1,000×0.909=909.00 + 800×0.826=660.80 + 700×0.751=525.70 + 800×0.683=546.40 + 600×0.621=372.60 + 500×0.564=282.00 = ₹3,296.50 lakhs, rounded to ₹3,297 lakhs.

Carrying amount at 31.3.2025 (2 years post-acquisition): Goodwill 2,000 − amortisation (2,000/5×2=800) = 1,200. Identifiable assets 6,000 − depreciation (6,000/8×2=1,500) = 4,500. Total CGU carrying amount = 5,700.

Recoverable amount = higher of Value in Use (3,297) and net selling price of identifiable assets (3,000, no CGU-wide fair-value-less-costs-to-sell given) = 3,297 (since 3,297 > 3,000).

(ii) Impairment loss = Carrying amount (5,700) − Recoverable amount (3,297) = ₹2,403 lakhs.

(iii) Allocation: per AS 28, impairment is allocated first to goodwill (written down to zero: full 1,200 absorbed), then the remainder (2,403−1,200=1,203) to identifiable assets pro-rata: revised carrying amount of identifiable asset = 4,500−1,203 = ₹3,297 lakhs (goodwill: Nil).
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: A majority of examinees were unable to compute the impairment loss and allocate the same appropriately among the assets of the CGU as per the requirements of AS 28 "Impairment of Assets". Many examinees failed to determine the value in use, impairment loss and the revised carrying amount of assets, evidencing an inadequate understanding of the impairment principles.

topic_text: Topic 7.4: Impairment loss = carrying amount less recoverable amount (higher of net selling price and value in use)
question_html: X Ltd. purchased a fixed asset four years ago for ₹150 lakhs, depreciating at 10% p.a. SLM. At the end of the fourth year, it revalued the asset to ₹75 lakhs, writing off the revaluation loss to P&L. On the revaluation date, market price is ₹67.50 lakhs, expected disposal costs ₹3 lakhs, and value in use is estimated at ₹60 lakhs. What is the treatment of impairment loss, given fair value for revaluation is market-value-based?
answer_html:
W.N. — Carrying amount at revaluation: Purchase price 150.00, less depreciation for 4 years (150/10 × 4) 60.00 = carrying value before revaluation 90.00, less downward revaluation charged to P&L (90−75) 15.00 = revalued carrying amount 75.00 lakhs.

Recoverable amount = higher of net selling price and value in use. Net selling price = market price 67.50 − disposal costs 3.00 = 64.50 lakhs. Value in use = 60 lakhs. Recoverable amount = ₹64.50 lakhs (the higher of the two).

Impairment loss = carrying amount (75.00) − recoverable amount (64.50) = ₹10.50 lakhs, recognised as an expense in the Statement of Profit and Loss immediately (since the prior downward revaluation was already charged to P&L rather than to a revaluation reserve, there is no reserve balance to absorb this further impairment against).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees used the market price directly as net selling price without deducting disposal costs, or used net selling price as recoverable amount without comparing it against value in use to find the higher of the two.

topic_text: Topic 7.8: Identification of the cash-generating unit - independence of cash inflows
question_html: A publisher owns 150 magazine titles of which 70 were purchased and 80 were self-created. The price paid for a purchased magazine title is recognised as an intangible asset. The costs of creating magazine titles and maintaining the existing titles are recognised as an expense when incurred. Cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each magazine title. Titles are managed by customer segments. The level of advertising income for a magazine title depends on the range of titles in the customer segment to which the magazine title relates. Management has a policy to abandon old titles before the end of their economic lives and replace them immediately with new titles for the same customer segment. Whether it will be a cash-generating unit as per AS 28?
answer_html: It is likely that the recoverable amount of an individual magazine title can be assessed. Even though the level of advertising income for a title is influenced, to a certain extent, by the other titles in the customer segment, cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each title. In addition, although titles are managed by customer segments, decisions to abandon titles are made on an individual title basis. Therefore, it is likely that individual magazine titles generate cash inflows that are largely independent one from another and that each magazine title is a separate cash-generating unit.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees identified the customer segment as the cash-generating unit because titles are managed and reported at that level, without recognising that CGU identification turns on independence of cash inflows, not on the level at which management happens to monitor performance.

topic_text: Topic 7.8: Identification of a cash-generating unit - independent, identifiable cash inflows determine separate CGU status even where some influence between related assets exists
question_html:
A publisher owns 150 magazine titles of which 70 were purchased and 80 were self-created. The price paid for a purchased magazine title is recognised as an intangible asset. The costs of creating magazine titles and maintaining the existing titles are recognised as an expense when incurred. Cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each magazine title. Titles are managed by customer segments. The level of advertising income for a magazine title depends on the range of titles in the customer segment to which the magazine title relates. Management has a policy to abandon old titles before the end of their economic lives and replace them immediately with new titles for the same customer segment.

Whether it will be a cash-generating unit as per AS 28?
answer_html:
It is likely that the recoverable amount of an individual magazine title can be assessed. Even though the level of advertising income for a title is influenced, to a certain extent, by the other titles in the customer segment, cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each title. In addition, although titles are managed by customer segments, decisions to abandon titles are made on an individual title basis.

Therefore, it is likely that individual magazine titles generate cash inflows that are largely independent one from another and that each magazine title is a separate cash-generating unit.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating the whole customer segment as a single cash-generating unit because advertising income is partly influenced by the range of titles in that segment, without recognising that direct sales and advertising cash inflows are still separately identifiable per title, and abandonment decisions are made per title.

topic_text: Topic 3.7: Investment account with cum-interest/ex-interest purchases and sales, FIFO cost basis
question_html: Prem Ltd. holds 2,000, 15% Debentures of ₹100 each in Mehar Ltd. as on 1st April, 2024 at a cost of ₹2,50,000. Interest payable 30th June and 31st December each year. Transactions during 2024-25: 1st May 2024, 1,000 debentures purchased cum-interest at ₹1,05,000; 1st November 2024, 1,200 debentures sold ex-interest at ₹1,28,200; 30th November 2024, 500 debentures purchased ex-interest at ₹54,500; 31st December 2024, 900 debentures sold cum-interest for ₹1,18,000. Prepare the Investment Account showing holdings on 31st March, 2025 at cost, using FIFO.
answer_html:
15% Debentures (Investment) Account, FIFO basis — closing balance as on 31.3.25: 1,400 debentures, face value ₹1,40,000, cost ₹1,44,500 (900 from the opening 2,000 + 500 purchased 30.11.24: opening lot after the 1.11.24 sale of 1,200 leaves 800 of the original 2,000 plus the 1,000 bought 1.5.24 minus what's sold, reconciled via FIFO issue order; net closing units 1,400 as shown in the working note below).

W.N.1 — Loss on sale 1.11.24: Cost of 1,200 sold (FIFO, from opening lot) = 2,50,000/2,000 × 1,200 = ₹1,50,000. Sale proceeds ₹1,28,200. Loss = ₹21,800, charged to P&L.

W.N.2 — Profit on sale 31.12.24: Cost of 900 sold (FIFO: 800 remaining from opening lot + 100 from the 1.5.24 purchase) = (2,50,000/2,000 × 800) + (1,00,000/1,000 × 100) = 1,00,000 + 10,000 = ₹1,10,000. Sale proceeds (cum-interest, less accrued interest component) net to ₹1,11,250 principal. Profit = ₹1,250.

W.N.3 — Closing balance: 900 debentures remaining from the 1.5.24 purchase (1,000−100 sold) at ₹90,000 (proportionate cost) + 500 debentures from the 30.11.24 purchase at ₹54,500 = 1,400 debentures, ₹1,44,500.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees applied weighted-average cost instead of the FIFO method the question specifically requires, or failed to separate the interest component from cum-interest purchase/sale prices before computing the capital gain/loss on disposal.

topic_text: Topic 3.5: Cost of investments - bonus shares (no separate cost), rights shares subscribed vs renounced, and weighted-average cost on partial disposal

Dividends for the year ended 31.03.2022 at the rate of 20% were declared by XYZ Ltd. and received by Sanket on 31.10.2022. Dividend amount for shares acquired by him on 01.06.2022 are to be adjusted against the cost of purchase.

On 15.11.2022, Sanket sold 25,000 equity shares at premium ₹12 per share.

You are required to prepare in books of Sanket. (i) Investment Account; (ii) Profit & Loss Account (Extract for Investment). Books of accounts are closed by Sanket on 31.12.2022 and market price of shares on that date is ₹20 per share. (10 Marks)

2. Right Shares = (50,000+10,000+10,000)/7 × 3 = 30,000 shares × 2/3 = 20,000 shares.

topic_text: Topic 3.6/3.8: Investment account on average-cost basis with cum-interest purchase, partial disposal, and part-conversion into equity shares

topic_text: Topic 3.4/3.6: Current investment (held under one year, at lower of cost and fair value) vs long-term investment (at cost, absent other-than-temporary decline)
question_html:
Innovative Garments Manufacturing Company Limited invested in the shares of another company on 1st October, 2022 at a cost of ₹2,50,000. It also earlier purchased Gold of ₹4,00,000 and Silver of ₹2,00,000 on 1st March, 2020. Market value as on 31st March, 2023 of above investments are as follows:

Particulars₹
Shares2,25,000
Gold6,00,000
Silver3,50,000

How above investments will be shown in the books of accounts of Innovative Garments Manufacturing Company Limited for the year ending 31st March, 2023 as per the provisions of Accounting Standard 13 "Accounting for Investments"?
answer_html:
As per AS 13 (Revised) "Accounting for Investments", for investment in shares, if the investment is purchased with an intention to hold for short-term period (less than one year), then it will be classified as current investment and to be carried at lower of cost and fair value, i.e. in case of shares, at lower of cost (₹2,50,000) and market value (₹2,25,000) as on 31st March 2023, i.e. ₹2,25,000.

If equity shares are acquired with an intention to hold for long term period (more than one year), then it should be considered as long-term investment to be shown at cost in the Balance Sheet of the company. However, provision for diminution should be made to recognise a decline, if other than temporary, in the value of the investments.

Gold and silver are generally purchased with an intention to hold it for long term period (more than one year) until and unless given otherwise. Hence, the investment in Gold and Silver (purchased on 1st March, 2020) should continue to be shown at cost (since there is no "other than temporary" diminution) as on 31st March, 2023, i.e. ₹4,00,000 and ₹2,00,000 respectively, though their market values have increased.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is applying the same "lower of cost and market value" treatment to the gold and silver holdings as to the shares, without first checking the intended holding period — long-term investments (like the gold/silver, held since 2020) stay at cost even when market value rises, and are written down only for an other-than-temporary decline, never simply marked to the lower of cost and current market value the way current investments are.

topic_text: Topic 3.9: Reclassification transfers - LT to current at lower of cost/carrying amount; current to LT at lower of cost/fair value
question_html: On 15th June, 2024, Y limited wants to re-classify its investments in accordance with AS 13 (revised). Decide and state the amount of transfer, based on the following information: (1) A portion of long term investments purchased on 1st March, 2023 are to be re-classified as current investments. The original cost of these investments was ₹14 lakhs but had been written down by ₹2 lakhs (to recognise 'other than temporary' decline in value). The market value of these investments on 15th June, 2024 was ₹11 lakhs. (2) A portion of current investments purchased on 15th March, 2024 for ₹7 lakhs are to be re-classified as long term investments, as the company has decided to retain them. The market value of these investments on 31st March, 2024 was ₹6 lakhs and fair value on 15th June 2018 was ₹8.5 lakhs.
answer_html:
As per AS 13 (Revised) 'Accounting for Investments', where long-term investments are reclassified as current investments, transfers are made at the lower of cost and carrying amount at the date of transfer; and where investments are reclassified from current to long term, transfers are made at lower of cost and fair value on the date of transfer. Accordingly, the re-classification will be done on the following basis:

(i) In this case, carrying amount of investment on the date of transfer is less than the cost; hence this re-classified current investment should be carried at ₹12 lakhs in the books (cost ₹14 lakhs less the ₹2 lakh write-down = ₹12 lakhs carrying amount, which is lower than the ₹14 lakh original cost).

(ii) In this case, reclassification of current investment into long-term investments will be made at ₹7 lakhs as cost is less than its fair value of ₹8.5 lakhs on the date of transfer.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is applying the same transfer rule in both directions — e.g. using "lower of cost and fair value" for the long-term-to-current reclassification too, instead of the correct "lower of cost and carrying amount" test that applies specifically to that direction.

topic_text: Topic 3.9: Reclassification of investments - long-term to current at lower of cost and carrying amount; current to long-term at lower of cost and fair value
question_html:
Kunal Securities Ltd. wants to reclassify its investments in accordance with AS-13 (Revised). State the values, at which the investments have to be reclassified in the following cases:

  1. Long term investment in Company A, costing ₹10.5 lakhs is to be re-classified as current investment. The company had reduced the value of these investments to ₹9 lakhs to recognize a permanent decline in value. The fair value on the date of reclassification is ₹9.3 lakhs.
  2. Long term investment in Company B, costing ₹14 lakhs is to be re-classified as current investment. The fair value on the date of reclassification is ₹16 lakhs and book value is ₹14 lakhs.
  3. Current investment in Company C, costing ₹12 lakhs is to be re-classified as long term investment as the company wants to retain them. The market value on the date of reclassification is ₹13.5 lakhs.
  4. Current investment in Company D, costing ₹18 lakhs is to be re-classified as long term investment. The market value on the date of reclassification is ₹16.5 lakhs.
answer_html:
As per AS 13 (Revised) ‘Accounting for Investments’, where long-term investments are reclassified as current investments, transfers are made at the lower of cost and carrying amount at the date of transfer. And where investments are reclassified from current to long term, transfers are made at lower of cost and fair value on the date of transfer.

Accordingly, the re-classification will be done on the following basis:

  1. In this case, carrying amount of investment on the date of transfer is less than the cost; hence this re-classified current investment should be carried at ₹9 lakhs in the books.
  2. The carrying/book value of the long-term investment is same as cost i.e., ₹14 lakhs. Hence this long-term investment will be reclassified as current investment at book value of ₹14 lakhs only.
  3. In this case, reclassification of current investment into long-term investments will be made at ₹12 lakhs as cost is less than its market value of ₹13.5 lakhs.
  4. Market value of the investment is ₹16.5 lakhs, which is lower than its cost i.e., ₹18 lakhs. Therefore, the transfer to long term investments should be done in the books at the market value i.e., ₹16.5 lakhs.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is applying a single reclassification rule across all four cases rather than switching direction with the transfer – long-term-to-current uses the lower of cost and carrying amount (not fair value), while current-to-long-term uses the lower of cost and fair value (not carrying amount); mixing these up produces the wrong transfer value in at least two of the four cases.
