topic_text: Topic 1.5: Adjusting vs non-adjusting events - physical possession vs mere date determines cheque treatment
question_html: Zenith Industries Ltd., preparing FY2024-25 financial statements. After year-end: (a) Fire on 10th April, 2025 destroyed uninsured stock worth ₹10,00,000, salvage recovered ₹2,00,000. (b) Legal claim filed 18th April, 2025 alleging misleading advertisement, damages claimed ₹20,00,000. (c) Cheques in Hand: company proposes recognising all cheques dated 31st March, 2025 or earlier received from stockists as "Cheques in Hand" under Cash and Cash Equivalents, reducing Trade Receivables — but two categories exist: (i) cheques physically collected by marketing personnel on/before 31st March, 2025; (ii) cheques sent by courier on/before 31st March but received only in April 2025. All cheques were deposited and realized in April 2025. Comment on the accounting treatment for each.
answer_html:
(a) Fire and loss of uninsured stock: occurred after the balance sheet date and does not relate to any condition existing on 31st March, 2025 — a non-adjusting event. Given its materiality (uninsured stock, future risk exposure), the fire and uninsured position must be disclosed, including its nature, estimated financial effect, and future vulnerability if determinable.

(b) Legal suit: initiated after the balance sheet date, no additional evidence of a pre-existing condition — also non-adjusting. Per AS 4 para 16, disclose as a contingent liability, including the nature of the contingency, estimated financial effect, and outcome uncertainties.

(c)(i) Cheques collected by marketing personnel: physically collected on or before 31st March, 2025 — since marketing personnel act as company representatives, this constitutes receipt by the company itself, discharging the stockist's liability. This is an adjusting event: reduce Trade Receivables and recognise as Cheques in Hand under Cash and Cash Equivalents, with appropriate accounting-policy disclosure.

(c)(ii) Cheques sent by courier, received only in April: though dated on/before 31st March, they were not in the company's possession until after the balance sheet date — a non-adjusting event. Account for these in the period actually received (April 2025), regardless of the cheque date; no disclosure needed since the event does not materially affect the financial position.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees treated all cheques dated on or before 31st March as adjusting events based on the cheque date alone, missing that physical possession by the company (or its representative) by the balance sheet date, not the cheque's date, is what actually determines adjusting vs. non-adjusting treatment.
chapter_label: AS 4: Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date

topic_text: Topic 1.2: A suit filed after the balance sheet date does not relate to a condition existing at that date - non-adjusting event, disclosable as a contingent liability
question_html: Surya Limited follows the financial year from April to March. A suit against the Company's Advertisement was filed by a party on 5th April, 2023, claiming damages of ₹5 lakhs. Keeping in view the provisions of AS-4, you are required to state with reasons whether the above event is to be treated as a Contingency, an Adjusting Event or a Non-Adjusting Event occurring after the Balance Sheet date.
answer_html: Suit filed against the company is a contingent liability, but it was not existing as on date of balance sheet date as the suit was filed on 5th April after the balance sheet date. As per AS 4, 'Contingencies' is restricted to conditions or situations at the balance sheet date, the financial effect of which is to be determined by future events which may or may not occur. However, it may be disclosed with the nature of contingency, being a contingent liability. This event does not pertain to conditions on the balance sheet date. Hence, it will have no effect on the financial statement and will be a non-adjusting event.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is treating a suit filed after the balance sheet date as an adjusting event or an outright provision, rather than recognising it as a non-adjusting contingency arising from a post-year-end condition.
chapter_label: AS 4: Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date

topic_text: Topic 1.5: A mere sale proposal at year end, with the deed registered only after the balance sheet date, is a non-adjusting event - no adjustment to the financial statements
question_html: Surya Limited follows the financial year from April to March. Company sends a proposal to sell an immovable property for ₹45 lakhs in March 2023. The book value of the property is ₹30 lakhs as on year end date. However, the Deed was registered on 15th April, 2023. Keeping in view the provisions of AS-4, you are required to state with reasons whether the above event is to be treated as a Contingency, an Adjusting Event or a Non-Adjusting Event occurring after the Balance Sheet date.
answer_html: In this case, no adjustment to assets and liabilities is required as the event does not affect the determination and the condition of the amounts stated in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2023. There was just a proposal before 31st March, 2023 and hence sale cannot be shown in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2023. Sale of immovable property is an event occurring after the balance sheet date is a non-adjusting event.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is recognising the sale in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March on the basis that a proposal existed by that date, without checking whether the sale was actually completed (deed registered) before or after the balance sheet date.
chapter_label: AS 4: Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date

topic_text: Topic 1.4/1.5: Adjusting vs non-adjusting events applied across four independent post-year-end scenarios for one company
question_html:
Smart Ltd. closes its books of accounts every year on 31st March. The financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2024 are to be approved by the approving authority on 30th June 2024. During the first quarter of 2024-2025, the following events/transactions have taken place. The accountant of the company seeks your guidance for the following:

  1. Smart Ltd. has an inventory of 50 stitching machines costing at ₹5,500 per machine as on 31st March, 2024. The company is expecting a heavy decline in the demand in next year. The inventories are valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower. During the month of April 2024, due to fall in demand, the prices have gone down drastically. The company has sold 5 machines during this month at a price of ₹4,000 per machine.
  2. A fire has broken out in the company's godown on 15th April, 2024. The company has estimated a loss of ₹25 lakhs of which 75% is recoverable from the Insurance company.
  3. The company has entered into a sale agreement on 30th March, 2024 to sell a property for a consideration of ₹7,50,000 which is being carried in the books at ₹5,50,000 at the year end. The transfer of risk and reward and sale is complete in the month of May 2024 when conveyance and possession get completed.
  4. The company has received, during the year 2022-2023, a government grant of ₹15 lakhs for purchase of a machine. The company has received a notice for refund of the said grant on 15th June, 2024 due to violation of some of the conditions of grant during the year 2023-2024.

You are required to state with reasons, how the above transactions will be dealt with in the financial statement for the year ended 31st March 2024.
answer_html:
Events occurring after the balance sheet date are significant events, favourable or unfavourable, occurring between the balance sheet date and the date on which the financial statements are approved. Assets and liabilities should be adjusted for such events only if they provide additional evidence of conditions existing at the balance sheet date, or indicate the going-concern assumption is no longer appropriate. Here, the financial statements are approved on 30th June 2024.

  1. Since on 31st March 2024 Smart Ltd. was already expecting a heavy decline in demand, the price fall during April 2024 is considered an adjusting event, providing further evidence of the condition (declining net realisable value) existing at the balance sheet date. Inventory should be written down to ₹4,000 per machine: 50 machines × ₹4,000 = ₹2,00,000.
  2. The fire took place after the balance sheet date (during FY 2024-25), so the financials for FY 2023-24 are not adjusted for the fire loss. However, the going-concern assumption should be evaluated in light of the fire; if it remains appropriate, no disclosure is required in the financial statements.
  3. Since the transfer of risk and reward and completion of sale occurred only in May 2024 (conveyance and possession), no revenue should be recognised for this in the FY 2023-24 financial statements – this is a non-adjusting event, though disclosure of the agreement should be given.
  4. Since the refund notice was received after 31st March but before the 30th June 2024 approval date, and the violation of grant conditions took place during FY 2023-24 (a condition the company must have been aware of), the grant refund is an adjusting event and shall be adjusted in the FY 2023-24 financial statements.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating item (i)'s post-year-end price fall as a non-adjusting event because the sale itself happened after the year end, missing that the company's own pre-year-end expectation of a demand decline is what makes the subsequent price evidence adjusting rather than the sale transaction itself.
chapter_label: AS 4: Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date

topic_text: Topic 1.5: Non-adjusting event - conditions not existing at balance sheet date
question_html: While preparing its financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2025, B Limited has come across the following events which took place after 31st March, 2025. The financial statements of the company were approved by the Board of Directors on 30th May, 2025: B Limited started negotiations with S Limited during 2024-25 to acquire their Consumer Durables Business for ₹400 lakhs. The deal was finalized on 20th April, 2025 and B Limited invested ₹275 lakhs before 30th May, 2025. You are required to state with reasons, whether the aforesaid event is an adjusting or non-adjusting event as per the provisions of the relevant AS.
answer_html:
AS 4 (Revised) defines “Events Occurring after the Balance Sheet Date” as those significant events, both favourable and unfavourable, that occur between the balance sheet date and the date on which the financial statements are approved by the Approving Authority in the case of a company.

The acquisition of Consumer Durables Business of S Limited by B Limited is an event occurring after the balance sheet date. However, it is a non-adjusting event as it does not affect the determination and the condition of the amounts stated in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2025. The disclosure should be made in the report of the approving authority about the investment of ₹275 lakhs to enable the users of financial statements to make proper evaluations and decisions.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees classified the acquisition as an adjusting event on the basis that negotiations had begun during 2024-25, not recognising that the deal was only finalised after the balance sheet date and so does not reflect conditions existing at 31st March, 2025.
chapter_label: AS 4: Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date

topic_text: Topic 1.4: Adjusting event - fraud relating to the accounting period, discovered before approval
question_html: During the course of audit for the year ended 31st March, 2025, the auditor discovered a fraud of ₹1,25,000 done by the accountant of the company. The fraud was discovered on 20th April, 2025. The accountant of the company had left the job and absconded on 29th March, 2025. You are required to state with reasons, whether the aforesaid event is an adjusting or non-adjusting event as per the provisions of the relevant AS.
answer_html: This is an adjusting event. If a fraud of the accounting period is detected after the balance sheet date but before approval of the financial statements, it is necessary to recognize the loss of ₹1,25,000 and adjust the accounts of the company for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees treated the fraud's discovery date (after year end) as decisive and classified it as non-adjusting, rather than recognising that the fraud itself related to the accounting period under audit and so required recognition in that period's accounts.
chapter_label: AS 4: Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date

topic_text: Topic 1.5: Non-adjusting event - loss did not exist at the balance sheet date
question_html: A fire engulfed the warehouse of B Limited on 13th April, 2025 and destroyed inventory worth ₹15 lakhs lying there. You are required to state with reasons, whether the aforesaid event is an adjusting or non-adjusting event as per the provisions of the relevant AS.
answer_html: This is a non-adjusting event. The destruction of warehouse due to fire did not exist on the balance sheet date i.e. 31st March, 2025. Therefore, loss occurred due to fire is not to be recognized in the financial year 2024-25. Considering that the going concern assumption is still valid, the fact of fire together with a loss of ₹15 lakhs should be disclosed in the report of the approving authority for 2024-25 to enable the users of financial statements to make proper evaluations and decisions.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A few examinees recognised the fire loss directly in the 2024-25 financial statements instead of treating it as a non-adjusting, disclosure-only event, incorrectly assuming any post-year-end loss of this size must be adjusted for.
chapter_label: AS 4: Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date

topic_text: Topic 1.4/1.5: Adjusting vs non-adjusting events after the balance sheet date across five illustrative scenarios
question_html:
For five companies whose financial year ended on 31st March, 2023, the financial statements were approved by their approving authority on 15th June, 2023.

During 2023-2024, the following material events took place:

  1. A Ltd. sold a major property which was included in the balance sheet at ₹1,00,000 and for which contracts had been exchanged on 15th March, 2023. The sale was completed on 15th May, 2023 at a price of ₹2,50,000.
  2. On 30th April, 2023, a 100% subsidiary of B Ltd. declared a dividend of ₹3,00,000 in respect of its own shares for the year ended on 31st March, 2023.
  3. On 31st May, 2023, the mail order activities of C Ltd. (a retail trading group) were shut down with closure costs amounting to ₹2.5 million.
  4. On 1st July, 2023 the discovery of sand under D Ltd.'s major civil engineering contract site causes the cost of the contract to increase by 25% for which there would be no corresponding recovery from the customer.
  5. A fire, on 2nd April, 2023, completely destroyed a manufacturing plant of E Ltd. It was expected that the loss of ₹10 million would be fully covered by the insurance company.

You are required to state with reasons, how each of the above items numbered (a) to (e) should be dealt with in the financial statement of the various companies for the year ended 31st March, 2023.
answer_html:
Treatment as per AS 4 ‘Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date’

CompanyTreatment
(a)A Ltd.The sale of property should be treated as an adjusting event since contracts had been exchanged prior to the year-end. The effect of the sale would be reflected in the financial statements ended on 31.3.2023 and the profit on sale of property ₹1,50,000 would be treated as an extraordinary item.
(b)B Ltd.The declaration of dividend on 30th April, 2023 of ₹3,00,000 would be treated as a non-adjusting event in the financial statements of 2022-2023. This is because, the dividend has been declared after the balance sheet date and no conditions existed on the balance sheet date for such declaration of dividend. Further as per AS 9, right to receive dividend is established when it is declared and not before that.
(c)C Ltd.A closure not anticipated at the year-end would be treated as a non-adjusting event. Memorandum disclosure would be required for closure of mail order activities since non disclosure would affect user's understanding of the financial statements.
(d)D Ltd.The event took place after the financial statements were approved by the approving authority and is thus outside the purview of AS 4. However, in view of its significance of the transaction, the directors may consider publishing a separate financial statement/additional statement for the attention of the members in general meeting.
(e)E Ltd.The event is a non-adjusting event since it occurred after the year-end and does not relate to the conditions existing at the year-end. However, it is necessary to consider the validity of the going concern assumption having regard to the extent of insurance cover. Also, since it is said that the loss would be fully recovered by the insurance company, the fact should be disclosed by way of a note to the financial statements.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating D Ltd.'s scenario as a normal non-adjusting event requiring disclosure in the 2022-2023 financial statements, without recognising that the event occurred after the accounts were already approved and is therefore entirely outside AS 4's scope for that year's statements.
chapter_label: AS 4: Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date

topic_text: Topic 2.5: Change in the method of estimating a provision is not a change in accounting policy, and the required disclosure note when the change is nonetheless made
question_html:
ABC Ltd. was making provision for non-moving inventories based on no issues for the last 12 months up to 31.3.2021.

The company wants to provide during the year ending 31.3.2022 based on technical evaluation:

Particulars₹
Total value of inventory100 lakhs
Provision required based on 12 months issue3.5 lakhs
Provision required based on technical evaluation2.5 lakhs

Does this amount to change in Accounting Policy? Can the company change the method of provision? (5 Marks)
answer_html:
The decision of making provision for non-moving inventories on the basis of technical evaluation does not amount to change in accounting policy. Accounting policy of a company may require that provision for non-moving inventories should be made. The method of estimating the amount of provision may be changed in case a more prudent estimate can be made. In the given case, considering the total value of inventory, the change in the amount of required provision of non-moving inventory from ₹3.5 lakhs to ₹2.5 lakhs is also not material. The disclosure can be made for such change in the following lines by way of notes to the accounts in the annual accounts of ABC Ltd. for the year 2021-22:

“The company has provided for non-moving inventories on the basis of technical evaluation unlike preceding years. Had the same method been followed as in the previous year, the profit for the year and the corresponding effect on the year end net assets would have been lower by ₹1 lakh.”
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating any change in the basis of a provision estimate as automatically a change in accounting policy requiring restatement, without distinguishing a genuine policy change from a change in accounting estimate (moving to a more prudent estimation method for an existing policy of providing for non-moving inventory).
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies

topic_text: Topic 2.5: Distinguishing a change in accounting estimate, a policy for new/immaterial transactions, and a genuine change in accounting policy
question_html:
The accountant of Moon Limited provides you the following information: (i) Provision for doubtful debts was created @3% till 31st March, 2025; from FY 2025-26, the rate has been changed to 5%. (ii) During the year ended 31st March, 2026 the management has introduced a formal gratuity scheme in place of ad-hoc ex-gratia payments to employees on retirement. (iii) During 2025-26, there was change in cost formula in measuring the cost of inventories. (iv) Management decided to pay pension to employees who have retired after completing 5 years of service (₹25,000 per month); earlier there was no such pension scheme.

You are required to advise the accountant of Moon Limited, with valid reasons, whether the above transactions would be treated as change in accounting policy or not, for the year ended 31st March, 2026 in the context of AS 5. (4 Marks)
answer_html:
As per para 21 of AS 5, the preparation of financial statements involves making estimates based on circumstances existing when the statements are prepared; it may be necessary to revise an estimate in a subsequent period if circumstances change. Revision of an estimate, by its nature, does not bring the adjustment within the definitions of a prior period item or an extraordinary item. Change in Accounting estimate is not a change in accounting policy.

(i) Provision for doubtful debts rate change (3% to 5%): this is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy. Per para 27 of AS 5, a change in estimate with a material effect in the current period should be disclosed and quantified; any change expected to have a material effect in later periods should also be disclosed and quantified.

(ii) As per AS 5, adopting an accounting policy for events or transactions that differ in substance from previously occurring events or transactions is not considered a change in accounting policy. Accordingly, introduction of a formal retirement gratuity scheme in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments is not a change in accounting policy.

(iii) As per AS 2 and AS 5: the method of determining cost (FIFO/Weighted Average) is an accounting policy choice, and any change in it affects measurement of inventory and profit. Hence a change in cost formula in measuring the cost of inventories IS a change in Accounting Policy.

(iv) The adoption of a new accounting policy for events or transactions which did not occur previously, or that were immaterial, will not be treated as a change in accounting policy. Introducing a pension scheme where none previously existed is therefore not a change in accounting policy.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees classified the provision-rate change and the new gratuity/pension schemes as changes in accounting policy, not recognising AS 5's distinction between a genuine policy change (like the inventory cost-formula change) and a change in estimate or the adoption of a policy for a genuinely new type of transaction.
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies

topic_text: Topic 2.3: Prior period item vs current-year expense - depends on whether the underlying adjustment was determinable in the prior period or only becomes so via a later event
question_html: Sneha, an employee of Omre Limited, went on paid maternity leave for 9 months, 1st January 2024 to 30th September 2024, monthly pay ₹1,50,000. While preparing FY2023-24 financial statements, her salary for 3 months (Jan–Mar 2024) was omitted. When she joined 1st October 2024, the whole 9-month salary was paid. With reference to AS-5, determine if this is a prior period item and pass the FY2024-25 journal entry. Variant: Suppose Sneha was terminated 1st January 2024 and reinstated by court order on 30th September 2024, with the 9-month salary paid 1st October 2024 — what is the AS-5 treatment here, with journal entry?
answer_html:
Original scenario: Per AS 5, prior period items are income/expenses arising in the current period from errors or omissions in preparing prior periods' financial statements. The 3 months' salary (Jan–Mar 2024, ₹4,50,000) omitted from FY2023-24 is a prior period item in FY2024-25.

Journal entry (FY2024-25): Salary A/c (₹1,50,000×6) Dr. 9,00,000; Prior Period Item A/c (₹1,50,000×3) Dr. 4,50,000; To Bank A/c 13,50,000.

Variant (termination/reinstatement): AS 5 states "prior period items" does not include adjustments necessitated by circumstances that, though related to prior periods, are determined only in the current period. Since Sneha's reinstatement (with retrospective salary) was ordered by the court only in FY2024-25, the ₹4,50,000 (Jan–Mar 2024) is not a prior period item — the entire ₹13,50,000 is a current-year expense.

Journal entry (variant): Salary A/c (₹1,50,000×9) Dr. 13,50,000; To Bank A/c 13,50,000.
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: A majority of examinees were unable to determine whether the given item constituted a prior period item under AS 5 "Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies". Many of them also failed to pass the correct journal entry.
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies

topic_text: Topic 2.2: Prior period items arise only from errors or omissions in preparing earlier financial statements - a provision write-back from a genuinely unusual event is an extraordinary item instead
question_html:
During the course of the last three years, a company owning and operating Helicopters lost four Helicopters. The company's accountant felt that after the crash, the maintenance provision created in respect of the respective helicopters was no longer required, and proposed to write it back to the Profit and Loss account as a prior period item.

Is the company's proposed accounting treatment correct? Discuss.
answer_html:
The balance amount of maintenance provision written back to profit and loss account, no longer required due to crash of the helicopters, is not a prior period item because there was no error in the preparation of previous periods' financial statements. The term "prior period items", as defined in AS 5 (revised) "Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies", refer only to income or expenses which arise in the current period as a result of errors or omissions in the preparation of the financial statements of one or more prior periods. The balance amount left in the provision created earlier is not as a result of error in the past. So it will not be considered as a prior period item. Such write back of provision is not an ordinary feature of the business; it shall be considered as an extra-ordinary item.

As per paragraph 8 of AS 5, extraordinary items should be disclosed in the Statement of Profit and Loss as a part of net profit or loss for the period. The nature and the amount of each extraordinary item should be separately disclosed in the Statement of Profit and Loss in a manner that its impact on current profit or loss can be perceived. Hence, the amount so written-back (if material) should be disclosed as an extraordinary item as per AS 5 rather than as a prior period item.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating the reversal of a no-longer-required provision as a prior period item merely because the original provision was created in an earlier year, missing AS 5's requirement that prior period items arise specifically from errors or omissions in preparing earlier financial statements — a provision correctly created and later found unnecessary due to a genuinely unusual event is an extraordinary item, not a prior period correction.
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies

topic_text: Topic 2.3: Classification exercise across accounting policy changes, estimate changes, extraordinary items, and prior period items
question_html: Identify each of the following as Change in Accounting Policy / Change in Accounting Estimate / Extraordinary Item / Prior Period Item / Ordinary Activity: (i) Non-provision for salary already due in an earlier year. (ii) Attachment of the property of the enterprise. (iii) Introduction of a new pension scheme for employees. (iv) Change in Reserve for obsolete inventory. (v) Settlement of a litigation case. (vi) Legislative changes with long-term retrospective application. (vii) Change from Cost Model to Revaluation Model for PPE measurement. (viii) Government-sanctioned grant received this year for expenses incurred in a previous year.
answer_html:
1. Prior period item.
  2. Extraordinary item.
  3. Ordinary activity (not a change in accounting policy).
  4. Change in accounting estimate.
  5. Ordinary activity, but requires separate disclosure.
  6. Extraordinary item requiring separate disclosure.
  7. Change in accounting policy.
  8. Prior period item.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees classified the change from Cost to Revaluation Model as a change in estimate rather than a change in accounting policy, and conversely treated the pension-scheme introduction as a policy change rather than recognising it as a new ordinary business decision, not a change to an existing policy.
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies

topic_text: Topic 2.4: Tax demands from ordinary business activity are not extraordinary items
question_html: Best Ltd., a consultancy services provider, received a GST department demand notice of ₹2,50,000 on consultancy services provided; the company paid the demand and recorded it as extraordinary expenditure. Can this payment of a tax demand be recognised as an extraordinary item?
answer_html: No. Per AS 5, extraordinary items arise from events clearly distinct from ordinary activities and are not expected to recur frequently or regularly. Providing consultancy services is Best Ltd.'s ordinary business activity, and the GST liability arises directly from these ordinary transactions. Paying a tax demand raised by the taxation authority is part of normal business operations. Recording it as extraordinary is therefore not correct — it should be recognised as part of profit or loss from ordinary activities.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees accepted the company's own extraordinary-item classification uncritically, not testing it against AS 5's actual definition (an event clearly distinct from, and not part of, the ordinary business activity).
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies

topic_text: Topic 2.5: Classification exercise distinguishing accounting-estimate changes, non-policy-changes (new events), and genuine accounting-policy changes
question_html:
The Accountant of Heera Ltd. has sought your opinion with relevant reasons, whether the following transactions will be treated as change in Accounting Policy or not for the year ended 31st March, 2024. Please advise him in the following situations in accordance with the provisions of relevant Accounting Standard:

  1. Till the previous year the furniture was depreciated on straight line basis over a period of 5 years. From current year, the useful life of furniture has been changed to 3 years.
  2. Management decided to pay pension to those employees who have retired after completing 5 years of service in the organization. Such employees will get pension of ₹20,000 per month. Earlier there was no such scheme of pension in the organization.
  3. During the year ended 31st March, 2024, there was change in cost formula in measuring the cost of inventories.
answer_html:
1. Change in useful life of furniture from 5 years to 3 years is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy.
  2. Adoption of a new accounting policy for events or transactions which did not occur previously (there was no pension scheme before) should not be treated as a change in an accounting policy. The introduction of the new pension scheme is therefore not a change in accounting policy.
  3. Change in the cost formula used in measuring the cost of inventories is a change in accounting policy.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is classifying the new pension scheme as a change in accounting policy simply because it is a new accounting treatment being adopted, missing AS 5's specific rule that adopting a policy for an event that did not previously occur is not a change in an existing policy.
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies

topic_text: Topic 2.5: Adoption of a policy for events/transactions that did not previously occur is not a change in accounting policy
question_html:
Explain whether the following will constitute a change in accounting policy or not as per AS 5:

  1. Introduction of a formal retirement gratuity scheme by an employer in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments to employees on retirement.
  2. Management decided to pay pension to those employees who have retired after completing 5 years of service in the organistaion. Such employees will get pension of ₹20,000 per month. Earlier there was no such scheme of pension in the organization.
answer_html:
As per para 31 of AS 5 ‘Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies’, the adoption of an accounting policy for events or transactions that differ in substance from previously occurring events or transactions, will not be considered as a change in accounting policy.

  1. Accordingly, introduction of a formal retirement gratuity scheme by an employer in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments to employees on retirement is not a change in an accounting policy.
  2. Similarly, the adoption of a new accounting policy of paying pension to retired employees is a policy for events or transactions which did not occur previously. Hence, it will not be treated as a change in an accounting policy.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating both scenarios as changes in accounting policy simply because the amount charged to profit or loss will differ going forward, without checking whether the underlying event or transaction itself is genuinely new rather than merely a change in the treatment of the same recurring event.
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies

topic_text: Topic 2.3: Definition of a prior period item - errors/omissions in prior financial statements, not later-determined adjustments
question_html: When can an item qualify to be a prior period item as per AS 5?
answer_html: Per AS 5 para 16, prior period items are income or expenses that arise in the current period as a result of errors or omissions in the preparation of financial statements of one or more prior periods. The term does not include other adjustments necessitated by circumstances that, though related to prior periods, are determined only in the current period (e.g. arrears payable to workers from a retrospective wage revision).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A direct definitional question; the key nuance examinees often miss is the exclusion for items only determinable in the current period despite relating to an earlier one.
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies

topic_text: Topic 2.4: Correcting an omitted-inventory error from a prior period, added to opening stock as a prior period item
question_html: A Ltd. finds that the stock sheets of 31.3.2024 did not include two pages containing details of inventory worth ₹20 lakhs. How should this be dealt with in the accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2025, per AS 5?
answer_html: This omission is a prior period item under AS 5 para 16. Per para 19, prior period items are normally included in determining the current period's net profit or loss — so ₹20 lakhs should be added to the opening stock as at 1.4.2024. Alternatively, such items may be shown in the statement of profit and loss after the current period's net profit/loss has been determined. Either presentation must clearly indicate the effect of the item on the current period's profit or loss.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees treated the omission as a current-year adjustment to closing stock rather than correcting the prior year's opening stock figure, misplacing the correction in the wrong period.
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies

topic_text: Topic 1.4: Adjusting versus non-adjusting events after the balance sheet date, across five distinct fact patterns   +   Topic 2.2: Extraordinary item discovered after financial statements are approved, treated in the subsequent period
question_html:
State with reasons, how the following events would be dealt with in the financial statements of Hari Ltd. for the year ended 31st March, 2024 (accounts were approved on 25th July, 2024):

  1. Negotiations with another company for acquisition of its business was started on 21st January, 2024. Hari Ltd. invested ₹40 lakh on 22nd April, 2024.
  2. The company made a provision for bad debts @ 4% of its total debtors (as per trend followed from the previous years). In the second week of March 2024, a debtor for ₹2,50,000 had suffered heavy loss due to an earthquake; the loss was not covered by any insurance policy. In May, 2024 the debtor became bankrupt.
  3. During the year 2023-24, Hari Ltd. was sued by a competitor for ₹13 lakhs for infringement of a trademark. Based on the advice of the company's legal counsel, Hari Ltd. provided for a sum of ₹8 lakhs in its financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2024. On 26th May, 2024, the Court decided in favour of the party alleging infringement of the trademark and ordered Hari Ltd. to pay the aggrieved party a sum of ₹12 lakhs.
  4. Cashier of Hari Ltd. embezzled cash amounting to ₹3,00,000 during March, 2024. However the same comes to the notice of Company management during August, 2024.
  5. Cheques dated 31st March, 2024 collected in the month of April, 2024. All cheques are presented to the bank in the month of April, 2024 and are also realized in the same month in the normal course after deposit in the bank.
answer_html:
1. As per AS 4 'Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date', disclosure should be made in the report of the approving authority of those events occurring after the balance sheet date that represent material changes and commitments affecting the financial position of the enterprise; the investment of ₹40 lakhs in April, 2024 in the acquisition of another company should be disclosed in the report of the Board of Directors to enable users of financial statements to make proper evaluations and decisions.
  2. As per AS 4, adjustment to assets and liabilities are required for events occurring after the balance sheet date that provide additional information materially affecting the determination of the amounts relating to conditions existing at the Balance Sheet date. A debtor for ₹2,50,000 suffered heavy loss due to earthquake in the second week of March, 2024 which was not covered by insurance. This information with its implications was already known to the company. The fact that he became bankrupt in May, 2024 (after the balance sheet date) is only an additional information related to the existing condition on the balance sheet date. Accordingly, full provision for bad debts amounting ₹2,50,000 should be made, to cover the loss arising due to the insolvency of a debtor, in the final accounts for the year ended 31st March 2024.
  3. As per AS 4, adjustments to assets and liabilities are required for events occurring after the balance sheet date that provide additional information materially affecting the determination of the amounts relating to conditions existing at the balance sheet date. In the given case, since Hari Ltd. was sued by a competitor for infringement of a trademark during the year 2023-24 for which the provision was also made by it, the decision of the Court on 26th May, 2024, for payment of the penalty will constitute as an adjusting event because it is an event occurred before approval of the financial statements. Therefore, Hari Ltd. should adjust the provision upward by ₹4 lakhs to reflect the award decreed by the Court to be paid by them to its competitor.
  4. As the embezzlement of cash comes to the notice of company management only after approval of financial statements by board of directors of the company, then the treatment will be done as per the provisions of AS 5 "Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies" and the same will not be adjusted in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2024. This being an extra-ordinary item should be disclosed in the statement of profit and loss as a part of loss for the year ending March, 2025, in a manner, that its impact on current profit or loss can be perceived.
  5. Collection of cheques after balance sheet date is not an adjusting event even if the cheques bear the date of 31st March. Recognition of cheques in hand is therefore not consistent with requirements of AS 4. Moreover, the collection of cheques after balance sheet date does not represent any material change or commitments affecting financial position of the enterprise and no disclosure of such collections in the Directors' Report is necessary.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating all five items uniformly as either "always adjust" or "always disclose only", rather than separately testing each event against AS 4's adjusting-versus-non-adjusting distinction on its own facts — in particular, confusing the Court's post-year-end decision (an adjusting event, since it relates to a liability that already existed and was already provided for at the balance sheet date) with the cashier's embezzlement discovered after the accounts were approved (a subsequent-period item under AS 5, not an adjustment to the year already closed).
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies

topic_text: Topic 3.6: Forward contract premium amortised over the contract period; monetary item restated at each balance sheet date and on settlement
question_html: Jared Limited purchased a machine for US$20,000 on 31st December 2024, payment due after four months. The company entered a four-month forward contract at ₹78.85 per US$; the spot rate on 31st December 2024 was ₹77.50 per US$. (i) How should Jared recognise the profit or loss on the forward contract for the year ended 31st March, 2025? (ii) Trade payables include an amount due to Sterling Limited of ₹9,75,000, recorded at US$1=₹75.00 on the purchase date. Exchange rate on balance-sheet date (31st March 2025): US$1=₹79.00. Payment made 1st May 2025 at US$1=₹78.30. Calculate the exchange difference as at 31st March 2025 and on settlement (1st May 2025), and explain the accounting treatment per AS 11.
answer_html:
(i) Forward contract premium/loss: Forward rate 78.85 − Spot rate 77.50 = premium of ₹1.35/US$. Total loss on contract = 20,000 × 1.35 = ₹27,000. Contract period 4 months, of which 3 months fall in the year ended 31st March, 2025: loss to be recognised = 27,000 × 3/4 = ₹20,250 in the year ended 31st March, 2025 (the balance ₹6,750 recognised in the following year).

(ii) Exchange difference on trade payable to Sterling Ltd.: Initial recognition: US$13,000 (9,75,000/75) at ₹75. Balance sheet date rate ₹79 — exchange loss = 13,000 × (79−75) = ₹52,000, charged to the Statement of Profit & Loss for the year ended 31st March, 2025 (per AS 11, monetary item restatement differences are recognised as they arise). Settlement date rate ₹78.30 — exchange gain on settlement = 13,000 × (79−78.30) = ₹9,100, credited to the Statement of Profit & Loss for the year ended 31st March, 2026 (the year of settlement).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees recognised the full forward-contract loss in the year of inception rather than time-apportioning it over the contract period falling in each accounting year, or netted the balance-sheet-date exchange loss against the later settlement-date gain instead of recognising each in its own accounting period.
chapter_label: AS 11: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates

topic_text: Topic 3.2/3.4: Definition of monetary item and reporting of foreign currency monetary/non-monetary items at each balance sheet date
question_html: "Explain "monetary item" as per Accounting Standard 11. How are foreign currency monetary items to be recognized at each Balance Sheet date? Classify the following as monetary or non-monetary item: (i) Share Capital (ii) Trade Receivables (iii) Investments (iv) Fixed Assets.
answer_html:
As per AS 11 'The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates', Monetary items are money held and assets and liabilities to be received or paid in fixed or determinable amounts of money.

Foreign currency monetary items should be reported using the closing rate at each balance sheet date. However, in certain circumstances, the closing rate may not reflect with reasonable accuracy the amount in reporting currency that is likely to be realised from, or required to disburse, a foreign currency monetary item at the balance sheet date. In such circumstances, the relevant monetary item should be reported in the reporting currency at the amount which is likely to be realised from or required to disburse, such item at the balance sheet date.

ItemClassification
Share capitalNon-monetary
Trade receivablesMonetary
InvestmentsNon-monetary
Fixed assetsNon-monetary
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is classifying Investments as a monetary item because they are eventually realised in cash, missing that AS 11 tests whether the amount to be received is fixed or determinable in monetary terms at the reporting date, not merely whether the asset will ultimately convert to cash.
chapter_label: AS 11: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates

topic_text: Topic 3.5: Exchange differences on restatement of a monetary trade receivable at the balance sheet date are recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss
question_html: Trade receivables of PP Ltd. include amount receivable from Preksha Ltd., ₹20,00,150 recorded at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of sales, transaction recorded at US $1 = ₹73.40. The exchange rate on balance sheet date (31.03.2023) is US $1 = ₹73.60. Exchange rate on 1st April, 2022 is US $1 = ₹74.00. You are required to calculate the amount of exchange difference and also explain the accounting treatment needed in the above two cases as per AS 11 in the books of PP Ltd.
answer_html:
Trade Receivables

Foreign Currency / Rate₹
Initial recognitionUS $27,250 (20,00,150/73.40) at 1 US $ = ₹73.4020,00,150
Rate on Balance sheet date1 US $ = ₹73.60
Exchange Difference Gain [US $27,250 × (73.60−73.40)]5,450

As per AS 11 "The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates", exchange differences on trade receivables amounting ₹5,450 is required to be transferred to Profit and Loss A/c.

Treatment needed in this case: Credit Profit and loss account by ₹5,450.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is recognising the exchange gain on the monetary trade receivable directly in a reserve, rather than crediting the full amount to the Statement of Profit and Loss for the period as AS 11 requires for monetary-item restatement differences.
chapter_label: AS 11: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates

topic_text: Topic 3.2/3.5: Monetary vs non-monetary classification, and exchange difference on restatement of a monetary trade payable recognised in profit and loss
question_html:
(i) Classify the following items into Monetary and Non-monetary: Share capital; Trade Payables; Cash balance; Property, plant and equipment.

(ii) Trade payables of CAT Ltd. include amount payable to JBB Ltd., ₹10,00,000 recorded at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of transaction, transaction recorded at US $1 = ₹80.00. The exchange rate on balance sheet date (31.03.2024) was US $1 = ₹85.00. You are required to calculate the amount of exchange difference and also explain the accounting treatment needed for this as per AS 11 in the books of CAT Ltd.
answer_html:
(i) Share capital – Non-monetary; Trade Payables – Monetary; Cash balance – Monetary; Property, plant and equipment – Non-monetary.

(ii) Amount of Exchange difference and its Accounting Treatment

ParticularsForeign Currency / Rate₹
Trade payables — Initial recognitionUS $12,500 (₹10,00,000/80), 1 US $ = ₹8010,00,000
Rate on Balance sheet date1 US $ = ₹85
Exchange Difference lossUS $12,500 × ₹(85−80)62,500

Treatment: Debit Profit and Loss A/c by ₹62,500 and Credit Trade Payables. Thus, the Exchange Difference on trade payables amounting ₹62,500 is required to be transferred to Profit and Loss.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is classifying Property, Plant and Equipment as monetary because it has a determinable rupee value, confusing "monetary" (a fixed or determinable number of currency units) with simply "having a value"; a second common error is deferring or capitalising the exchange loss instead of recognising it in profit and loss for the period.
chapter_label: AS 11: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates

topic_text: Topic 3.4/3.5: Balance sheet valuation of monetary/non-monetary items and exchange gain/loss on settlement
question_html:
Karna Ltd., an Indian Company, has the following foreign currency transactions during the financial year 2025-26:
(i) On 1st July, 2025, imported goods from Try Ltd., a German based company, amounting to ₹30,96,000.
(ii) On 1st October, 2025, imported plant and machinery from Lucy Ltd., a German based company, for €18,500. The amount was paid on the date of import itself. (Ignore depreciation).
(iii) On 1st December, 2025, exported good on credit to Cream Ltd., a German based company, amounting to ₹50,40,000.
All the above transactions were recorded in the books of account at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of the transactions. Ignore taxes and duty on the above transactions.
Payment due from Cream Ltd. and payment due to Try Ltd. is outstanding as on 31st March, 2026.
Rate of exchange between reporting currency (₹) and foreign currency (€) on different dates are as under: On 1st July, 2025, 1€ = ₹86; On 1st October, 2025, 1€ = ₹88; On 1st December, 2025, 1€ = ₹84; On 31st March, 2026, 1€ = ₹90.
You are required, as per AS-11: (i) To show value at which above items will appear in Balance sheet as on 31st March, 2026; (ii) To calculate the amount of gain/loss on each of above transactions on account of exchange differences, if any. (5 Marks)
answer_html:
As per AS 11 “The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates”, Foreign currency monetary items should be reported using the closing rate. Non-monetary items which are carried in terms of historical cost denominated in a foreign currency should be reported using the exchange rate at the date of the transaction. Exchange differences arising on the settlement of monetary items or on reporting an enterprise's monetary items at rates different from those at which they were initially recorded during the period, or reported in previous financial statements, should be recognised as income or as expenses in the period in which they arise.

(i) Items given in the question will appear in the Balance Sheet at the following values:
Trade Payables (30,96,000/86 = 36,000 German Currency) x ₹90 = ₹32,40,000
Plant and Machinery 18,500 German Currency x ₹88 = ₹16,28,000
Trade Receivables (50,40,000/84 = 60,000 German Currency) x ₹90 = ₹54,00,000

(ii) Amount of gain/loss on each transaction on account of exchange difference:
Exchange loss on Transaction of import of goods from Try Ltd. = ₹(1,44,000) [36,000 German Currency x ₹4 (i.e. 90−86)]
Exchange gain on Transaction of export of goods to Cream Ltd = ₹3,60,000 [60,000 German Currency x ₹6 (i.e. 90−84)]
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A significant number of examinees used the transaction-date rate instead of the closing rate to restate the outstanding trade payable and trade receivable at year end under AS 11, and some failed to translate the plant and machinery paid for on the date of import at the transaction-date rate.

topic_text: Topic 4.3: Exchange differences on a foreign-currency borrowing treated as a borrowing cost only to the extent they approximate the interest-rate differential against an equivalent local-currency loan   +   Topic 3.5: Exchange difference on restatement of a foreign-currency monetary borrowing at the closing rate, with the AS 16-eligible portion carved out of the total exchange loss and the remainder recognised under AS 11
question_html:
Omega Limited has borrowed a sum of US $10,00,000 at the beginning of Financial Year 2022-23 for its residential project at 4%. The interest is payable at the end of the Financial Year. At the time of availment of loan exchange rate was ₹56 per US $ and the rate as on 31st March, 2023 was ₹62 per US $. If Omega Limited had borrowed the loan in India in Indian Rupee equivalent, the pricing of loan would have been 10.50%.

You are required to compute Borrowing Cost and exchange difference for the year ending 31st March, 2023 as per applicable Accounting Standards.
answer_html:
1. Interest for the period 2022-23 = US $10 lakhs × 4% × ₹62 per US$ = ₹24.80 lakhs
  2. Increase in the liability towards the principal amount = US $10 lakhs × ₹(62 − 56) = ₹60 lakhs
  3. Interest that would have resulted if the loan was taken in Indian currency = US $10 lakhs × ₹56 × 10.5% = ₹58.80 lakhs
  4. Difference between interest on local currency borrowing and foreign currency borrowing = ₹58.80 lakhs − ₹24.80 lakhs = ₹34 lakhs.

Therefore, out of ₹60 lakhs increase in the liability towards principal amount, only ₹34 lakhs will be considered as the borrowing cost. Thus, total borrowing cost would be ₹58.80 lakhs being the aggregate of interest of ₹24.80 lakhs on foreign currency borrowings plus the exchange difference to the extent of difference between interest on local currency borrowing and interest on foreign currency borrowing of ₹34 lakhs.

Hence, ₹58.80 lakhs would be considered as the borrowing cost to be accounted for as per AS 16 and the remaining ₹26 lakhs (60 − 34) would be considered as the exchange difference to be accounted for as per AS 11.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating the entire ₹60 lakh increase in the rupee liability as either wholly a borrowing cost under AS 16 or wholly an exchange difference under AS 11, instead of splitting it at the interest-rate-differential figure of ₹34 lakhs.
chapter_label: AS 11: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates

topic_text: Topic 3.3/3.4: Measurement of a foreign-currency monetary payable at the transaction/settlement exchange rate, compared under two settlement options
question_html:
Trower Limited is an Indian importer. It imports goods from True View Limited situated at London. Trower Limited has a payable of £50,000 to True View Limited as on 31st March, 2023. True View Limited has given Trower Limited the following two options:

(i) Pay immediately with a cash discount of 1% on the payable.
(ii) Pay after 6 months with interest @ 5% p.a. on the payable.

The borrowing rate for Trower Limited in rupees is 15% p.a.

The following are the exchange rates:

Date₹/£
31st March, 202397
30th September, 202399

You are required to give your opinion to Trower Limited on which of the above two options to be chosen. (5 Marks)
answer_html:
Option (i) Pay immediately with Cash discount of 1% on the payable

₹
Total amount payable as on 31.3.2023 (50,000 × ₹97)48,50,000
Less: Cash discount(48,500)
(subtotal)48,01,500
Add: Borrowing cost @ 15% p.a. for 6 months3,60,112.50
If payment made immediate51,61,612.50

Option (ii) Pay after 6 months with interest @ 5% p.a. on the payable

₹
Total amount payable as on 31.3.2023 (50,000 × ₹99)49,50,000
Interest for 6 months @ 5%1,23,750
If payment made after 6 months50,73,750

Thus, Option (ii) is beneficial to Trower Limited as the Rupee outflow will be lower by ₹(51,61,612 − 50,73,750) = ₹87,862 in option (ii).

Option (ii): 50,000 + interest for 6 months @5% (50,000×5/100×6/12=1,250) = 51,250 units × ₹99 = ₹50,73,750. Same conclusion.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A significant number of examinees omitted the notional borrowing cost of paying immediately (interest on funds foregone at the company's own 15% p.a. rate) when comparing the two options, effectively comparing only the cash discount against the deferred interest without placing both options on a common date. This led many to conclude that immediate payment was cheaper, missing that Trower Limited's own high borrowing rate outweighs the 1% cash discount once time value is properly reflected.

topic_text: Topic 3.13: Para 46A option - exchange difference on foreign-currency loan capitalised to a depreciable asset, or accumulated in FCMITD if not asset-linked
question_html:
ABC Ltd, borrowed 10,000 US $ in foreign currency on 1st April, 2025 at 6% p.a. annual interest and acquired a depreciable asset. Exchange rates: 01-04-2025 ₹85.00/US$; 31-03-2026 ₹90.00/US$. (Assume interest accrued on 31st March, 2026 is paid on the same date.)

You are required to: (i) Pass the journal entries in case the option under Para 46A of AS 11 is availed by the company. (ii) Explain the difference in treatment of exchange difference if Para 46A of AS 11 is not availed. (iii) Would your answer be different regarding treatment of exchange difference if the loan was taken to finance the operations of the entity, not to procure a depreciable asset, and option under Para 46A of AS 11 is availed by the company? (4 Marks)
answer_html:
(i) Option under Para 46A availed – Journal Entries in the Books of ABC Ltd.:

2025 Apr. 01Bank Account (10,000×85) Dr.
  To Foreign Loan Account		8,50,0008,50,000
2026 Mar 31Finance Cost (USD 10,000×6%×₹90) Dr.
  To Bank Account		54,00054,000
2026 Mar 31Foreign Exchange Difference Account Dr.
  To Foreign Loan Account [10,000×(90−85)]		50,00050,000
2026 Mar 31Property, Plant and Equipment Dr.
  To Foreign Exchange Difference Account		50,00050,000

Since the option under Para 46A is availed, the Exchange Loss of ₹50,000 is capitalized in the cost of PPE, indirectly recognized in the P&L by way of increased depreciation over the remaining useful life of the asset.

(ii) If Para 46A is NOT availed: the Exchange Loss of ₹50,000 is recognised as an expense in the Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ending 31 March 2026 instead.

(iii) If the loan financed operations (not a depreciable asset) and Para 46A is availed: the Exchange Loss of ₹50,000 is accumulated in the FCMITD A/c, subsequently spread over and debited to P&L over the tenure of the loan (since there is no qualifying asset to capitalise it against).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees applied the same asset-capitalisation treatment to part (iii) as part (i), not recognising that Para 46A's asset-linked capitalisation route is only available when the borrowing financed a depreciable asset; where it instead financed operations, the FCMITD accumulation-and-amortisation route applies.

topic_text: Topic 3.3/3.4/3.5: Trade payable/receivable restated at closing rate vs. a non-monetary asset (plant, settled same day) held at transaction-date rate; exchange gain/loss recognised on each outstanding monetary item

answer_html:
As per AS 11 “The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates”, Foreign currency monetary items should be reported using the closing rate. Non-monetary items which are carried in terms of historical cost denominated in a foreign currency should be reported using the exchange rate at the date of the transaction. Exchange differences arising on the settlement of monetary items or on reporting an enterprise’s monetary items at rates different from those at which they were initially recorded during the period, or reported in previous financial statements, should be recognised as income or as expenses in the period in which they arise.

Some examinees also computed the exchange gain/loss by comparing the transaction-date rupee value to the closing-rate rupee value directly rather than isolating the per-unit rate movement on the outstanding foreign-currency amount, occasionally producing the correct final figure by an incorrect method.
