topic_text: Topic 3.4: Monetary items restated at the closing rate at each balance sheet date; the resulting exchange difference goes to profit and loss, never adjusted against the non-monetary cost already recorded
question_html:
Bansal Company Ltd. imported raw material worth US Dollars 12,000 on 15th January, 2024 when the exchange rate was ₹68 per US Dollar. The payment for the transaction was made on 5th May, 2024 when exchange rate was ₹64 per US Dollar. At the year end, 31st March, 2024, the rate of exchange was ₹65 per US Dollar. The accountant of the company passed entry on 31st March, 2024 adjusting the cost of raw material consumed for the difference between ₹64 and ₹68 per US Dollar.

Discuss whether this treatment is justified as per the provisions of AS-11 (Revised).
answer_html:
As per AS 11, "The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates", initial recognition of a foreign currency transaction is done in the reporting currency by applying the exchange rate at the date of the transaction. Accordingly, on 15th January, 2024, the raw material purchased and its creditors will be recorded at US dollar 12,000 × ₹68 = ₹8,16,000.

Also, on balance sheet date such transaction is reported at closing rate of exchange, hence it will be valued at the closing rate i.e. ₹65 per US dollar (USD 12,000 × ₹65 = ₹7,80,000) at 31st March, 2024, irrespective of the payment made for the same subsequently at a lower rate in the next financial year.

The difference of ₹3 (65 − 68) per US dollar i.e. ₹36,000 (USD 12,000 × ₹3) will be shown as an exchange gain in the profit and loss account for the year ended 31st March, 2024 and will not be adjusted against the cost of raw materials.

In the subsequent year on settlement date, the company would recognize or provide in the Profit and Loss account an exchange gain of ₹1 per US dollar, i.e. the difference from balance sheet date to the date of settlement between ₹65 and ₹64 per US dollar i.e. ₹12,000.

Hence, the accounting treatment adopted by the Accountant of the company is incorrect i.e. it is not in accordance with the provisions of AS 11.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is adjusting the cost of raw material consumed for the exchange difference between the transaction-date and settlement-date rates, missing that AS 11 requires monetary items to be restated at the closing rate at each balance sheet date, with the resulting exchange difference recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss, not adjusted against the non-monetary cost of raw material already recorded.
chapter_label: AS 11: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates

topic_text: Topic 3.5: Para 46A option to capitalise exchange differences on long-term foreign-currency monetary items into a depreciable asset's cost
question_html:
Legal Ltd. is engaged in the manufacturing of rubber. For its plant, it required machineries of latest technology. It usually resorts to Long Term Foreign Currency Borrowings for its fund requirements. On 1st April, 2023, it borrowed US $1 million from International Funding Agency, USA when the exchange rate was 1$ = ₹63. The funds were used for acquiring machineries, on the same date, to be used in three different plants. The useful life of the machineries is 10 years and their residual value is ₹30,00,000.

Earlier also the company used to purchase machineries out of foreign borrowings. The exchange differences arising on such borrowings were charged to profit and loss account and were not capitalized, even though the company had an option to capitalize it as per notified AS 11.

Now for this new purchase of machinery, Legal Ltd. is interested to avail the option of capitalizing the same to the cost of asset. Exchange rate on 31st March, 2024 is 1 US$ = ₹62. Assume that on 31st March, 2024, Legal Ltd. is not having any old long term foreign currency borrowings except for the amount borrowed for machinery purchased on 1st April, 2023.

Comment whether Legal Ltd. can capitalize the exchange difference to the cost of asset on 31st March, 2024. If yes, then calculate the depreciation amount on machineries as on 31st March, 2024.
answer_html:
As per paragraph 46A of AS 11, in respect of accounting periods commencing on or after 1st April, 2011, an enterprise (whether or not it had earlier exercised the option under paragraph 46, the option being irrevocable and applied to all such foreign currency monetary items) may add to or deduct from the cost of a depreciable capital asset the exchange differences arising on reporting long-term foreign currency monetary items relating to its acquisition, and depreciate this over the balance life of the asset.

Accordingly, though Legal Ltd. had not earlier exercised the option, it can still avail the option to capitalize the exchange difference to the cost of machinery by virtue of para 46A of AS 11. Further, since Legal Ltd. has no other long term foreign currency borrowings, it is not required to apply the capitalization option to any earlier borrowing.

Exchange difference to be capitalized and depreciation amount₹
Cost of the asset in $ (1 million); Exchange rate on 1st April, 2023 (₹63 = $1)—
Cost of the asset in ₹ (1 million × ₹63)63 million
Less: Exchange difference as on 31st March, 2024 – (63−62) × $1 million (Gain)(1 million)
Revised cost of asset62 million
Less: Depreciation for 2023-2024 – (62 million − 3 million) / 10 years(5.90 million)
Carrying amount as on 31st March, 202456.10 million
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is assuming the para 46A option is unavailable to Legal Ltd. because it never exercised it in earlier years, missing that the option is available for this new borrowing on its own facts, since Legal Ltd. has no other long-term foreign-currency borrowings that would otherwise force the irrevocable-election issue.
chapter_label: AS 11: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates

topic_text: Topic 3.5: Exchange differences on restatement/repayment of a long-term foreign-currency loan financing PPE, capitalised into the asset's carrying amount
question_html: Alfa Ltd. purchased an item of property, plant and equipment for US $ 50 lakh on 01.04.2023 and the same was fully financed by the foreign currency loan [i.e. US $] repayment in five equal instalments annually. (Exchange rate at the time of purchase was 1 US $ = ₹60]. As on 31.03.2024 the first instalment was paid when 1 US $ fetched ₹62.00. The entire loss on exchange was included in cost of goods sold. Alfa Ltd. normally provides depreciation on an item of property, plant and equipment at 20% on WDV basis and exercised the option to adjust the cost of asset for exchange difference arising out of loan restatement and payment. Calculate the amount of exchange loss and its treatment and depreciation.
answer_html:
Exchange differences arising on restatement or repayment of liabilities incurred for the purpose of acquiring an item of property, plant and equipment should be adjusted in the carrying amount of the respective item of property, plant and equipment as Alfa Ltd. has exercised the option and it is long term foreign currency monetary item.

Thus, the entire exchange loss due to variation of ₹20 lakh on 31.03.2023 on payment of US $ 10 lakh, should be added to the carrying amount of an item of property, plant and equipment and not to the cost of goods sold. Further, depreciation on the unamortized depreciable amount should also be provided.

Calculation of Exchange loss:

Foreign currency loan (in ₹) = (50 lakh $ × ₹60) = ₹3,000 lakh

Exchange loss on outstanding loan on 31.03.2024 = ₹40 lakh US $ × (62.00−60.00) = ₹80 lakh.

So, ₹80 lakh should also be added to cost of an item of property, plant and equipment with corresponding credit to outstanding loan in addition to ₹20 lakh on account of exchange loss on payment of instalment. The total cost of an item of property, plant and equipment to be increased by ₹100 lakh.

Total depreciation to be provided for the year 2023-2024 = 20% of (₹3,000 lakh + 100 lakh) = ₹620 lakh.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is leaving the exchange loss in the cost of goods sold (as the company's own initial treatment had done) rather than capitalising it into the carrying amount of the property, plant and equipment once the long-term-monetary-item option has been exercised, and consequently missing the resulting increase in the depreciation charge.
chapter_label: AS 11: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Conditions for recognising revenue on sale of goods - delayed delivery at buyer's request still recognised if buyer accepts billing and goods are ready
question_html: Indicate in each case whether revenue can be recognized and when it will be recognized as per AS-9. (1) Trade discount and volume rebate received. (2) Where goods are sold to distributors or others for resale. (3) Where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date. (4) Insurance agency commission for rendering services. (5) On 11-03-2024 cloths worth ₹50,000 were sold to X mart, but due to refurbishing of their showroom being underway, on their request, clothes were delivered on 12-04-2024.
answer_html:
1. Trade discounts and volume rebates received are not encompassed within the definition of revenue, since they represent a reduction of cost. Trade discounts and volume rebates given should be deducted in determining revenue.
  2. When goods are sold to distributor or others, revenue from such sales can generally be recognized if significant risks of ownership have passed; however, in some situations the buyer may in substance be an agent and in such cases the sale should be treated as a consignment sale.
  3. For transactions, where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date that are in substance a financing agreement, the resulting cash inflow is not revenue as defined and should not be recognized as revenue.
  4. Insurance agency commissions should be recognized on the effective commencement or renewal dates of the related policies.
  5. On 11.03.2024, if X mart takes title and accepts billing for the goods then it is implied that the sale is complete and all risk and reward on ownership has been transferred to the buyers. Revenue should be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2024 notwithstanding that physical delivery has not been completed so long as there is every expectation that delivery will be made and items were ready for delivery to the buyer at the time.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is recognising revenue on the physical delivery date rather than the date the buyer accepted billing with goods ready for delivery, or failing to identify a sale-with-repurchase arrangement as a financing transaction rather than a sale.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Revenue recognition timing across five distinct transaction types - approval-basis sale, delayed delivery, sale-repurchase, interest/royalty, consignment
question_html: Given the following information of Rainbow Ltd., you are required to advise, with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue under the provisions of AS-9: (i) On 15th November, goods worth ₹5,00,000 were sold on approval basis. The period of approval was 4 months after which they were considered sold. Buyer sent approval for 75% goods sold upto 31st January and no approval or disapproval received for the remaining goods till 31st March. (ii) On 31st March, goods worth ₹2,40,000 were sold to Bright Ltd. but due to refurnishing of their show-room being underway, on their request, goods were delivered on 10th April. (iii) Rainbow Ltd. supplied goods worth ₹6,00,000 to Shyam Ltd. and concurrently agrees to re-purchase the same goods on 14th April. (iv) Dew Ltd, used certain assets of Rainbow Ltd. Rainbow Ltd. received ₹7.5 lakhs and ₹12 as interest and royalties respectively from Dew Ltd. during the year 2023-24. (v) On 25th December, goods of ₹4,00,000 were sent on consignment basis of which 40% of the goods unsold are lying with the consignee at the year-end on 31st March.
answer_html:
1. As per AS 9 "Revenue Recognition", in case of goods sold on approval basis, revenue should not be recognized until the goods have been formally accepted by the buyer or the buyer has done an act adopting the transaction or the time period for rejection has elapsed or where no time has been fixed, a reasonable time has elapsed. Therefore, revenue should be recognized for the total sales amounting ₹5,00,000 as the time period for rejecting the goods had expired.
  2. The sale is complete but delivery has been postponed at buyer's request. The entity should recognize the entire sale of ₹2,40,000 for the year ended 31st March.
  3. Sale/repurchase agreements i.e. where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date, such transactions that are in substance a financing agreement, the resulting cash inflow is not revenue as defined and should not be recognized as revenue. Hence no revenue to be recognized in the given case.
  4. Revenue arising from the use by others of enterprise resources yielding interest and royalty should be recognized when no significant uncertainty as to measurability or collectability exists. The interest should be recognized on time proportion basis taking into account the amount outstanding and rate applicable. The royalty should be recognized on accrual basis in accordance with the terms of relevant agreement.
  5. 40% goods lying unsold with consignee should be treated as closing inventory and sales should be recognized for ₹2,40,000 (60% of ₹4,00,000). In case of consignment sale revenue should not be recognized until the goods are sold to a third party.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating goods sold on approval as sold immediately at the point of delivery instead of waiting for buyer acceptance or expiry of the approval period, and separately, recognising revenue on a sale-and-repurchase arrangement instead of identifying it as a financing transaction outside the scope of AS 9 revenue.

topic_text: Topic 1.6: Revenue recognition timing across five distinct transaction types
question_html: Indicate in each case whether revenue can be recognized and when, as per AS-9: (i) Delivery is delayed at buyer's request but buyer takes title and accepts billing. (ii) Instalment Sales. (iii) Trade discounts and volume rebates. (iv) Insurance agency commission for rendering services. (v) Advertising commission.
answer_html:
(i) Revenue is recognised notwithstanding the delayed physical delivery, so long as delivery is expected and the goods are on hand, identified, and ready for delivery at the time of sale recognition (not merely an intention to acquire/manufacture in time).

(ii) When consideration is receivable in instalments, revenue attributable to the sale price (excluding interest) is recognised at the date of sale; the interest element is recognised as revenue proportionately to the unpaid balance.

(iii) Trade discounts and volume rebates received are not revenue (they reduce cost); those given are deducted in determining revenue.

(iv) Insurance agency commissions are recognised on the effective commencement or renewal dates of the related policies.

(v) Advertising commission is recognised when the service is completed — media commission when the advertisement appears before the public (with the agency's intimation received); production commission when the project is completed.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees deferred revenue on the delayed-delivery sale entirely, missing that the goods being on-hand and ready is what matters, not the physical transfer date itself.

topic_text: Topic 2.7: Income from other sources - interest on a time-proportion basis, royalties on an accrual basis per the agreement
question_html: Y Ltd. used certain resources of X Ltd. In return X Ltd. received ₹10 lakhs and ₹15 lakhs as interest and royalties respectively from Y Ltd. during the year 2022-23. You are required to state whether and on what basis these revenues can be recognized by X Ltd.
answer_html: As per AS 9 on Revenue Recognition, revenue arising from the use by others of enterprise resources yielding interest and royalties should only be recognized when no significant uncertainty as to measurability or collectability exists. These revenues are recognized on the following bases: (i) Interest: on a time proportion basis taking into account the amount outstanding and the rate applicable. Therefore X Ltd. should recognize interest revenue of ₹10 Lakhs. (ii) Royalties: on an accrual basis in accordance with the terms of the relevant agreement. X Ltd. therefore should recognize royalty revenue of ₹15 Lakhs.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is applying the same recognition basis to both interest and royalty income, when AS 9 prescribes two distinct bases — time-proportion for interest, accrual per the agreement's terms for royalties.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Five specific-scenario tests for revenue recognition timing
question_html:
Indicate in each case whether revenue can be recognized and when it will be recognized as per AS-9.

  1. Trade discount and volume rebate received.
  2. Where goods are sold to distributors or others for resale.
  3. Where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date.
  4. Insurance agency commission for rendering services.
  5. On 11-03-2024 cloths worth ₹50,000 were sold to X mart, but due to refurbishing of their showroom being underway, on their request, clothes were delivered on 12-04-2024.
answer_html:
1. Trade discounts and volume rebates received are not encompassed within the definition of revenue, since they represent a reduction of cost. Trade discounts and volume rebates given should be deducted in determining revenue.
  2. When goods are sold to distributor or others, revenue from such sales can generally be recognized if significant risks of ownership have passed; however, in some situations the buyer may in substance be an agent and in such cases the sale should be treated as a consignment sale.
  3. For transactions, where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date that are in substance a financing agreement, the resulting cash inflow is not revenue as defined and should not be recognized as revenue.
  4. Insurance agency commissions should be recognized on the effective commencement or renewal dates of the related policies.
  5. On 11.03.2024, if X mart takes title and accepts billing for the goods then it is implied that the sale is complete and all risk and reward on ownership has been transferred to the buyers. Revenue should be recognized for year ended 31st March, 2024 notwithstanding that physical delivery has not been completed so long as there is every expectation that delivery will be made and items were ready for delivery to the buyer at the time.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is treating a sale to a distributor for resale, or a delayed-delivery sale made at the buyer's own request, as ineligible for revenue recognition, without checking whether the substantive risk-and-reward transfer conditions have actually been met.

topic_text: Topic 1.4: Trade discounts deducted from revenue, regardless of the reason for the discount
question_html: AB Limited purchased goods on credit from XY Limited for ₹150 lakhs for export. The export order was cancelled; AB Limited decided to sell the same goods locally with a price discount. XY Limited agreed to a 12% price discount requested by AB Limited. XY's chief accountant wants to adjust the sales figure to the extent of the discount. Discuss whether this treatment is as per the relevant Accounting Standard.
answer_html: Correct. Per AS 9, trade discounts given should be deducted in determining revenue. The 12% discount should be deducted from the turnover figure for revenue recognition purposes — XY Limited's adjustment of the sales figure to the extent of the discount is correct as per AS 9.
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: The responses of examinees to the requirements of AS 9 "Revenue Recognition" were unsatisfactory. Many were unable to correctly comment on the treatment of the four independent situations provided in the question, indicating inadequate conceptual clarity on timing and basis of revenue recognition.

topic_text: Topic 1.5: Dividend income recognised only when the right to receive payment is established (declaration, not mere proposal)
question_html: XY Limited recognized dividend income of ₹10 lakhs on accrual basis on securities of face value ₹100 lakhs held at 31st March 2025. The dividend (10%) was declared on 30th April 2025, having been proposed on 30th March 2025. Comment.
answer_html: Incorrect. Dividends from investments in securities are not recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss until the right to receive payment is established. Here, the dividend is proposed 30th March 2025 but declared only 30th April 2025 — the right to receive payment is established only on 30th April 2025. Recognising ₹10 lakhs on accrual basis at 31st March 2025 is not correct as per AS 9.
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: The responses of examinees to the requirements of AS 9 "Revenue Recognition" were unsatisfactory. Many were unable to correctly comment on the treatment of the four independent situations provided in the question, indicating inadequate conceptual clarity on timing and basis of revenue recognition.

topic_text: Topic 1.6: Sale on approval - revenue recognised on acceptance or expiry of the approval period, not at dispatch
question_html: XY Limited sold goods of ₹1,50,000 on approval basis on 15th December 2024; approval period 3 months, after which goods are considered sold. Buyer approved 60% of goods by 31st January 2025; no approval/disapproval received for the remainder by 31st March 2025. The accountant recognised ₹1,50,000 as revenue on 15th December, 2024. Comment.
answer_html: Incorrect as recognised. For goods sold on approval, revenue should not be recognised until formal acceptance, an act adopting the transaction, or expiry of the rejection period. Revenue for ₹90,000 (60%) should be recognised on 31st January, 2025 (date of approval); the remaining ₹60,000 should be recognised on 15th March, 2025, when the 3-month approval period lapsed without response (deemed acceptance) — not the full ₹1,50,000 on 15th December, 2024 as the accountant did.
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: The responses of examinees to the requirements of AS 9 "Revenue Recognition" were unsatisfactory. Many were unable to correctly comment on the treatment of the four independent situations provided in the question, indicating inadequate conceptual clarity on timing and basis of revenue recognition.

topic_text: Topic 1.7: Consignment sales - revenue recognised only when the consignee sells to a third party
question_html: In 2024-2025, XY Limited supplied goods worth ₹80,000 on consignment basis to ABC (a retail outlet). ABC sold goods worth ₹60,000 during the year; the rest remains in its store. XY recognizes ₹60,000 revenue in its books for 2024-2025. Comment.
answer_html: Correct. Unsold consignment goods (₹20,000) remain XY Limited's closing inventory; revenue on a consignment sale is recognised only when the goods are sold to a third party by the consignee. XY's recognition of ₹60,000 revenue is correct as per AS 9.
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: The responses of examinees to the requirements of AS 9 "Revenue Recognition" were unsatisfactory. Many were unable to correctly comment on the treatment of the four independent situations provided in the question, indicating inadequate conceptual clarity on timing and basis of revenue recognition.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Sale and repurchase arrangement with a pre-determined, holding-cost-covering resale price is accounted for as financing, not a sale
question_html: Mithya Ltd. entered into agreement with Satya Ltd. for sale of goods costing ₹8 lakh at a profit of 20% on cost. The sale transaction took place on 1st February, 2024. On the same day, Satya Ltd. entered into another agreement with Mithya Ltd. to resell the same goods at ₹10.80 lakh on 1st August, 2024. State the treatment of this transaction in the financial statements of Mithya Ltd. as on 31.03.2024. The predetermined re-selling price covers the holding cost of Satya Ltd. Give the Journal Entries as on 31.03.2024 in the books of Mithya Ltd.
answer_html:
In the given case, Mithya Ltd. concurrently agreed to repurchase the same goods from Satya Ltd. on 1st February, 2024. Also the re-selling price is pre-determined and covers purchasing and holding costs of Satya Ltd. Hence, the transaction between Mithya Ltd. and Satya Ltd. on 1st February, 2024 should be accounted for as financing rather than sale. The resulting cash flow of ₹9.60 lakh received by Mithya Ltd. cannot be considered as revenue as per AS 9 "Revenue Recognition".

Journal Entries in the books of Mithya Ltd. (₹ in lakh)

DateParticularsDr.Cr.
1.2.2024Bank Account Dr. To Advance from Satya Ltd. (Being advance received from Satya Ltd. amounting [₹8 lakh + 20% of ₹8 lakh = 9.60 lakh] under sale and re-purchase agreement)9.609.60
31.3.2024Financing Charges Account Dr. To Satya Ltd. (Financing charges for 2 months [(10.80 − 9.60) × 2/6])0.400.40
31.3.2024Profit and Loss Account Dr. To Financing Charges Account (Being amount of finance charges transferred to P&L Account)0.400.40

Note: the balance of Satya Ltd.'s account will be disclosed as an advance under the heading liabilities in the balance sheet of Mithya Ltd. as on 31st March, 2024.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is recognising the ₹9.60 lakh received by Mithya Ltd. as sale revenue, missing that a concurrent agreement to repurchase the same goods at a pre-determined price covering the buyer's holding cost converts the arrangement into a financing transaction under AS 9, not a genuine sale.

topic_text: Topic 1.2: Property sale by a real-estate dealer is ordinary-activity revenue, not extraordinary, even at unusual scale
question_html: Class Ltd., a real-estate developer, purchased land for ₹225 crore in FY2025 intending a residential complex, then sold it a few months later for ₹360 crore due to a strategic reallocation and favourable market conditions. All legal formalities completed. Advise on revenue recognition for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
answer_html:
AS 9 recognises revenue when earned with reasonable certainty of collection, arising from the enterprise's ordinary activities. Class Ltd. is in the business of buying and selling properties; the land forms part of its inventory. The ₹360 crore sale is therefore a transaction arising from ordinary activities, and revenue is recognised when the sale is completed and collection is reasonably certain.

Per AS 5, this is not an extraordinary item, since it arises in the ordinary course of business — though given its size, its nature and amount should be separately disclosed if relevant to explaining the enterprise's performance. The ₹360 crore is recognised as revenue in the year the sale is completed.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees treated the large, unusual sale as an extraordinary item given its size and the company's stated change in strategy, missing that dealing in land is Class Ltd.'s core ordinary business, so scale alone does not make a transaction extraordinary.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Revenue recognised where the sale is complete and only physical delivery is postponed at the buyer's own request, buyer having accepted billing
question_html: Goods of ₹2,00,000 sold to Den Ltd. on 20-03-2023 but at the request of the buyer these were delivered on 10-04-2023. You are required to advise the accountant of BS Products Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue in this case in the context of AS 9.
answer_html: The sale is complete, but delivery has been postponed at buyer's request. BS Products Ltd. should recognize the entire sale of ₹2,00,000 for the year ended 31st March, 2023.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is deferring revenue recognition to the actual delivery date, missing that the sale itself was already complete and delivery was postponed purely at the buyer's own request.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Consignment sale - revenue recognised only on sale by the consignee to a third party; unsold consignment goods remain closing inventory
question_html: On 15-01-2023 goods of ₹3,00,000 were sent on consignment basis, of which 20% of the goods unsold are lying with the consignee as on 31-03-2023. You are required to advise the accountant of BS Products Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue in this case in the context of AS 9.
answer_html: 20% goods lying unsold with consignee should be treated as closing inventory and sales should be recognized for ₹2,40,000 (80% of ₹3,00,000). In the case of consignment sale revenue should not be recognized until the goods are sold to a third party.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is recognising the full ₹3,00,000 as revenue on the date goods are sent on consignment, treating dispatch to the consignee as equivalent to a sale to the end customer.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Sale on approval basis - revenue recognised once formally accepted, an adopting act occurs, or the approval/rejection period has elapsed, whichever governs
question_html: ₹4,00,000 worth of goods were sold on approval basis on 01-12-2022. The period of approval was 3 months after which they were considered as sold. Buyer sent approval for 75% goods upto 31-01-2023 and no approval or disapproval received for the remaining goods till 31-03-2023. You are required to advise the accountant of BS Products Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue in this case in the context of AS 9.
answer_html: In case of goods sold on approval basis, revenue should not be recognized until the goods have been formally accepted by the buyer or the buyer has done an act adopting the transaction or the time period for rejection has elapsed or where no time has been fixed, a reasonable time has elapsed. Therefore, revenue should be recognized for the total sales amounting to ₹4,00,000 as the time period for rejecting the goods had expired.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is recognising revenue only for the 75% expressly approved by the buyer and continuing to treat the remaining 25% as unsold, missing that the stated 3-month approval period had already lapsed for that portion by the year end, which itself triggers recognition.

topic_text: Topic 2.9: Effect of collection uncertainty on revenue recognition - recognised only to the extent collection is reasonably certain, based on past collection experience
question_html: Apart from the above, BS Products Ltd. sells goods to dealers also. One of the conditions of sale is that interest is payable @ 2% p.m. for delayed payments by dealers. The percentage of interest recovery is only 10% i.e. ₹50,000 on such overdue outstanding due to various reasons. During the year 2022-23, the company wants to recognize the entire interest receivable of ₹60,000. You are required to advise the accountant of BS Products Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue in this case in the context of AS 9, and also determine the total revenue to be recognized for the year ending 31-03-2023.
answer_html:
As per the standard, "where the ability to assess the ultimate collection with reasonable certainty is lacking at the time of raising any claim, the revenue recognition is postponed to the extent of uncertainty involved. In such cases, the revenue is recognized only when it is reasonably certain that the ultimate collection will be made". In this case, interest should be recognized only if the ultimate collection is certain and the company expects to realize interest for the delayed payments for ₹50,000 only. Hence, based on the past experience, the realization of interest for the delayed payments by the agent is certain only to the extent of this amount and not ₹60,000. Therefore, the interest income of ₹50,000 should be recognized in the books for the year ended 31st March, 2023.

Thus, total revenue amounting ₹8,90,000 (2,00,000 + 2,40,000 + 4,00,000 + 50,000) will be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2023 in the books of BS Products Ltd.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is recognising the full contractually-computed interest of ₹60,000 rather than limiting recognition to the ₹50,000 actually supported by past collection experience, and separately failing to aggregate all four cases into the single total revenue figure the question asks for.

topic_text: Topic 2.8: Revenue-recognition timing across delayed delivery, consignment sale, and sale-on-approval scenarios
question_html:
Given below are the following information of B.S. Ltd.:

  1. Goods of ₹50,000 were sold on 18-03-2024 but at the request of the buyer these were delivered on 15-04-2024.
  2. On 13-01-2024 goods of ₹1,25,000 are sent on consignment basis, of which 20% of the goods unsold are lying with the consignee as on 31-03-2024.
  3. ₹1,00,000 worth of goods were sold on approval basis on 01-12-2023. The period of approval was 3 months after which they were considered sold. Buyer sent approval for 75% goods up to 31-01-2024 and no approval or disapproval received for the remaining goods till 31-03-2024.

You are required to advise the accountant of B.S. Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue for the year ended 31st March, 2024 in the above cases in the context of AS-9.
answer_html:
As per AS 9 'Revenue Recognition', in a transaction involving the sale of goods, performance should be regarded as being achieved when: (a) the seller has transferred to the buyer the property in the goods for a price, or all significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred and the seller retains no effective control of the goods to a degree usually associated with ownership; and (b) no significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of consideration to be derived from the sale.

Case (i): The sale is complete but delivery has been postponed at the buyer's request. B.S. Ltd. should recognize the entire sale of ₹50,000 for the year ended 31st March, 2024.

Case (ii): In case of a consignment sale, revenue should not be recognized until the goods are sold by the consignee to a third party. The 20% of goods lying unsold with the consignee should be treated as closing inventory, and sales should be recognized for ₹1,00,000 (80% of ₹1,25,000).

Case (iii): In case of goods sold on approval basis, revenue should not be recognized until the goods have been formally accepted by the buyer, or the buyer has done an act adopting the transaction, or the time period for rejection has elapsed (or, where no time has been fixed, a reasonable time has elapsed). Since the 3-month approval period had already expired by 31st March, 2024, revenue should be recognized for the full ₹1,00,000 (including the portion neither approved nor disapproved, since the approval window itself had lapsed).

Thus, total revenue amounting to ₹2,50,000 (50,000 + 1,00,000 + 1,00,000) will be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2024 in the books of B.S. Ltd.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error in case (iii) is withholding revenue recognition on the un-responded-to 25% of goods on the reasoning that no explicit acceptance was received, missing that AS 9 treats the mere expiry of the stated rejection period as itself sufficient for revenue recognition, with no separate acceptance needed.

topic_text: Topic 2.2: No revenue recognized on inter-divisional transfers since risks/rewards remain within the enterprise and there is no external consideration
question_html: When will the revenue be recognized in the case of inter divisional transfers?
answer_html: The Accounting Standard Board of ICAI has come up with an announcement in the earlier years wherein it clarified that the inter-divisional transfers/sales are not revenue as per AS 9 "Revenue Recognition". According to it, in case of inter-divisional transfers, risks and rewards remain within the enterprise and also there is no consideration from the point of view of the enterprise as a whole. Therefore, the recognition criteria for revenue recognition are also not fulfilled in respect of inter-divisional transfers. Hence, no revenue is recognized in the case of inter-divisional transfers.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating an inter-divisional transfer priced at a notional transfer price as genuine revenue, without recognising that the enterprise as a whole has not transacted with any outside party.

topic_text: Topic 1.7: Consignment sales - revenue recognised only on the consignee's actual sale to a third party
question_html: Tonk Tanners (leather shoes): On 31st December, 2024, shoes worth ₹3,20,000 were sent to Mohan Shoes for sale on consignment; 25% remained unsold with Mohan Shoes as on 31st March, 2025. Advise when revenue is recognised in 2024-25 per AS 9.
answer_html: Mohan Shoes is a consignee (agent), not a buyer — risk and reward remain with Tonk Tanners until Mohan Shoes sells to a third party. Revenue is recognised only for the goods actually sold by the consignee: ₹3,20,000 × 75% = ₹2,40,000 recognised as revenue in 2024-25; the remaining 25% (unsold) stays as Tonk Tanners' closing inventory.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees recognised the full ₹3,20,000 upon dispatch to the consignee, treating the consignment shipment itself as a completed sale.

topic_text: Topic 1.8: Sale-and-repurchase arrangements treated as financing, not revenue
question_html: On 10th January, 2025, Tonk Tanners supplied shoes worth ₹4,50,000 to Shani Shoes and concurrently agreed to repurchase the same goods on 11th April, 2025. Advise on revenue recognition.
answer_html: A sale with a concurrent agreement to repurchase the same goods is, in substance, a financing arrangement, not a genuine sale. The resulting cash inflow is not revenue and should not be recognised as revenue in 2024-25.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees recognised the ₹4,50,000 as ordinary sales revenue, not recognising the repurchase commitment as converting the transaction into a financing arrangement in substance.

topic_text: Topic 1.4: Delivery delayed at buyer's request - revenue still recognised once title/billing acceptance occurs
question_html: On 21st March, 2025, shoes worth ₹1,60,000 were sold to Shoe Shine, but due to their showroom refurbishment, delivery was made on 12th April, 2025 at their request. Advise on revenue recognition.
answer_html: If, on 21st March 2025, Shoe Shine took title and accepted billing for the goods, the sale is complete and all risks/rewards of ownership have transferred, even though physical delivery was delayed at the buyer's own request. Provided no significant uncertainty exists over the consideration, revenue is recognised in 2024-25, regardless of the delayed physical delivery.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees deferred revenue recognition to the actual delivery date (April 2025), not recognising that title transfer and billing acceptance, not physical delivery, is what matters here.

topic_text: Topic 1.6/1.9/1.10: Percentage-of-completion method with a mid-contract variation changing total contract value and estimated cost

Constructions Limited is engaged in the business of constructing Flyovers and Railway over bridges. It obtained a contract from Railway Authorities to construct a railway over bridge for ₹400 crores. The construction of the railway over bridge is expected to be completed in 4 years.

At the outset of the contract, it was estimated that the total costs to be incurred will be ₹370 crores but by the end of year 1, this estimate stands revised to ₹375 crores.

During year 3, the Construction Limited has requested for a variation in the contract which is approved by Railway Authorities and accordingly the total contract value will increase by ₹10 crores and costs will increase by ₹7 crores.

The Constructions Limited decided to measure the stage of completion on the basis of the proportion of contract costs incurred to the total estimated contract costs. Contract costs incurred at the end of each year is: Year 1 ₹98.8 crores; Year 2 ₹202.4 crores; Year 3 ₹310 crores (including unused material of 3 crores); Year 4 ₹382 crores.

You are required to: (1) Calculate stage of completion of contract for each year; (2) Profit to be recognised for each year.

topic_text: Topic 1.6/1.9/1.10: Percentage of completion method - stage of completion via costs-incurred-to-date/total-estimated-costs, revision of contract price and cost estimates mid-contract (change in estimate), profit recognised as revenue less cost incurred each year

topic_text: Topic 1.6: Percentage of completion method - stage of completion, revenue and profit recognition, updated for a contract-price escalation clause
question_html:
Rose Constructions undertake to construct a bridge for the Government of Uttar Pradesh. The construction commenced during the financial year ending 31.03.2024 and is likely to be completed by the next financial year. The contract is for a fixed price of ₹12 crore with an escalation clause. You are given the following information for the year ended 31.03.2024:

Cost incurred upto 31.03.2024₹4 crore
Cost estimated to complete the contract₹6 crore

Escalation in cost was by 5%. Hence, the contract price is also increased by 5%.

You are required to ascertain the stage of completion and compute the amount of revenue and profit to be recognized for the year as per AS 7.
answer_html:
Cost of construction of bridge incurred upto 31.3.2024₹4.00 crore
Add: Estimated future cost₹6.00 crore
Total estimated cost of construction₹10.00 crore
Contract Price (12 crore × 1.05)₹12.60 crore

Stage of completion: Percentage of completion till date to total estimated cost of construction = (4/10)×100 = 40%.

Revenue and Profit to be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2024 as per AS 7:

Proportion of total contract value recognized as revenue = Contract price × percentage of completion = ₹12.60 crore × 40% = ₹5.04 crore.

Profit for the year ended 31st March, 2024 = ₹5.04 crore − ₹4 crore = ₹1.04 crore.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is computing the percentage of completion using the original (pre-escalation) contract price or cost estimates instead of updating both cost incurred/estimated-to-complete and contract price for the 5% escalation before applying AS 7's percentage of completion formula.

topic_text: Topic 3.4: Percentage of completion method - unused stored materials excluded from the cost-incurred-to-date figure used to measure progress
question_html: A construction contractor entered a fixed-price contract of ₹18,000 lacs to construct a bridge within 3 years, with provisions for variations. (₹ in lacs): Year 1/2/3 — Initial revenue agreed 18,000/18,000/18,000; Variation in revenue (+)400/400 (Years 2,3); Contract costs incurred to date 4,186/12,336*/16,200**; Estimated profit for whole contract 1,900/2,000/2,000. *includes ₹200 lacs standard materials stored at site for use in Year 3. **excludes ₹200 lacs standard material brought forward from Year 2. Year 2's variation was approved by the customer. Compute year-wise: revenue recognised, expenses recognised, contract costs to complete, and profit/loss recognised.
answer_html:
Working — degree of completion each year (costs incurred, excluding unused stored materials, ÷ estimated total cost): Year 1: revenue after variations 18,000, less estimated profit 1,900 = estimated total cost 16,100; actual cost incurred 4,186; degree of completion = 4,186/16,100 = 26%. Year 2: revenue 18,400, less profit 2,000 = total cost 16,400; cost incurred (excluding the ₹200 lacs stored materials not yet used) 12,336−200=12,136; degree of completion = 12,136/16,400 = 74%. Year 3: revenue 18,400, total cost 16,400; cost incurred 16,200+200 (bringing forward the previously-excluded stored material, now used) = 16,400; degree of completion 100%.

topic_text: Topic 1.3: Conditions under which one contract document covering multiple assets is treated as separate construction contracts
question_html: AP Ltd., a construction contractor, undertakes the construction of a commercial complex for Kay Ltd. AP Ltd. submitted separate proposals for each of 3 units of the commercial complex. A single agreement is entered into between the two parties. The agreement lays down the value of each of the 3 units, i.e. ₹50 Lakh, ₹60 Lakh and ₹75 Lakh respectively. The agreement also lays down the completion time for each unit. Comment, with reference to AS-7, whether AP Ltd. should treat it as a single contract or three separate contracts.
answer_html:
As per AS 7 'Construction Contracts', when a contract covers a number of assets, the construction of each asset should be treated as a separate construction contract when: (a) separate proposals have been submitted for each asset; (b) each asset has been subject to separate negotiation and the contractor and customer have been able to accept or reject that part of the contract relating to each asset; and (c) the costs and revenues of each asset can be identified.

In the given case, AP Ltd. submitted separate proposals for each of the 3 units, the agreement lays down a separate value and separate completion time for each unit, and the costs/revenues of each unit are identifiable. Therefore, AP Ltd. is required to treat the construction of each unit as a separate construction contract, as the above-mentioned conditions of AS 7 are fulfilled in the given case – notwithstanding that a single agreement document was used.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is concluding it must be a single contract simply because only one agreement document was signed, missing that AS 7 looks at the three specific conditions (separate proposals, separate negotiability, identifiable costs/revenues) rather than the number of physical documents.

topic_text: Topic 1.6: Percentage-of-completion revenue recognition together with immediate recognition of the entire foreseeable loss on a loss-making contract
question_html: On 1st December, 2023, GR Construction Co. Ltd. undertook a contract to construct a building for ₹45 lakhs. On 31st March, 2024, the company found that it had already spent ₹32.50 lakhs on the construction. Additional cost of completion is estimated at ₹15.10 lakhs. What amount should be charged to revenue in the final accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2024 as per provisions of AS-7?
answer_html:
₹ in lakhs
Cost of construction incurred till date32.50
Add: Estimated future cost15.10
Total estimated cost of construction47.60

Percentage of completion till date to total estimated cost of construction = (32.50/47.60) × 100 = 68.28%.

Proportion of total contract value recognised as revenue for the year ended 31st March, 2024 per AS 7 (Revised) = Contract price × percentage of completion = ₹45 lakh × 68.28% = ₹30.73 lakhs.

₹ in lakhs
Total cost of construction47.60
Less: Total contract price(45.00)
Total foreseeable loss to be recognized as expense2.60

According to AS 7, when it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss should be recognized as an expense immediately (in full, not spread by percentage of completion).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is recognising only the current period's proportionate share of the ₹2.60 lakh foreseeable loss (via the 68.28% completion rate) rather than the entire foreseeable loss immediately, once it becomes probable that total costs will exceed total contract revenue.

topic_text: Topic 3.5: Expected loss on a construction contract recognised immediately in full, regardless of stage of completion
question_html: A company took a construction contract for ₹100 lakhs in January 2024; 80% completed at cost ₹92 lakhs by 31.3.2025; further ₹23 lakhs estimated to complete; expected loss ₹15 lakhs. Can the company recognise the loss in the FY2024-25 financial statements?
answer_html: Yes. Per AS 7 paras 31 and 35, an expected loss on a construction contract must be recognised as an expense immediately, regardless of (i) whether work has commenced; (ii) the stage of completion; or (iii) profits expected on other contracts. The company must recognise the ₹15 lakh loss immediately in the year ended 31.3.2025.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees deferred the loss recognition to future periods or spread it across the remaining completion percentage, missing AS 7's requirement for immediate full recognition.

topic_text: Topic 1.6: Presentation of grants related to specific fixed assets - Method I (grant deducted from asset's gross value), and treatment when the deducted grant exceeds the asset's remaining book value
question_html:
D Ltd. acquired a machine on 01-04-2017 for ₹20,00,000. The useful life is 5 years. The company had applied on 01-04-2017, for a subsidy to the tune of 80% of the cost. The sanction letter for subsidy was received in November 2020. The Company's Fixed Assets Account for the financial year 2020-21 shows a credit balance as under:

Particulars₹
Machine (Original Cost)20,00,000
Less: Accumulated Depreciation (from 2017-18 to 2019-20 on Straight Line Method)12,00,000
8,00,000
Less: Grant received(16,00,000)
Balance(8,00,000)

You are required to explain how should the company deal with this asset in its accounts for 2020-21? (5 Marks)
answer_html:
From the above account, it is inferred that the Company has deducted grant from the book value of asset for accounting of Government Grants. Accordingly, out of the ₹16,00,000 that has been received, ₹8,00,000 (being the balance in Machinery A/c) should be credited to the machinery A/c.

The balance ₹8,00,000 may be credited to P&L A/c, since already the cost of the asset to the tune of ₹12,00,000 had been debited to P&L A/c in the earlier years by way of depreciation charge, and ₹8,00,000 transferred to P&L A/c now would be partial recovery of that cost.

There is no need to provide depreciation for 2020-21 or 2021-22 as the depreciable amount is now Nil.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A frequent slip is treating the entire ₹16,00,000 grant as available to write down the asset's book value below zero, without recognising that once the asset's book value is reduced to nil, the excess grant amount must instead be recognised as income (a partial recovery of the depreciation already charged in earlier years) rather than left as a negative asset balance.

topic_text: Topic 1.9: Refund of a government grant related to a specific fixed asset increases the asset's book value, depreciated prospectively
question_html: Caseworker Limited received a specific grant of ₹6 crore for acquiring the plant of ₹30 crore on 1.4.2016 having useful life of 10 years. At the beginning of the financial year 2021-2022, due to non-compliance of conditions laid down for the grant of ₹6 crore, the company had to refund the grant to the Government. What should be the treatment of the refund if grant was deducted from the cost of the plant during financial year 2016-2017? Assume depreciation is charged on fixed assets as per Straight Line Method.
answer_html:
As per AS 12, the amount refundable in respect of grant related to specific fixed assets should be recorded by increasing the book value of the asset or by reducing the capital reserve or the deferred income balance, as appropriate, by the amount refundable. Where the book value of the asset is increased, depreciation on the revised book value should be provided prospectively over the residual useful life of the asset.

Where grant was deducted from the cost of the asset, initial value of the plant after deduction of grant amount of ₹6 crore would have been = ₹30 crore − ₹6 crore = ₹24 crore.

Carrying value of the plant after 5 years on 1.4.2021 = [(₹24 crore / 10 years) × 5 years] = ₹12 crore.

Annual depreciation charge would be ₹2.4 crore.

On refund of grant to the Government, the book value of the plant shall be increased by ₹6 crore i.e. ₹12 crore + ₹6 crore = ₹18 crore. The increased cost of ₹18 crore of the plant should be amortised prospectively over remaining 5 years of useful residual life. Depreciation charge in the year 2021-2022 would be ₹18 crore / 5 years = ₹3.6 crore instead of earlier ₹2.4 crore.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is reversing the refund entry against the original grant-deduction entry retrospectively (restating prior years), rather than increasing the asset's current book value prospectively and depreciating the revised amount only over the remaining useful life.

topic_text: Topic 1.6/1.9: Refund of a grant credited to Deferred Grant Account under the deferred-income method - refund entry splitting the outstanding deferred-grant balance and the shortfall to Profit and Loss, with the related fixed asset's own carrying amount and remaining depreciation charge unaffected by the refund
question_html: Ram Ltd. purchased machinery for ₹80 lakhs (useful life 4 years and residual value ₹8 lakhs). Government grant received was ₹32 lakhs. The grant had to be refunded at the beginning of third year. Show the Journal Entry to be passed at the time of refund of grant and the value of the fixed assets in the third year and the amount of depreciation for remaining two years, if the grant had been credited to Deferred Grant A/c.
answer_html:
As per AS 12 ‘Accounting for Government Grants,’ income from Deferred Grant Account is allocated to Profit and Loss account usually over the periods and in the proportions in which depreciation on related assets is charged. Accordingly, in the first two years (₹32 lakhs /4 years) = ₹8 lakhs x 2 years = ₹16 lakhs will be credited to Profit and Loss Account and ₹16 lakhs will be the balance of Deferred Grant Account after two years. Therefore, on refund of grant, following entry will be passed:

Particulars₹₹
Deferred Grant A/cDr.16 lakhs
Profit & Loss A/cDr.16 lakhs
  To Bank A/c32 lakhs
(Being Government grant refunded)

1. Value of Fixed Assets after two years but before refund of grant

Fixed assets initially recorded in the books = ₹80 lakhs
Depreciation for each year = (₹80 lakhs − ₹8 lakhs)/4 years = ₹18 lakhs per year
Book value of fixed assets after two years = ₹80 lakhs − (₹18 lakhs x 2 years) = ₹44 lakhs

2. Value of Fixed Assets after refund of grant

On refund of grant the balance of deferred grant account will become nil. The fixed assets will continue to be shown in the books at ₹44 lakhs.

3. Amount of depreciation for remaining two years

Depreciation will continue to be charged at ₹18 lakhs per annum for the remaining two years.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is writing the refund entry entirely against the Deferred Grant Account balance without recognising that only ₹16 lakhs remains there after two years' amortisation, forcing the shortfall of ₹16 lakhs to be debited to Profit and Loss; a related error is reducing the fixed asset's own book value on refund, when AS 12 requires the asset's carrying amount and future depreciation to continue unchanged since the grant was never netted against the asset's cost under the deferred-income method.

topic_text: Topic 1.9: Refund of a government grant recognised as Deferred Grant Account and Profit and Loss, asset carrying amount unaffected
question_html: Smile Ltd. purchased machinery for ₹80 lakhs (useful life 4 years and residual value ₹8 lakhs). Government grant received was ₹32 lakhs. The grant had to be refunded at the beginning of third year. Show the Journal Entry to be passed at the time of refund of grant and the value of the fixed assets in the third year and the amount of depreciation for remaining two years, if the grant had been credited to Deferred Grant A/c.
answer_html:
As per AS 12 ‘Accounting for Government Grants’, income from a Deferred Grant Account is allocated to Profit and Loss usually over the periods and in the proportions in which depreciation on the related asset is charged. In the first two years, (₹32 lakhs/4 years) = ₹8 lakhs × 2 years = ₹16 lakhs is credited to P&L, leaving ₹16 lakhs as the balance of the Deferred Grant Account after two years. On refund of the grant:

AccountDr (₹ lakhs)Cr (₹ lakhs)
Deferred Grant A/c Dr.16
Profit & Loss A/c Dr.16
  To Bank A/c32
(Being Government grant refunded)

1. Value of fixed assets after two years but before refund of grant: initial cost ₹80 lakhs; depreciation per year = (₹80 lakhs − ₹8 lakhs)/4 years = ₹18 lakhs; book value after two years = 80 − (18×2) = ₹44 lakhs.

2. Value of fixed assets after refund of grant: on refund the Deferred Grant Account balance becomes nil, but the fixed asset continues to be shown in the books at ₹44 lakhs (unchanged — the refund does not restate the asset's carrying amount).

3. Depreciation for remaining two years: continues to be charged at ₹18 lakhs per annum for the remaining two years.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is restating the fixed asset's carrying amount upward on refund of the grant, rather than recognising that the refund is charged to the Deferred Grant Account balance and Profit and Loss, leaving the asset's carrying amount unaffected.

topic_text: Topic 1.6: Depreciation impact of the asset-deduction, deferred-income and promoter's-contribution presentation methods, including a mid-life grant refund
question_html: On 1st April 2023, Eleanor Limited purchased a manufacturing Plant for ₹60 lakhs, which has an estimated useful life of 10 years with a salvage value of ₹10 lakhs. On purchase of the Plant, a grant of ₹20 lakhs was received from the government. You are required to calculate the amount of depreciation as per AS 12 for the financial year 2024-25 in the following cases: (i) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant. (ii) If the grant is treated as deferred income. (iii) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, but at the end of the year 2024-2025 grant is refunded to the extent of ₹4 lakhs, due to non-compliance of certain conditions. (iv) If the grant is treated as the promoter's contribution. (Assume depreciation on the basis of Straight-Line Method.)
answer_html:
(i) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹3,00,000 p.a.

(ii) If the grant is treated as deferred income, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹5,00,000 p.a.

(iii) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, but at the end of the year 2024-25 grant is refunded to the extent of ₹4 lakh: depreciation for year 2023-24 remains (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹3,00,000; for the year 2024-25, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000 − ₹3,00,000) ÷ 9 years = ₹3,00,000.

Note: It is assumed that the depreciation for the year has been charged on the book value of the plant before making adjustment for the grant refund. Alternatively, if depreciation is charged after making adjustment for the grant refund, depreciation for 2024-25 will be (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000 + ₹4,00,000 − ₹3,00,000) ÷ 9 years = ₹3,44,444.

(iv) If the grant is treated as the promoter's contribution, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹5,00,000 p.a.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is treating the partial grant refund in case (iii) as a fresh transaction requiring the original 10-year schedule to be unwound, rather than simply adding the refunded amount back to the asset's remaining book value and re-spreading it over the remaining useful life.

topic_text: Topic 1.6/1.9: Four presentation methods for a fixed-asset grant (deducted from cost / deferred income / refunded / promoter's contribution) and refund treatment
question_html:
On 1st April 2021, Eleanor Limited purchased a manufacturing Plant for ₹60 lakhs, which has an estimated useful life of 10 years with a salvage value of ₹10 lakhs. On purchase of the Plant, a grant of ₹20 lakhs was received from the government.

You are required to calculate the amount of depreciation as per AS-12 for the financial year 2022-23 in the following cases: (i) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant. (ii) If the grant is treated as deferred income. (iii) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, but at the end of the year 2022-2023 grant is refunded to the extent of ₹4 lakhs, due to non-compliance of certain conditions. (iv) If the grant is treated as the promoter's contribution. (Assume depreciation on the basis of Straight-Line Method.) (5 Marks)
answer_html:
Calculation of depreciation as per AS 12 for the financial year 2022-23:

(i) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, then the amount of depreciation will be ₹3,00,000 p.a. (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000) / 10 year.

(ii) If the grant is treated as deferred income, then amount of depreciation will be ₹5,00,000 p.a. (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000) / 10 year.

(iii) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of plant, but at the end of the year 2022-23 grant is refunded to the extent of ₹4 lakh then the amount of depreciation will be ₹3,00,000 p.a. (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000) /10 year for year 2021-22 and for the year 2022-23 depreciation will be ₹3,00,000 calculated as follows, (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000 − ₹3,00,000) / 10 years.

Note: It is assumed that the depreciation for the year has been charged on the book value on the plant before making adjustment for grant. Alternatively, if it is considered otherwise then the depreciation will be charged after making adjustment for grant. In that case depreciation for the year 2022-23 will be ₹3,44,444 calculated as follows: [(₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000 + 4,00,000 − ₹3,00,000) / 9 years].

(iv) If the grant is treated as promoter's contribution, then the amount of depreciation will be ₹5,00,000 p.a. (₹60,00,000 − 10,00,000) /10 year.

topic_text: Topic 1.7: Refund of a grant previously deducted from asset cost - added back to the asset's carrying amount
question_html: Mediwell Hospitals Ltd. acquired 40 Doppler Scan Machines from Holiver Inc., USA, at US$1,65,100/unit at the start of FY2022-23, exchange rate ₹50/US$. Partly financed by a government grant of ₹5 crores (specific condition: refund on change in management/ownership control). In April 2025, 51% shareholding acquired by an overseas investor — management control changed, grant refund now due. Useful life 5 years, SLM at 20% p.a. Also: Bank charges US$4,000 (whole import), Sea freight ₹7,500/unit. No Capital Reserve or Deferred Income Account was maintained for the grant. Advise the accounting treatment for the grant refund per AS 12.
answer_html:
The grant was received towards a fixed asset; the capital (deduction-from-cost) approach was adopted (confirmed by the absence of a Capital Reserve or Deferred Income Account).

mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees expensed the refunded grant amount directly to the P&L, not applying AS 12's specific rule that a refund of a grant deducted from asset cost is added back to the carrying amount of that asset.

topic_text: Topic 1.8: Grants in the nature of promoters' contribution credited to Capital Reserve, never treated as revenue/deferred income
question_html: XYZ Limited has set-up its business in a designated backward area which entitles the company to receive from the Government of India a subsidy of 20% of the cost of investment. Having fulfilled all the conditions under the scheme, the company on its investment of ₹75 crore received ₹15 crore as subsidy from the Government in January 2024. The company wants to treat this receipt as an item of revenue and thereby reduce the losses for the year ended on 31st March, 2024. Keeping in view the relevant Accounting Standard, examine whether this action is justified or not.
answer_html:
As per para 10 of AS 12 'Accounting for Government Grants', where government grants are in the nature of promoters' contribution – i.e. they are given with reference to the total investment in an undertaking, or by way of contribution towards its total capital outlay, and no repayment is ordinarily expected in respect thereof – the grants are treated as Capital Reserve, which can be neither distributed as dividend nor considered as deferred income.

In the given case, the subsidy received (20% of the cost of investment) is neither in relation to a specific fixed asset nor in relation to revenue – it is linked to the total investment made in the backward-area undertaking. It is therefore inappropriate to recognise this government grant in the profit and loss statement, since it is not earned but represents an incentive provided by the government without related costs.

The correct treatment is to credit the ₹15 crore subsidy to Capital Reserve. Therefore, the accounting treatment (treating it as revenue to reduce the reported loss) followed by the company is not proper.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating any cash subsidy received as revenue income by default, without first testing whether it meets AS 12's specific "promoters' contribution" characterisation (tied to total investment, not a specific asset or specific revenue item), which mandates Capital Reserve treatment instead.

topic_text: Topic 1.4: Recognition of a government grant requires reasonable assurance of both compliance and receipt - mere application is insufficient
question_html:
Energy Ltd. has acquired a generator on 1.4.2023 for ₹100 lakh. On 2.4.2023, it applied to Indian Renewal Energy Development Authority (IREDA) for a subsidy. The subsidy was granted in June, 2024 after the accounts for 2023-2024 were finalized. The company has not accounted for the subsidy for the year ended 31.3.2024.

State

  1. Is this a prior period item?
  2. How should the subsidy be accounted in the accounting year 2024-2025?
answer_html:
The answer is in para 13 of AS 12 "Accounting for Government Grants" which permits recognition of grant only when there is reasonable assurance that –

  1. the enterprise will comply with the conditions attached to them and
  2. the subsidy will be received.

Mere making of an application does not provide the reasonable assurance that the subsidy will be received. Letter of sanction from IREDA is required to provide this assurance. Since, the subsidy was granted in June, 2024 after approval of accounts, non-recognition of grant in 2023-2024 will not be considered as an error. Hence, this is not a prior period item. Therefore, the company was right in not recognizing the grant.

Further, AS 4 requires adjustment of events occurring after the balance sheet date only upto the date of approval of accounts by the Board of Directors. In view of this, the company is correct in not adjusting the same in the accounts in the year 2023-2024.

(ii) The subsidy should be deducted from the cost of the generator. The revised unamortised amount of generator should be written off over the remaining useful life.

Alternatively, the same may be treated as ‘deferred income’ and allocated over the remaining useful life in the proportion in which depreciation is charged.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating the mere filing of a subsidy application as sufficient grounds to recognize the grant, or alternatively treating the later grant of the subsidy as a prior period item requiring restatement of the already-approved 2023-2024 accounts.

topic_text: Topic 1.3: Revenue grants credited to P&L (or netted against the related expense)
question_html: Zenith Industries Ltd. received ₹65 lakhs from a local authority to develop medical facilities for employees at its new township. Explain the accounting treatment per AS 12.
answer_html: This is a grant in the nature of a revenue grant (related to employee welfare expenditure, not a specific fixed asset). Such grants are generally presented as a credit in the Statement of Profit and Loss, either separately or under "Other Income." Alternatively, the ₹65 lakhs may be deducted from the related expense (employee benefit expenses) instead.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees treated this as a capital grant since it funds facilities at a "newly built" site, missing that the grant's purpose (employee welfare) rather than the site's newness determines its revenue-grant classification.

topic_text: Topic 1.8: Promoters'-contribution grants credited to Capital Reserve
question_html: Zenith Industries Ltd. also received ₹82 lakhs as a Central Government subsidy for establishing a new production unit in a notified backward area, classified as being in the nature of promoters' contribution, intended to support long-term development. Explain the treatment per AS 12.
answer_html: Per AS 12, grants in the nature of promoters' contribution — given with reference to total investment/capital outlay, with no repayment ordinarily expected — are treated as Capital Reserve, which can neither be distributed as dividend nor treated as deferred income. Since this ₹82 lakh subsidy is neither tied to a specific fixed asset nor to revenue, the full amount should be credited to Capital Reserve.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees treated this as deferred income to be amortised, not recognising the promoters'-contribution characterisation that requires direct Capital Reserve treatment.

topic_text: Topic 4.3: Definitions of Timing Difference and Permanent Difference
question_html: Write short note on Timing difference and Permanent Difference as per AS 22.
answer_html:
Matching of taxes against revenue for a period poses special problems arising from the fact that in a number of cases, taxable income may be different from the accounting income. The divergence between taxable income and accounting income arises due to two main reasons: firstly, there are differences between items of revenue and expenses as appearing in the statement of profit and loss and the items which are considered as revenue, expenses or deductions for tax purposes, known as Permanent Difference. Secondly, there are differences between the amount in respect of a particular item of revenue or expense as recognised in the statement of profit and loss and the corresponding amount which is recognised for the computation of taxable income, known as Timing Difference.

Permanent differences are the differences between taxable income and accounting income which arise in one accounting period and do not reverse subsequently. For example, an income exempt from tax or an expense that is not allowable as a deduction for tax purposes.

Timing differences are those differences between taxable income and accounting income which arise in one accounting period and are capable of reversal in one or more subsequent periods. For e.g., Depreciation, Bonus, etc.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is treating any book-tax gap as a timing difference by default; only differences capable of reversing in a future period (like depreciation) are timing differences, while items that never reverse (like a permanently tax-exempt income) are permanent differences and never generate deferred tax.
chapter_label: AS 22: Accounting for Taxes on Income

topic_text: Topic 4.5: Deferred tax liability remeasured each year using the tax rate enacted or substantively enacted as at that balance sheet date
question_html:
ABC Ltd. prepares its accounts annually on 31st March. On 1st April, 2022, it purchases a machine at a cost of ₹1,50,000. The machine has a useful life of three years and an expected scrap value of zero. Although it is eligible for a 100% first year depreciation allowance for tax purposes, the straight line method is considered appropriate for accounting purposes. ABC Ltd. has profits before depreciation and taxes of ₹2,00,000 each year and corporate tax rate is 40 percent each year.

The purchase of machine at a cost of ₹1,50,000 in 2022 gives rise to a tax saving of ₹60,000. The corporate tax rate has been assumed to be same in each of the three years. Calculate deferred tax and pass necessary journal entries.

What will be the amount of deferred tax, if the substantively enacted tax rates for 2022, 2023 and 2024 are 40%, 35% and 38% respectively.
answer_html:
If the cost of machine is spread over three years of its life for accounting purposes, the amount of the tax saving should also be spread over the same period as shown below:

In 2022, the amount of depreciation allowed for tax purposes exceeds the amount of depreciation charged for accounting purposes by ₹1,00,000 and, therefore, taxable income is lower than the accounting income — giving rise to a deferred tax liability of ₹40,000. In 2023 and 2024, accounting income is lower than taxable income because the amount of depreciation charged for accounting purposes exceeds the amount allowed for tax purposes by ₹50,000 each year; deferred tax liability is reduced by ₹20,000 in each of those years.

The amount debited (credited) to the profit and loss account for each year is accordingly: 31st March, 2022 Debit ₹40,000; 31st March, 2023 (Credit) ₹(22,500); 31st March, 2024 (Credit) ₹(17,500).

topic_text: Topic 5.5: Basic EPS restated for a rights issue's bonus element using the theoretical ex-rights fair value adjustment factor
question_html: Following information is supplied by K Ltd.: Number of shares outstanding prior to right issue - 2,50,000 shares. Right issue - two new share for each 5 outstanding shares (i.e. 1,00,000 new shares). Right issue price - ₹98. Last date of exercising rights - 30-06-2023. Fair value of one equity share immediately prior to exercise of right on 30-06-2023 is ₹102. Net Profit to equity shareholders: 2022-2023 - ₹50,00,000; 2023-2024 - ₹75,00,000. You are required to calculate the basic earnings per share as per AS-20 Earnings per Share.
answer_html:
Theoretical ex-rights fair value per share = (Fair value of shares immediately prior to exercise of rights + Total amount received from exercise) / (Number of shares outstanding prior to exercise + Number of shares issued in the exercise) = (₹102 × 2,50,000 shares + ₹98 × 1,00,000 shares) / 3,50,000 shares = ₹100.86.

Computation of adjustment factor = Fair value per share prior to exercise of rights / Theoretical ex-rights value per share = 102/100.86 = 1.01.

Computation of earnings per share:

EPS for the year 2022-23 as originally reported: ₹50,00,000/2,50,000 shares = ₹20.

EPS for the year 2022-23 restated for rights issue: ₹50,00,000/(2,50,000 shares × 1.01) = ₹19.80.

EPS for the year 2023-24 including effects of rights issue: EPS = ₹75,00,000/3,25,625* = ₹23.03.

* [(2,50,000 × 1.01 × 3/12) + (3,50,000 × 9/12)] = 63,125 + 2,62,500 = 3,25,625 shares.

Note: Financial year (ended 31st March) is considered as accounting year while giving the above answer.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is using the raw share count and nominal rights-issue price directly, without first computing the theoretical ex-rights fair value and applying the resulting adjustment factor to the pre-rights weighted average.

topic_text: Topic 5.6: Diluted EPS from convertible debentures, with partly-paid shares weighted by proportion paid
question_html: On 1st April, 2025, ABC Limited: 50,000 equity shares of ₹100 each (₹80 paid up by all shareholders) ₹40,00,000; 2,00,000 8% Preference shares of ₹10 each ₹20,00,000; 10,000 12% Debentures of ₹100 each (each convertible into 3 equity shares of ₹100 each) ₹10,00,000. On 1st July 2025, remaining ₹20 called up and paid by all shareholders except one holding 10,000 equity shares. Profit after tax for 2025-26: ₹3,44,000. Tax rate 30%. Compute Basic and Diluted EPS.
answer_html:
Basic EPS: Net profit attributable to equity = 3,44,000 − preference dividend (8% × 20,00,000 = 1,60,000) = 1,84,000. Weighted average equity shares: 1 Apr–30 Jun (50,000 shares × 80/100 paid × 3/12) = 10,000 + 1 Jul–31 Mar (40,000 fully-paid shares × 9/12) = 30,000 + (10,000 shares still ₹80-paid × 80/100 × 9/12) = 6,000; total = 46,000. Basic EPS = 1,84,000 / 46,000 = ₹4 per share.

Diluted EPS: Interest on 10,000 12% debentures = 1,20,000; tax relief @30% = 36,000; net interest add-back = 84,000. Adjusted net profit = 1,84,000 + 1,20,000 − 36,000 = 2,68,000. Shares from conversion (10,000 debentures × 3) = 30,000. Diluted shares = 46,000 + 30,000 = 76,000. Diluted EPS = 2,68,000 / 76,000 = ₹3.53 per share (approx).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees forgot to add back the after-tax interest saving on the convertible debentures to net profit when computing diluted EPS, or omitted weighting the partly-paid shares by the proportion actually paid up.

topic_text: Topic 5.3: Weighted average number of shares - the effective date to use for shares issued under six different circumstances
question_html:
In the following list of shares issued, for the purpose of calculation of weighted average number of shares, from which date, weight is to be considered:

  1. Equity Shares issued in exchange of cash,
  2. Equity Shares issued as a result of conversion of a debt instrument,
  3. Equity Shares issued in exchange for the settlement of a liability of the enterprise,
  4. Equity Shares issued for rendering of services to the enterprise,
  5. Equity Shares issued in lieu of interest and/or principal of an other financial instrument,
  6. Equity Shares issued as consideration for the acquisition of an asset other than in cash.
answer_html:
The following dates should be considered for weights for the purpose of calculation of weighted average number of shares in the given situations:

  1. Date of Cash receivable
  2. Date of conversion
  3. Date on which settlement becomes effective
  4. When the services are rendered
  5. Date when interest ceases to accrue
  6. Date on which the acquisition is recognised.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is defaulting to "date of allotment" for every scenario, without distinguishing situations where AS 20 specifies a different effective date, e.g. shares issued in lieu of interest are weighted from when interest ceases to accrue, not the allotment date.

topic_text: Topic 5.4: Inclusion-date rules for shares issued under various circumstances, for weighted average share count
question_html: In the following list of shares issued, for the purpose of calculation of weighted average number of shares, from which date, weight is to be considered: (i) Equity Shares issued in exchange of cash, (ii) Equity Shares issued as a result of conversion of a debt instrument, (iii) Equity Shares issued in exchange for the settlement of a liability of the enterprise, (iv) Equity Shares issued for rendering of services to the enterprise, (v) Equity Shares issued in lieu of interest and/or principal of an other financial instrument, (vi) Equity Shares issued as consideration for the acquisition of an asset other than in cash. (5 Marks)
answer_html: (i) Date of Cash receivable. (ii) Date of conversion. (iii) Date on which settlement becomes effective. (iv) When the services are rendered. (v) Date when interest ceases to accrue. (vi) Date on which the acquisition is recognised.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees used the date of the board resolution or agreement for several of these cases instead of the specific triggering event AS 20 identifies (e.g. date of conversion, date services are rendered), inflating or understating the weighted average share count.
