topic_text: Topic 2.6: Fixed asset acquisitions and disposals reported gross, not netted, in the cash flow statement
question_html: Garden Ltd. acquired plant and machinery for ₹20 lakhs and sold furniture and fixtures for ₹5 lakhs in the same year. Can the company disclose net cash outflow towards purchase of fixed assets in the cash flow statement per AS 3?
answer_html: No. Per AS 3 para 21, major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments from investing and financing activities must be reported separately, except for the specific items permitted to be reported net under paras 22 and 24 — acquisition and disposal of fixed assets is not among those permitted items. The company cannot net the ₹20 lakh purchase against the ₹5 lakh disposal; both must be shown as separate gross cash flow lines.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees assumed netting was acceptable since both items relate to fixed assets, not checking the specific, limited list of items AS 3 actually permits to be reported net.

topic_text: Topic 3.5: Treatment of interest for segment reporting, including overdraft/operating-liability interest and interest capitalised into segment-asset inventory
question_html:
Whether interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should be included in the segment expense or not?

In case interest is included as a part of the cost of inventories where it is so required as per AS 16, read with AS 2, and those inventories are part of segment assets of a particular segment, state whether such interest would be considered as a segment expense.
answer_html:
The interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should not be included as a part of the segment expense unless the operations of the segment are primarily of a financial nature or unless the interest is included as a part of the cost of inventories.

In case interest is included as part of the cost of inventories where it is so required as per AS 16 "Borrowing Costs", read with AS 2 "Valuation of Inventories", and those inventories are part of segment assets of a particular segment, such interest should be considered as a segment expense.

In this case, the amount of such interest and the fact that the segment result has been arrived at after considering such interest should be disclosed by way of a note to the segment result.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is treating all segment-identified interest expense the same way, without recognising the specific carve-out where interest capitalised into inventory cost under AS 16/AS 2 does count as a segment expense even though ordinary overdraft interest generally does not.

topic_text: Topic 3.9: Identifying reportable segments - 10% revenue/asset threshold and 75% cumulative external revenue test
question_html:
Garnet Limited has 4 operating segments. The total revenue (internal and external) and assets are set out as below:

SegmentInter Segment SalesExternal SalesTotal Assets
Fan3,20010,90023,700
Light2001,40013,200
Lamp01,5004,200
Printer1,1002003,400
TOTAL4,50014,00044,500

How many reportable segments does Garnet Limited have as per the Revenue and Assets criteria given in AS 17? State Reasons for your answer. (4 Marks)
answer_html:
As per AS 17 ‘Segment Reporting’, a business segment or geographical segment should be identified as a reportable segment if: its revenue from sales to external customers and from other transactions with other segments is 10% or more of the total revenue – external and internal of all segments; or its segment assets are 10% or more of the total assets of all segments.

If the total external revenue attributable to reportable segments constitutes less than 75% of total enterprise revenue, additional segments should be identified as reportable segments even if they do not meet the 10% thresholds until at least 75% of total enterprise revenue is included in reportable segments. This is not applicable in the given case. In the given case 75% of External Revenue is ₹10,500 Lakhs (₹14,000 × 75%) and the total External Revenue from Reportable segments is ₹12,300 Lakhs. So, no need to add Reportable segments.

On the basis of turnover criteria segment Fan is reportable segment as its sales are more than 1,850 lakhs (10% of ₹18,500 lakhs). Moreover, total external revenue attributable to reportable segment is also more than 75% of the total enterprise revenue.

On the basis of asset criteria, Fan and Light are reportable segments as their assets are more than 4,450 lakhs (10% of ₹44,500 lakhs).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees applied only the 10% revenue or asset threshold test and omitted to check the 75% cumulative external-revenue test for identifying reportable segments under AS 17.

topic_text: Topic 3.6: Inter-segment transfer pricing may be based on any consistently-applied and disclosed basis - cost, below cost, or market price
question_html:
A Company has an inter-segment transfer pricing policy of charging at cost less 5%. The market prices are generally 20% above cost.

You are required to examine whether the policy adopted by the company is correct or not?
answer_html: AS 17 "Segment Reporting" requires that inter-segment transfers should be measured on the basis that the enterprise actually used to price these transfers. The basis of pricing inter-segment transfers and any change therein should be disclosed in the financial statements. Hence, the enterprise can have its own policy for pricing inter-segment transfers and hence, inter-segment transfers may be based on cost, below cost or market price. However, whichever policy is followed, the same should be disclosed and applied consistently. Therefore, in the given case the inter-segment transfer pricing policy adopted by the company is correct if followed consistently.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is concluding that any inter-segment transfer price other than market price is automatically non-compliant with AS 17, missing that the standard permits any consistently-applied and disclosed pricing basis, including cost, below cost, or market price.

topic_text: Topic 3.3: Reportable segment thresholds - 10% revenue or assets test, plus the 75% external-revenue coverage check
question_html: Garnet Limited has 4 operating segments (₹ in appropriate units): Fan — Inter-segment sales 3,200, External sales 10,900, Total assets 23,700; Light — 200, 1,400, 13,200; Lamp — 0, 1,500, 4,200; Printer — 1,100, 200, 3,400; Total — 4,500, 14,000, 44,500. How many reportable segments does Garnet Limited have per the Revenue and Assets criteria in AS 17? State reasons.
answer_html:
A segment is reportable if its revenue (external + inter-segment) is ≥10% of total revenue (external + internal, all segments), OR its assets are ≥10% of total assets.

Total revenue basis (external 14,000 + internal 4,500 = 18,500): 10% threshold = 1,850. Fan's total revenue (3,200+10,900=14,100) far exceeds 1,850 — Fan is reportable. (Light: 200+1,400=1,600, below threshold; Lamp: 0+1,500=1,500, below; Printer: 1,100+200=1,300, below.)

Assets basis (total 44,500): 10% threshold = 4,450. Fan (23,700) and Light (13,200) both exceed this — both are reportable on the assets criterion.

75% external-revenue test: reportable segments' external revenue must cover ≥75% of total external revenue (75% × 14,000 = 10,500). Fan and Light's combined external revenue (10,900+1,400=12,300) already exceeds 10,500, so no additional segments need to be added to meet the 75% threshold.

Conclusion: Garnet Limited has 2 reportable segments — Fan and Light (Fan qualifies on both revenue and assets; Light qualifies on assets only, but that alone is sufficient).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees tested the 10% revenue threshold against external sales alone, omitting inter-segment sales from the revenue base used for that specific test.

topic_text: Topic 3.5: Treatment of interest for segment reporting - overdraft/operating-liability interest
question_html: Whether interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should be included in the segment expense or not?
answer_html: The interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should not be included as a part of the segment expense unless the operations of the segment are primarily of a financial nature or unless the interest is included as a part of the cost of inventories.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees included all interest expense indiscriminately in segment expense, overlooking the two exceptions (segment primarily financial in nature, or interest forming part of inventory cost) under which such interest is included.

topic_text: Topic 3.5: Interest on overdrafts/operating liabilities excluded from segment expense unless the segment is primarily of a financial nature or the interest is part of inventory cost
question_html: Whether interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should be included in the segment expense or not?
answer_html: The interest expense relating to overdrafts and other operating liabilities identified to a particular segment should not be included as a part of the segment expense unless the operations of the segment are primarily of a financial nature or unless the interest is included as a part of the cost of inventories.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is including all interest expense identified to a segment as a matter of course, without checking the two specific exceptions (financial-nature segment, or interest forming part of inventory cost) that would actually justify inclusion.

topic_text: Topic 3.3: A segment need only satisfy one of the three reportability tests - checking all three can expand the reportable set well beyond the most obvious single segment
question_html: Cotton Garments Limited, 5 segments (₹ Crore): Segment Assets A/B/C/D/E 40/15/10/10/5 (Total 80); Segment Results (95)/5/5/(5)/15 (Total −75); Segment Revenue 310/40/30/40/30 (Total 450). The Chief Accountant believes only segment "A" should be reported. Examine this opinion per AS 17.
answer_html:
Per AS 17 para 27, a segment is reportable if: (i) its revenue (external+internal) is ≥10% of total revenue; or (ii) its result (profit or loss) is ≥10% of the combined result of all profit-making segments or all loss-making segments, whichever is greater in absolute amount; or (iii) its assets are ≥10% of total assets. If reportable segments cover <75% of total external revenue, additional segments must be added until 75% is reached.

(a) Revenue test (10% of 450 = 45): only A (310) qualifies.

(b) Result test: combined profit-segments (B+C+E = 5+5+15=25) vs. combined loss-segments (A+D = 95+5=100, in absolute terms); greater = 100; 10% = 10. Segments with |result| ≥10: A (95) and E (15) qualify.

(c) Assets test (10% of 80 = 8): A, B, C, D (40,15,10,10) qualify; only E (5) falls short.

Since every segment (A through E) satisfies at least one of the three tests, all five segments must be reported per AS 17. The Chief Accountant's opinion that only segment A is reportable is therefore wrong.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees checked only the revenue test (which favours only segment A) and stopped there, missing that the result and assets tests bring in the remaining segments too.

topic_text: Topic 4.3/4.4: Related-party status ceasing mid-year, directors serving in an individual professional capacity, and sole-customer economic dependence not amounting to related-party status
question_html: Answer the following with respect to AS 18: (i) ABC Ltd. sold goods of ₹2,00,000 to its associate company for the 1st quarter ending 30.06.2025. After that the related party relationship ceased to exist. However, goods were supplied to any other ordinary customer. Decide whether transactions of the entire year have to be disclosed as related party transaction. (ii) If the majority of directors of Arjun Ltd. constitute the majority of the Board of another Company Bheem Ltd. in their individual capacity as professionals (and not by virtue of their being Directors in Arjun Ltd.). Are both the companies related? (iii) Asha Ltd. sells all the manufactured furniture of ₹1,00,00,000 to Sasha Ltd, as per agreement. Sasha Ltd. is the only customer to Asha Ltd. In the financial statements, Asha Ltd. wants to present Sasha company as a related party. Comment on the disclosure requirement.
answer_html:
(i) As per AS 18, parties are considered related if at any time during the reporting period one party has the ability to control the other or exercise significant influence over the other. Transactions of ABC Ltd. with its associate company for the first quarter ending 30.06.2025 only are required to be disclosed as related party transactions, as the company had the ability to exercise significant influence only until 30.6.2025. The transactions for the period in which the related party relationship did not exist need not be reported.

(ii) Arjun Ltd. cannot be said to control the composition of the board of directors of Bheem Ltd., as the directors have been appointed in their individual capacity as professionals and not by virtue of their being directors in Arjun Ltd. Hence, it cannot be concluded that the companies are related merely because the majority of the directors of one company became the majority of the directors of the second in their individual capacity as professionals.

(iii) In the context of AS 18, a single customer, supplier, franchiser, distributor, or general agent with whom an enterprise transacts a significant volume of business cannot be construed as a Related Party Relationship merely by virtue of the resulting economic dependence. There is economic dependence between the companies, but no one controls or exercises significant influence on the other. Asha Ltd. need not report Sasha Company as its related party in its financial statements.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is over-extending "related party" to any relationship of economic significance — mere economic dependence on a sole customer, or directors overlapping only in an unrelated individual professional capacity, does not by itself create control or significant influence under AS 18.

topic_text: Topic 4.3: Related party relationships as per AS 18, including indirect significant influence through an intermediate holding and disclosure limited to the period the relationship existed
question_html:
The following information is provided for the year ended 31st March, 2024: (i) AX Limited holds 70% shares of BX Limited. (ii) BX Limited holds 30% shares of CX Limited. (iii) DX Limited holds 40% shares of in CX Limited. (iv) DX Limited holds 49% shares in EX Limited.

You are required to: (i) Identify the related parties for the reporting entities – AX Limited, CX Limited and EX Limited. (ii) If DX Limited would have sold its investment in EX Limited on 1st October, 2023, but goods were continued to be supplied by DX Limited to EX Limited throughout the year, will this scenario change your answer with respect to any of the reporting entity mentioned in point (i)? Give reasons for your answer as per AS 18. (4 Marks)
answer_html:
(i)

Reporting entityRelated party
AX LimitedBX Limited (AX Limited controls BX Limited directly as holding company); CX Limited (AX Limited has significant influence in CX Limited indirectly through BX Limited)
CX LimitedAX Limited (AX Limited has significant influence in CX Limited indirectly through BX Limited); BX Limited (BX Limited has significant influence in CX Limited); DX Limited (DX Limited holds 40% shares, means substantial interest of more than or equal to 20%, hence significant influence exists in this case)
EX LimitedDX Limited (DX Limited holds 49% shares, means substantial interest of more than or equal to 20%, hence significant influence exists in this case)

(ii) No, DX would still be a related party of EX Limited. EX Limited will report DX Limited as a related party as per AS 18. However, the transaction for the period in which the related party relationship exists will only be disclosed.
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: Some examinees failed to correctly identify the related parties for the three reporting entities.

topic_text: Topic 4.6: A related party transaction requires disclosure whether or not a price is actually charged for the transfer of resources or obligations
question_html:
Will transactions with related parties, for services provided/received free of cost, be required to be disclosed?

A Limited has a corporate communications department, which centralises the public relations function for the whole group of A Limited and its subsidiaries. No charges are, however, levied by A Limited on its subsidiaries and accordingly, these transactions are not given accounting recognition. Would these constitute related party transactions requiring disclosure under AS 18 in the standalone financial statements of A Limited?
answer_html: These transactions would require disclosure under AS 18 in the standalone financial statements of A Limited. As per paragraph 10 of AS 18, a related party transaction is "a transfer of resources or obligations between related parties, regardless of whether or not a price is charged". In the given situation, there is a transfer of resources from A Limited to its subsidiaries, though no price is charged for the same. Hence, it will constitute a related party transaction and will require disclosure in the financial statements of A Ltd.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is concluding that a related party transaction requires disclosure under AS 18 only if a price is actually charged, missing that the standard's own definition explicitly covers a transfer of resources or obligations between related parties regardless of whether or not a price is charged.

topic_text: Topic 4.6: Expense reimbursement to a KMP is not remuneration and does not require AS 18 disclosure
question_html: Mr. Rajiv, a KMP of Raijada Limited, received a cheque of ₹70,000 towards reimbursement of expenses incurred on hotel stay, conference expenses, etc. while attending a meeting on behalf of the company. Is this transaction covered under AS-18?
answer_html: Mr. Rajiv, as a KMP, is a related party of Raijada Limited under AS 18. However, a reimbursement of expenses actually incurred on the company's behalf is not in the nature of remuneration or a related-party transaction requiring disclosure — it is simply the company bearing its own cost, routed through the KMP. Hence, this reimbursement need not be disclosed as a related-party transaction under AS 18.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees concluded disclosure was required simply because Mr. Rajiv is a related party, without separately testing whether the specific transaction (a cost reimbursement, not remuneration) actually falls within AS 18's disclosure scope.

topic_text: Topic 4.3: Related-party status requires either a voting-power interest giving control/significant influence, or the ability to direct/instruct the board (key management personnel) - day-to-day management alone under a fee contract does not qualify
question_html: A Ltd. enters into an agreement with Mr. Bhola for running a business for a fixed amount payable to the later every year. The contract states that the day-to-day management of the business will be handled by Mr. Bhola, while all financial and operating policy decisions are taken by the Board of Directors of the Company. Mr. Bhola does not have any voting power in A Limited. You are required to suggest how this transaction will be treated as at the closing date i.e. on 31st March, 2023 for the purposes of AS 18 'Related Party Disclosures'.
answer_html: Mr. Bhola will not be considered as a related party of A Ltd. in view of provisions of AS 18 "Related Party Disclosures" which states, "individuals owning, directly or indirectly, an interest in the voting power of the reporting enterprise that gives them control or significant influence over the enterprise, and relatives of any such individual are related parties". In the given case, in the absence of share ownership, Mr. Bhola would not be considered to exercise significant influence on A Limited, even though there is an agreement giving him the power to manage the company. Further, the fact that Mr Bhola does not have the ability to direct or instruct the board of directors does not qualify him as a key management personnel.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is treating anyone contractually responsible for day-to-day management as automatically a related party, without checking for an actual voting-power interest or the ability to control the board's financial and operating policy decisions.

topic_text: Topic 4.7: Related-party disclosure applies if the relationship existed at any time during the reporting period, even if it has since ended before year-end
question_html: Shri Manoj a relative of key management personnel received remuneration of ₹3,50,000 for his services in the company for the period from 1st April, 2022 to 30th June, 2022. On 1st July, 2022, he left the service. You are required to suggest how this transaction will be treated as at the closing date i.e. on 31st March, 2023 for the purposes of AS 18 'Related Party Disclosures'.
answer_html: According to AS 18 on 'Related Party Disclosures', parties are considered to be related if at any time during the reporting period one party has the ability to control the other party or exercise significant influence over the other party in making financial and/or operating decisions. Hence, Shri Manoj, a relative of key management personnel should be identified as related party for disclosure in the financial statements for the year ended 31.3.2023 as he received remuneration for his services in the company for the period from 1st April, 2022 to 30th June, 2022.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is excluding the transaction from disclosure on the reasoning that Shri Manoj was no longer employed as at the balance sheet date, missing that AS 18's "at any time during the reporting period" test is satisfied by the relationship having existed for even part of the year.

topic_text: A day-to-day hotel manager with no voting power and no control over financial/operating policy decisions is not a related party under AS 18
question_html: SP Hotels Limited enters into an agreement with Mr. A for running its hotel for a fixed return payable to the latter every year. The contract involves the day-to-day management of the hotel, while all financial and operating policy decisions are taken by the Board of Directors of the company. Mr. A does not own any voting power in SP Hotels Limited. Would he be considered as a related party of SP Hotels Limited?
answer_html: Mr. A will not be considered as a related party of SP Hotels Limited, in view of paragraph 3(c) of AS 18, which states: "individuals owning, directly or indirectly, an interest in the voting power of the reporting enterprise that gives them control or significant influence over the enterprise, and relatives of any such individual." In the given case, in the absence of share ownership, Mr. A would not be considered to exercise significant influence over SP Hotels Limited, even though there is an agreement giving him the power to manage the day-to-day operations of the company. Further, the fact that Mr. A does not have the ability to direct or instruct the Board of Directors (which retains all financial and operating policy decisions) means he does not qualify as a key management personnel either.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating Mr. A as a related party simply because he has day-to-day management authority over the hotel, without separately testing whether he has the voting power or board-level control that AS 18 actually requires for related-party or key-management-personnel status.

topic_text: Topic 4.4: Only transactions during the period the related party relationship actually existed require disclosure
question_html: X Ltd. sold goods to its associate company for the 1st quarter ending 30.6.2024, priced as it would for any ordinary customer. After that quarter, the related party relationship ceased to exist. Decide whether transactions for the entire year have to be disclosed as related party transactions.
answer_html: No. Per AS 18 para 23, only the transactions during the period the related party relationship actually existed — here, the first quarter ending 30.6.2024 — need be disclosed as related party transactions. Transactions in the remaining periods, after the relationship ceased, need not be disclosed as such.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees required disclosure for the whole year merely because a related party relationship existed at some point during it, not applying the period-specific test AS 18 actually uses.

topic_text: Topic 6.2: Gradual phasing out without a formal approved plan does not meet the discontinuing-operation definition
question_html: Kumar Ltd. manufactures both passenger cars and commercial vehicles. Management has an informal long-term strategic vision to shift focus toward commercial vehicles over 5 years, reducing passenger car production by ~20% annually and establishing a new commercial-vehicle facility, with employees to be transferred in phases. However, no specific or approved plan exists for sale, closure, or discontinuance of the passenger car division; no formal disposal plan, no Board approval; the new factory has not commenced operations, no binding commitments made. Comment on whether this gradual scaling down, without a formal approved plan, can be regarded as a 'Discontinuing Operation' under AS 24.
answer_html:
Mere gradual phasing out is not considered a discontinuing operation as defined under AS 24. Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy the definition on their own (though they might in combination with other circumstances) include: gradual/evolutionary phasing out of a product line; discontinuing several products within an ongoing line of business; shifting production/marketing activities between locations; and closing a facility for productivity improvements or cost savings.

On these facts: the strategic plan has no final Board approval via resolution; there is no specific, time-bound plan for asset/employee transfer; and the new commercial-vehicle segment has not started operations. Kumar Ltd.'s passenger-car scale-down is therefore not a discontinuing operation under AS 24.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees treated the mere existence of a strategic intention as sufficient for AS 24 classification, missing that a specific, Board-approved plan with a defined implementation timeline is required.

topic_text: Topic 6.2-6.3: Gradual phasing out without a formal approved plan vs. a time-bound Board-resolved closure plan
question_html:
Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of Passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the Passenger car segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. It also plans to commence another new factory for the manufacture of commercial vehicles plus transfer of employees in a phased manner.

  1. You are required to comment if mere gradual phasing out in itself can be considered as a ‘Discontinuing Operation' within the meaning of AS 24.
  2. If the company passes a resolution to sell some of the assets in the passenger car division and also to transfer few other assets of the passenger car division to the new factory, does this trigger the application of AS 24?
  3. Would your answer to the above be different if the company resolves to sell the assets of the Passenger Car Division in a phased but time bound manner?
answer_html:
Mere gradual phasing out is not considered as discontinuing operation as defined under para 3 of AS 24, ‘Discontinuing Operations'.

Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include: (1) Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service; (2) Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business; (3) Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and (4) Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

A Reportable business segment or geographical segment as defined in AS 17, would normally satisfy criteria (b) of the definition.

In view of the above the answers are:

(i) No, the companies' strategic plan has no final approval from the board through a resolution and there is no specific time bound activities like shifting of assets and employees. Above all, the new segment i.e. commercial vehicle production line in a new factory has not started.

(ii) No, the resolution is salient about stoppage of the Car segment in definite time period. Though, sale of some assets and some transfer proposal were passed through a resolution to the new factory, closure road map and new segment starting roadmap are missing. Hence, AS 24 will not be applicable.

(iii) Yes, phased and time bound programme resolved in the board clearly indicates the closure of the passenger car segment in a definite time frame and will constitute a clear roadmap. Hence, this action will attract compliance of AS 24.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error across all three parts of this question is treating any board resolution touching the passenger car division as sufficient to trigger AS 24, without checking whether it actually specifies a definite, time-bound closure roadmap for the division as a whole, as distinct from partial asset sales/transfers alongside an ongoing, open-ended strategic shift.

topic_text: Topic 6.5: Presentation and disclosure requirements for a discontinuing operation
question_html: Analyse the disclosure and presentation requirements of AS 24 for Discontinuing Operations (any five). (5 Marks)
answer_html:
An enterprise should include the following information relating to a discontinuing operation in its financial statements beginning with the financial statements for the period in which the initial disclosure event occurs:

  1. A description of the discontinuing operation(s).
  2. The business or geographical segment(s) in which it is reported as per AS 17.
  3. The date and nature of the initial disclosure event.
  4. The date or period in which the discontinuance is expected to be completed if known or determinable.
  5. The carrying amounts, as of the balance sheet date, of the total assets to be disposed of and the total liabilities to be settled.
  6. The amounts of revenue and expenses in respect of the ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period.
  7. The amount of pre-tax profit or loss from ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period, and the income tax expense related thereto.
  8. The amounts of net cash flows attributable to the operating, investing, and financing activities of the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees omitted the requirement to disclose the amount of net cash flows attributable to the operating, investing and financing activities of the discontinuing operation, listing only the descriptive disclosures under AS 24.

topic_text: Topic 6.5: Initial disclosure event - the eight required disclosure items
question_html: What is the initial disclosure information of AS-24 for discontinuing operations? (4 Marks)
answer_html: An enterprise should include the following information relating to a discontinuing operation in its financial statements beginning with the financial statements for the period in which the initial disclosure event occurs: (a) A description of the discontinuing operation(s). (b) The business or geographical segment(s) in which it is reported as per AS 17. (c) The date and nature of the initial disclosure event. (d) The date or period in which the discontinuance is expected to be completed if known or determinable. (e) The carrying amounts, as of the balance sheet date, of the total assets to be disposed of and the total liabilities to be settled. (f) The amounts of revenue and expenses in respect of the ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period. (g) The amount of pre-tax profit or loss from ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period, and the income tax expense related thereto. (h) The amounts of net cash flows attributable to the operating, investing, and financing activities of the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period.
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees faced difficulty in stating the initial disclosure requirements for discontinuing operations as per AS 24. Instead of addressing the required disclosures, they described the circumstances under which a business may be discontinued.

topic_text: Topic 6.2: Definition of a discontinuing operation - single plan, piecemeal disposal, separate major line of business
question_html:
Oasis Limited runs a famous chain of super markets and restaurants. Restaurant division constitutes 35% of total group revenue. The management of the company decides to close the business of restaurants as the company has been experiencing declining profitability due to increased competition. On 1st April, 2025, the management announced its intention to discontinue the restaurant business and concentrate on Super market segment only. The decision was made through strategic review and the management started actively seeking buyers for the restaurant division. During the year 2025-26, the company has sold 5 restaurants out of 12 restaurants so far as part of the sale.

Comment, whether it will be considered as discontinuing operation or not as per the provisions of AS-24? (10 Marks)
answer_html:
As per AS 24, a discontinuing operation is a component of an enterprise: that the enterprise, pursuant to a single plan, is disposing of substantially in its entirety, or disposing of piecemeal, or terminating through abandonment; and which represents a separate major line of business or geographical area of operations.

Hence the restaurant division's closure by Oasis Limited will be considered a discontinuing operation as per the provisions of AS 24. This is due to the fact that the assets are sold off as part of a single plan, and that the business represents a separate major line of business, and can be distinguished both operationally and for financial reporting purposes.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees concluded this was not a discontinuing operation because the disposal was piecemeal (5 of 12 restaurants sold rather than the whole division at once), not recognising that AS 24 explicitly includes piecemeal disposal pursuant to a single plan within its definition.

topic_text: Topic 6.5: Disclosure and presentation requirements for a discontinuing operation, and activities that only satisfy the AS 24 criteria in combination with other circumstances
question_html:
What are the disclosure and presentation requirements of AS 24 for discontinuing operations?

Give four examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion (a) of paragraph 3 of AS 24, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances.
answer_html:
(i) An enterprise should include the following information relating to a discontinuing operation in its financial statements beginning with the financial statements for the period in which the initial disclosure event (as defined in paragraph 15) occurs:

  1. a description of the discontinuing operation(s);
  2. the business or geographical segment(s) in which it is reported as per AS 17, Segment Reporting;
  3. the date and nature of the initial disclosure event;
  4. the date or period in which the discontinuance is expected to be completed if known or determinable;
  5. the carrying amounts, as of the balance sheet date, of the total assets to be disposed of and the total liabilities to be settled;
  6. the amounts of revenue and expenses in respect of the ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period;
  7. the amount of pre-tax profit or loss from ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period, and the income tax expense related thereto; and
  8. the amounts of net cash flows attributable to the operating, investing, and financing activities of the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period.

(ii) Para 3 of AS 24 "Discontinuing Operations" explains the criteria for determination of discontinuing operations. According to Paragraph 9 of AS 24, examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion (a) of paragraph 3, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include:

  1. Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service;
  2. Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business;
  3. Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and
  4. Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

An example in relation to consolidated financial statements is selling a subsidiary whose activities are similar to those of the parent or other subsidiaries.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating any product-line phase-out or facility closure as an automatic discontinuing operation under AS 24, missing that paragraph 9's listed activities only qualify in combination with other circumstances that independently satisfy the AS 24 criteria for a distinct, separately identifiable major line of business or geographical area.

topic_text: Topic 6.2: Gradual/evolutionary phasing out of a product line does not by itself meet the definition of a discontinuing operation; needs a specific plan, board approval, and time-bound implementation
question_html: Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the passenger car segment to the commercial vehicles segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan, it has planned that it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. It also plans to commence another new factory for the manufacture of commercial vehicles plus transfer of employees in a phased manner. These plans have not been approved from the Board of Directors and the new factory for manufacture of commercial vehicles has not yet started. You are required to comment if mere gradual phasing out in itself can be considered as a 'Discontinuing Operation' within the meaning of AS 24.
answer_html:
Mere gradual phasing out is not considered as discontinuing operation as defined under AS 24, 'Discontinuing Operations'. Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include:

  1. Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service;
  2. Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business;
  3. Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and
  4. Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

In view of the above, mere gradual phasing out in itself cannot be considered as discontinuing operation. The companies' strategic plan also has no final approval from the board through a resolution and there is no specific time bound activities like shifting of assets and employees. Moreover, the new segment, i.e. the commercial vehicle production line in a new factory has not started.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is concluding that any strategic segment shift automatically meets AS 24's discontinuing-operation definition, without checking for a formally approved, specific, time-bound plan for disposal or discontinuance of the operation and its assets.

topic_text: Topic 6.2/6.3: Definition of a discontinuing operation and what triggers the initial disclosure event
question_html:
Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of Passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the Passenger car segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. (ii) If the company passes a resolution to sell some of the assets in the passenger car division and also to transfer few other assets of the passenger car division to the new factory, does this trigger the application of AS 24?

(iii) Would your answer to the above be different if the company resolves to sell the assets of the Passenger Car Division in a phased but time bound manner?

Mere gradual phasing out is not considered as discontinuing operation as defined under para 3 of AS 24, ‘Discontinuing Operations'.

Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include: (1) Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service; (2) Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business; (3) Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and (4) Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

In view of the above the answers are:

(i) No, the companies' strategic plan has no final approval from the board through a resolution and there is no specific time bound activities like shifting of assets and employees. Above all, the new segment i.e. commercial vehicle production line in a new factory has not started.

mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees answered part (iii) without properly building on the reasoning already established in parts (i) and (ii), missing that a phased-but-time-bound board resolution is precisely the missing ingredient (a definite closure roadmap) that parts (i) and (ii) found absent, and so overlooked the requirement for a clear sale plan with time-bound actions when applying AS 24.

topic_text: Topic 6.2: Mere gradual/evolutionary phasing out, without a definite time-bound board resolution, is not a discontinuing operation
question_html:
Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of Passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the Passenger car segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include:

topic_text: Topic 1.9: Minority interest turning negative - losses absorbed by holding company, recouped from future minority profits
question_html: GB Limited acquired 80% of equity shares of TB Limited on 1st April, 2018 at a cost of ₹58,00,000, when TB Limited had Equity Share Capital of ₹50,00,000 and Reserves and Surplus of ₹4,64,000. Yearly profit/(loss) of TB Limited: 2018-19 (14,50,000); 2019-20 (23,20,000); 2020-21 (29,00,000); 2021-22 (6,96,000); 2022-23 1,90,000; 2023-24 6,80,000; 2024-25 12,70,000. You are required to calculate the minority interest and cost of control at the end of each year for the purpose of consolidation.
answer_html:
W.N. — Minority Interest and Goodwill on 1.4.2018: Share Capital 50,00,000 (80%: 40,00,000; 20%: 10,00,000) + Reserves 4,64,000 (80%: 3,71,200; 20%: 92,800) = Holding's share 43,71,200, Minority 10,92,800. Cost of investment 58,00,000 − 43,71,200 = Goodwill 14,28,800.

Since minority interest (20%) turns negative during the loss-making years 2018-19 through 2020-21, AS 21 requires losses beyond the minority's own interest to be absorbed by the holding company (Cost of Control account), then recouped from future minority profits before minority interest is credited again:

YearProfit/(Loss)Minority share (20%)Minority interest balanceCost of Control (holding co. absorption)
2018-19(14,50,000)(2,90,000)8,02,800—
2019-20(23,20,000)(4,64,000)3,38,800—
2020-21(29,00,000)(5,80,000)Nil (excess 2,41,200 absorbed by holding co.)2,41,200
2021-22(6,96,000)(1,39,200)Nil (absorbed by holding co.)3,80,400 (cumulative)
2022-231,90,00038,000Nil (profit share adjusted against losses absorbed by holding co.)3,42,400 (cumulative)
2023-246,80,0001,36,000Nil (profit share adjusted against holding co.'s absorbed balance)2,06,400 (cumulative)
2024-2512,70,0002,54,00047,600 (2,54,000 − 2,06,400 remaining absorbed balance recouped)Nil

Cumulative Minority Interest at 31.3.2025 (Balance Sheet figure, excluding the P&L movement column): ₹12,22,400 (i.e. opening 10,92,800 plus the net minority share of profits across the full period, after the loss-absorption/recoupment mechanism above).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A very common error across multiple sittings on this exact pattern: continuing to show a negative (debit) minority interest balance in the consolidated balance sheet, instead of transferring the excess loss to the holding company (Cost of Control) and recouping it against the minority's later profit shares before crediting minority interest again.

topic_text: Topic 1.15-1.16: Preparation of the Consolidated Statement of Profit and Loss, line-by-line addition with elimination of inter-company rent, dividend and expense transactions
question_html:
Birds Ltd. and its subsidiary Rooster Ltd provided the following information for the year ended 31/03/2025 (₹): Equity Share Capital – Birds 10,00,000, Rooster 3,00,000. Sales – Birds 28,40,000, Rooster 10,40,000. Purchases (Finished Goods) – Birds 9,15,000, Rooster 1,75,000. Salaries – Birds 7,75,000, Rooster 3,78,000. Rent received – Birds 5,40,000. General and Administration expenses – Birds 2,81,500, Rooster 1,98,000. Selling and Distribution Expenses – Birds 2,21,000, Rooster 90,000. Dividend Income – Birds 1,35,000, Rooster 28,000. Finished Goods Inventory on 01/04/2024 – Birds 3,35,000, Rooster 1,20,000. Finished Goods Inventory on 31/03/2025 – Birds 7,85,000, Rooster 2,90,000. Other Non-operating Income – Birds 2,38,000, Rooster 57,000.

Other Information: On 1st April 2022 Birds Ltd. acquired 2,500 shares of ₹100 each fully paid up in Rooster Ltd. Rooster Ltd. paid a dividend of 12% for the year ended 31/03/2024, correctly accounted for by Birds Ltd. Rooster Ltd. pays ₹11,250 per month to Birds Ltd. towards rent for the portion of premises occupied. Selling and Distribution Expenses of Rooster Ltd. include ₹15,000 received from Birds Ltd.

Prepare Consolidated Profit and Loss Account of Birds Ltd. and its subsidiary Rooster Ltd. for the year ended 31/03/2025. (10 Marks)
answer_html:
Consolidated Statement of Profit and Loss of Birds Ltd. and its subsidiary Rooster Ltd. for the year ended 31st March, 2025:

Other Income working: Dividend income – Birds 1,35,000 less dividend received from Rooster (2,500×100×12%=30,000) = 1,05,000; plus Rooster 28,000 = 1,33,000. Other Non-operating Income (2,38,000+57,000)=2,95,000. Rent received – Birds 5,40,000 less rent received from Rooster (11,250×12=1,35,000) = 4,05,000. Total Other Income = 1,33,000+2,95,000+4,05,000 = 8,33,000.

Other expenses working: General & Admin – Birds 2,81,500 + (Rooster 1,98,000 less rent paid to Birds 1,35,000 = 63,000) = 3,44,500. Selling & Distribution – Birds 2,21,000 less paid to Rooster (15,000) = 2,06,000; plus (Rooster 90,000 add received from Birds 15,000 = 1,05,000) = 3,11,000. Total Other expenses = 3,44,500+3,11,000 = 6,55,500.

topic_text: Topic 1.11: Calculation of Goodwill/Capital Reserve (cost of control) at acquisition date, with a pre- vs post-acquisition dividend treatment adjusting the cost of investment
question_html:
Rubber Ltd. purchased 70% of shares of Tyre Ltd. on 31/03/2024 for ₹4,05,000. The following is the position of Tyre Ltd. as on that date: Issued share capital of Tyre Ltd. on 31/03/2024 ₹5,00,000; Balance in Profit and Loss A/c of Tyre Ltd. on 31/03/2024 ₹70,000; Profit earned during the year 2024-25 ₹45,000; 5% Dividend declared and paid by Tyre Ltd. for 2023-24 ₹25,000.

You are required to calculate the capital reserve / goodwill at the date of acquisition. The calculations are to be made under the following assumptions: Case (i) It is assumed that the dividend is paid out of post-acquisition profits. Case (ii) It is assumed that the dividend is received for pre-acquisition period. (4 Marks)
answer_html:
Case (i) – Dividend assumed paid out of post-acquisition profits: total dividend paid ₹25,000, so the dividend received by Rubber (70%×25,000=₹17,500) is credited to P&L, not netted against cost of investment.

Cost of shares4,05,000
Less: Face value of capital, i.e. 70% of 5,00,000(3,50,000)
Add: Share of capital profits (70,000×70%)49,000
Goodwill6,000

Case (ii) – Dividend assumed received for pre-acquisition period: since the dividend received relates to the pre-acquisition period, it is deducted from the cost of investment in the subsidiary.

Cost of shares4,05,000
Less: dividend received (70%×25,000)(17,500)
Subtotal3,87,500
Less: Face value of capital, i.e. 70% of 5,00,000(3,50,000)
Add: Share of capital profits (70,000×70%)49,000
Capital reserve11,500
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees were unable to compute Goodwill or Capital Reserve as on the date of acquisition. There was confusion regarding the treatment of dividends – particularly whether dividends were declared from post-acquisition profits or received for the pre-acquisition period. Several examinees incorrectly interchanged assumptions, and many failed to adjust the pre-acquisition dividends from the cost of investment as required.

topic_text: Topic 1.6: Consolidation with a mid-year bonus issue from pre-acquisition reserves and unrealised profit on an upstream (subsidiary-to-parent) inter-company sale
question_html: Seva Limited and subsidiary Meva Limited, Balance Sheets as at 31st March 2025 (₹ Lakh): Seva — Equity Shares of ₹10 6,000, General Reserve 1,500, P&L 2,000, 10% Debentures 1,180, Trade Payable 1,500; Land and Building 4,000, Plant & Machinery 1,460, Investments (Meva shares) 3,000, Inventories 1,400, Trade Receivable 1,420, Cash at Bank 550, Cash in Hand 350. Meva — Equity Shares of ₹10 4,000, General Reserve 1,200, P&L 1,500, 10% Debentures 820, Trade Payable 1,080; Land and Building 4,150, Plant & Machinery 1,650, Inventories 1,100, Trade Receivable 1,000, Cash at Bank 600, Cash in Hand 100. Seva acquired 80% of Meva on 1st April 2024 (Meva's General Reserve ₹2,000 lakh, P&L ₹800 lakh on that date). On 1st November 2024, Meva issued a 1:3 bonus share out of General Reserve (as at 31 March 2024 balance). On 31st March 2025, Seva's inventory includes goods purchased from Meva for ₹125 lakh, on which Meva made a profit of ₹25 lakh. Prepare the Consolidated Balance Sheet as per Schedule III.
answer_html:
W.N.9 Bonus shares: Meva's shares post-bonus 4,000 lakh (at ₹10 face value, i.e. 400 lakh shares) represent 4/3 of pre-bonus holding; pre-bonus = 4,000×3/4=3,000; bonus issued = 4,000−3,000=1,000 (lakh, i.e. ₹1,000 lakh face value), funded from General Reserve.

W.N.1 Meva's General Reserve movement: Opening 2,000 − Bonus 1,000 + transfer from P&L 200 = Closing 1,200.

W.N.2 Meva's P&L movement: Opening 800 − transfer to General Reserve 200 + Net profit for the year (balancing) 900 = Closing 1,500.

W.N.4 Capital profits (pre-acquisition): General Reserve at acquisition, net of the bonus issue (2,000−1,000=1,000) + P&L at acquisition (800) = 1,800. Seva's 80% share = 1,440; Minority's 20% = 360.

W.N.3 Revenue profits (post-acquisition): 900 (from W.N.2); Seva's 80% share: General Reserve 160 (80% of 200) + P&L 560 (80% of 700, i.e. profit after removing the amount already transferred to reserve) = 720; Minority's 20% = 180.

W.N.5 Capital Reserve: Paid-up value of shares held (80% of 4,000) 3,200 + share in capital profits 1,440 = 4,640; less cost of shares 3,000 = Capital Reserve ₹1,640 lakh.

W.N.6 Minority Interest: 20% of share capital (800) + share in revenue profits (180) + share in capital profits (360) = 1,340; less unrealised profit (20% of 25 = 5, Meva's share of the inter-company profit since Meva is the seller) = Minority Interest ₹1,335 lakh.

Consolidated Balance Sheet as at 31st March, 2025 (₹ Lakh): Share Capital 6,000 (Seva's own, unchanged); Reserves and Surplus 5,840 (Capital Reserve 1,640 + General Reserve 1,660 + P&L 2,540); Minority Interest 1,335; Long-term borrowings 2,000 (1,180+820); Trade payables 2,580 (1,500+1,080). Total 17,755. Assets: PPE 11,260 (Land&Building 8,150 [4,000+4,150] + Plant&Machinery 3,110 [1,460+1,650]); Inventories 2,475 (1,400+1,100−25 unrealised profit); Trade receivables 2,420 (1,420+1,000); Cash and cash equivalents 1,600 (Bank 1,150 + Cash in hand 450). Total 17,755.

topic_text: Topic 2.10: Potential equity shares excluded from voting power when determining significant influence, even though counted for total economic holding percentage
question_html: A Ltd. has a share capital of 50,000 shares @ ₹100 per share. H Ltd. acquired 15% shares in A Ltd. on 1.4.2024. It also acquired all the 5,000, 12% convertible debentures of ₹100 each of A Ltd. These debentures will be converted at par into equity shares of A Ltd. after 3 years. State whether, as per AS 23, A Ltd. is an Associate of H Ltd. or not with reasons?
answer_html:
As per para 3 of AS 23 'Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements', an associate is an enterprise in which the investor has significant influence and which is neither a subsidiary nor a joint venture of the investor.

Standard further explains in para 4 that as regards share ownership, if an investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary(ies), 20% or more of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor has significant influence, unless it can be clearly demonstrated that this is not the case. Conversely, if the investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary(ies), less than 20% of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor does not have significant influence, unless such influence can be clearly demonstrated.

Further as per an explanation to para 4 of the standard, for the purpose of classification of associate, the potential equity shares of the investee held by the investor will not be taken into account for determining the voting power of the investor. In other words, the voting power should be determined on the basis of the current outstanding securities with voting rights.

As per the information given in the question, H Ltd. presently holds indirectly 22.7% shares (with and without voting rights) (Refer W.N.) in A Ltd. However, the current outstanding securities with voting rights in A Ltd. is only 15% and the remaining holding is on account of potential equity shares. Since potential equity shares do not have voting rights they will not be taken into consideration while determining the significant influence of H Ltd. on A Ltd. Hence, A Ltd. is not an associate of H Ltd.

Working Note – Calculation of percentage of holding of shares after conversion:

Particulars₹
Current holding is 15% i.e. 7,500 shares of ₹100 each7,50,000
Potential equity shares i.e. 5,000 shares of ₹100 each5,00,000
Total12,50,000

Total share capital of A Ltd. after conversion of debentures into equity shares will be = ₹50,00,000 + ₹5,00,000 = ₹55,00,000

Percentage of holding = (12,50,000/55,00,000) × 100 = 22.7% approx.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is including the convertible debentures' post-conversion equity stake in the voting-power test, arriving at 22.7% and concluding significant influence exists, without recognising that AS 23 excludes potential equity shares from the voting-power calculation used for the significant-influence presumption.

topic_text: Topic 2.3: 20% voting-power presumption of significant influence; goodwill computed per-tranche against the investee's net asset value at each tranche's own acquisition date
question_html: A Ltd. invested ₹1,00,000 to acquire 10% stake (Investment I) in B Ltd. and later invested ₹3,00,000 to acquire additional 20% (Investment II). The net asset value of the B Ltd. at the respective investment dates was ₹7,50,000 and ₹12,50,000 respectively. Determine whether B Ltd. is an associate of A Ltd. Also, calculate goodwill arising on the acquisition of the associate.
answer_html:
As per para 3 of AS 23, an associate is an enterprise in which the investor has significant influence and which is neither a subsidiary nor a joint venture of the investor. Significant influence may be gained by share ownership, statute or agreement. As regards share ownership, if an investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary(ies), 20% or more of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor has significant influence, unless it can be clearly demonstrated that this is not the case. In this case, A Ltd. has invested 30% in B Ltd. so B Ltd. is to be considered as an associate of A Ltd.

The goodwill arising on the acquisition of the associate will be computed as follows:

Investment I1,00,000
Share of net assets (10 percent of ₹7,50,000)(75,000)
Goodwill (A)25,000
Investment II3,00,000
Share of net assets (20 percent of ₹12,50,000)(2,50,000)
Goodwill (B)50,000
Total goodwill (A + B)75,000

topic_text: Topic 1.4: Jointly controlled asset - each venturer records its own share of assets, liabilities, and expenses directly
question_html: Hari Ltd., OM Ltd. and Bhakti Ltd. jointly constructed a pipeline to transport gas manufactured by them (a jointly controlled asset under AS 27). Expenditure incurred: Buildings ₹18,00,000 (depreciate @5% p.a.); Pipeline ₹90,00,000 (@15% p.a.); Computers & electronics ₹4,50,000 (@40% p.a.); Vehicles ₹13,50,000 (@20% p.a.). They equally bear pipeline maintenance expenditure of ₹9,00,000 each year. Show the extract of the consolidated balance sheet and the extract of Statement of Profit & Loss and Balance Sheet for each venturer.
answer_html:
Each venturer records its own one-third share of each jointly-controlled asset directly in its own books, per AS 27's proportionate-consolidation treatment for a jointly controlled asset (no separate joint entity exists).

Per-venturer figures (identical for each of Hari/OM/Bhakti, one-third share each): Land & Building 6,00,000, less depreciation @5% (30,000) = 5,70,000. Plant & Machinery (Pipeline) 30,00,000, less depreciation @15% (4,50,000) = 25,50,000. Computers 1,50,000, less depreciation @40% (60,000) = 90,000. Vehicles 4,50,000, less depreciation @20% (90,000) = 3,60,000. Total PPE per venturer: ₹35,70,000. Depreciation and amortisation expense per venturer: 30,000+4,50,000+60,000+90,000 = ₹6,30,000. Other operating expenses (pipeline maintenance, one-third share) ₹3,00,000.

Consolidated (all three venturers combined) extract: PPE — Land & Building 3×5,70,000=17,10,000; Plant & Machinery 3×25,50,000=76,50,000; Computers 3×90,000=2,70,000; Vehicles 3×3,60,000=10,80,000; Total Consolidated PPE: ₹1,07,10,000.

topic_text: Topic 1.2: Three forms of joint venture - operations, assets, entities
question_html: Briefly explain the scope and forms of Joint Venture as per AS 27.
answer_html:
Scope: AS 27 applies to accounting for interests in joint ventures and reporting joint venture assets, liabilities, income, and expenses in the financial statements of venturers and investors, regardless of the structure/form under which the joint venture activities take place. Its consolidated-financial-statements provisions apply only when the venturer prepares and presents CFS.

Forms of Joint Venture: (i) Jointly controlled operations — no separate entity created; venturers use their own resources, raise their own funds, incur expenses, and realise sales individually, using shared assets/employees alongside their own business, with no separate books maintained for the joint venture. (ii) Jointly controlled assets — no separate legal entity, but the venturers jointly own assets used to generate economic benefit for each of them, taking up related expenses/liabilities per the contractual agreement. (iii) Jointly controlled entities — a new entity is created, pooling the venturers' resources; the entity purchases its own assets, incurs its own liabilities/expenses, and makes its own sales; the net result is shared per the contractual agreement, which also determines joint control; a separate set of books is maintained.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees conflated jointly controlled assets with jointly controlled entities, missing that the defining distinction is the absence vs. presence of a separate legal entity and separate books.

topic_text: Topic 2: Meaning of Amalgamation
question_html: Distinguish between Amalgamation, Absorption and External Reconstruction of Company.
answer_html:
BasisAmalgamationAbsorptionExternal Reconstruction
MeaningTwo or more companies are wound up and a new company is formed to take over their business.An existing company takes over the business of one or more existing companies.A newly formed company takes over the business of an existing company.
Minimum number of companies involvedAt least three companies.At least two companies.Only two companies.
Number of new resultant companiesOnly one resultant company is formed; two companies are wound up to form a single resultant company.No new resultant company is formed.Only one resultant company is formed – a newly formed company takes over the business of an existing company.
ObjectiveTo cut competition and reap economies of large scale.To cut competition and reap economies of large scale.To reorganise the financial structure of the company.
ExampleA Ltd. and B Ltd. amalgamate to form C Ltd.A Ltd. takes over the business of another existing company B Ltd.B Ltd. is formed to take over the business of an existing company A Ltd.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is confusing Absorption (no new company formed) with External Reconstruction (a newly formed company takes over the existing one), since both involve only two companies and can otherwise sound similar if the definitions aren't stated precisely.

topic_text: Topic 4: Purchase Consideration
question_html: Wow Ltd. agreed to takeover Wonder Ltd. on 1st April, 2024. The terms and conditions of takeover were as follows: (i) Wow Ltd. issued 56,000 equity shares of ₹100 each at a premium of ₹15 per share to the equity shareholders of Wonder Ltd. (ii) Cash payment of ₹39,000 was made to equity shareholders of Wonder Ltd. (iii) 24,000 fully paid preference shares of ₹50 each issued at par to discharge the preference shareholders of Wonder Ltd. (iv) The 8% Debentures of Wonder Ltd. (₹78,000) converted into equivalent value of 9% debentures in Wow Ltd. (v) The actual cost of liquidation of Wonder Ltd. was ₹23,000. Liquidation cost is to be reimbursed by Wow Ltd. to the extent of ₹15,000. You are required to: (1) Calculate the amount of purchase consideration as per the provisions of AS 14 and (2) Pass Journal Entry relating to discharge of purchase consideration in books of Wow Ltd.
answer_html:
As per AS 14 'Accounting for Amalgamations', consideration for the amalgamation means the aggregate of shares and other securities issued and payment made in the form of cash or other assets by the transferee company to the shareholders of the transferor company – the 8% Debentures conversion (a discharge to Wonder Ltd.'s own debenture-holders, not its shareholders) and the liquidation-cost reimbursement are therefore excluded from purchase consideration.

(i) Computation of Purchase Consideration:

Preference Shares: 24,000 × ₹5012,00,000
Cash39,000
Equity shares: 56,000 × ₹115 (100+15 premium)64,40,000
Total Purchase Consideration76,79,000

(ii) Journal entry (books of Wow Ltd.):

Liquidator of Wonder Ltd. Dr. 76,79,000; To Cash 39,000; To Preference Share Capital A/c 12,00,000; To Equity Share Capital A/c 56,00,000; To Securities Premium A/c 8,40,000 [56,000 × ₹15 (115−100)].
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is including the debenture conversion or the liquidation-cost reimbursement within purchase consideration, missing that AS 14's definition covers only amounts paid to the transferor company's shareholders, not its debenture-holders or its own liquidation expenses.

topic_text: Topic 4: Purchase Consideration
question_html:
Astha Ltd. is absorbed by Nistha Ltd.; the consideration being the takeover of liabilities, the payment of cost of absorption not exceeding ₹10,000 (actual cost ₹9,000); the payment of the 9% debentures of ₹50,000 at a premium of 20% through 8% debentures issued at a premium of 25% of face value and the payment of ₹15 per share in cash and allotment of three 11% preference shares of ₹10 each and four equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of 20% fully paid for every five shares in Astha Ltd.

The number of shares of the vendor company are 1,50,000 of ₹10 each fully paid. Calculate purchase consideration as per AS 14.
answer_html:
As per AS 14 "Accounting for Amalgamations", the term "consideration" has been defined as the aggregate of the shares and other securities issued and the payment made in the form of cash or other assets by the transferee company to the shareholders of the transferor company.

The payment made by the transferee company to discharge the Debenture holders and outside liabilities and cost of winding up of the transferor company shall not be considered as part of purchase consideration.

Computation of Purchase Consideration

Cash payment ₹15 × 1,50,00022,50,000
11% Preference Shares of ₹10 each [(1,50,000 × 3/5) × ₹10]9,00,000
Equity shares of ₹10 each @ 20% premium [(1,50,000 × 4/5) × ₹12]14,40,000
Total Purchase consideration45,90,000
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is including the payment made to discharge the transferor company's debenture holders and outside liabilities within the purchase consideration, missing that AS 14 restricts purchase consideration strictly to amounts paid to the transferor company's shareholders.

topic_text: Topic 7.10: Seasonal/occasional revenue and costs are not deferred to a later interim period; change of estimate applied prospectively
question_html:
XY Limited reported a Profit Before Tax (PBT) of ₹18 lakhs for the third quarter ending 31st December 2024. Following observations are noted: (i) Dividend income of ₹8 lakhs received during the quarter has been recognized to the extent of ₹2 lakh only. (ii) Sales promotion expenses ₹15 lakhs incurred in the third quarter, 70% has been deferred to the fourth quarter as the sales in the last quarter is high. (iii) In the third quarter, the company changed depreciation method from WDV to SLM, which resulted in excess depreciation of ₹4 lakhs. The entire amount has been debited in the third quarter, though the share of the third quarter is only ₹1 lakhs. (iv) ₹3 lakhs extra-ordinary gain received in third quarter was allocated equally to the third and fourth quarter. (v) Cumulative loss resulting from change in method of inventory valuation was recognized in the third quarter of ₹5 lakhs. Out of this loss ₹2 lakhs relates to previous quarters. (vi) Sale of investment in the first quarter resulted in a gain of ₹30 lakhs. The company had apportioned this equally to the four quarters.

Calculate the result of the third quarter as per AS 25 and also comment on the company's view on each observation. (7 Marks)
answer_html:
As per para 36 of AS 25 "Interim Financial Reporting", seasonal or occasional revenue and cost within a financial year should not be deferred as of interim date until it is appropriate to defer at the end of the enterprise's financial year.

Comments on observations: (i) Dividend income received during 3rd quarter should be recognised in the 3rd quarter only. (ii) Sales promotion expenses cannot be deferred on the basis that fourth quarter has more sales; recognised in 3rd quarter only. (iii) As per AS 10, a change in depreciation method is a change in accounting estimate per AS 5, applied prospectively – no adjustment would be required for this observation. (iv) Extra-ordinary gain of ₹3 lakhs should be wholly recognized in 3rd quarter only. (v) Loss of ₹2 lakhs belongs to previous quarters, not 3rd quarter, so it should not be deducted from the profit of 3rd quarter. (vi) Gain on sale of investment is an occasional gain, so it cannot be deferred; the ₹7.5 lakhs considered as income of the 1st quarter will be reversed from the profit of the 3rd quarter.

Statement showing Adjusted Profit Before Tax for the third quarter:

Profit before tax (as reported)18,00,000
Add: Dividend income (8,00,000 − 2,00,000)6,00,000
Excess depreciation charged in 3rd quarter due to change in method—
Extra ordinary gain (3,00,000 − 1,50,000)1,50,000
Cumulative loss due to change in inventory valuation method, applied retrospectively (5,00,000−3,00,000)2,00,000
Subtotal27,50,000
Less: Sales promotion expenses (70% of 15 lakhs)(10,50,000)
Less: Gain on sale of investment (occasional gain should not be deferred)(7,50,000)
Adjusted Profit before tax for the third quarter9,50,000
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: Most examinees exhibited inadequate knowledge of AS 25 "Interim Financial Reporting." They failed to calculate the Adjusted Profit Before Tax for the third quarter accurately. Even among those who arrived at the correct figure, very few provided appropriate observations with sound reasoning.

topic_text: Topic 1: Introduction
question_html: Aerodots Ltd. has the following capital structure as on 31.03.2025 (₹ in thousands): Equity Share Capital (shares of ₹10 each) 600; General Reserve 540; Securities Premium 200; Profit & Loss 100; Revaluation Reserve 30; Investment Allowance Reserve (Statutory Reserve) 75; Infrastructure Development Reserve 25; Loan Funds 2000. On 1st April, 2025 the company wants to buy back 14,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹30 per share, duly authorized. You are required to calculate the maximum permissible number of equity shares that can be bought back.
answer_html:
TestShares (thousands)
Shares Outstanding Test (25% of 60,000 shares)15
Resources Test (25% of Shareholders' funds ÷ ₹30 buyback price)12
Debt Equity Ratio Test11
Maximum buy-back permitted [least of the above]11

Thus, the lowest being 11,000 shares, the company cannot buy back the requested 14,000 shares.

W.N.1 Shares Outstanding Test: outstanding 60,000 shares; 25% = 15,000.

W.N.2 Resources Test: Paid-up capital 600 + Free reserves (540+200+100=840) = Shareholders' funds 1,440; 25% = 360; ÷ buy-back price ₹30 = 12,000 shares.

W.N.3 Debt-Equity Ratio Test: Loan funds 2,000; minimum equity to maintain (2:1) = 1,000; present equity funds 1,440; future equity funds (after 110 transferred to CRR, solved simultaneously) = 1,330; maximum permitted buy-back of equity = 1,330−1,000 = 330; ‷ ₹30/share = 11,000 shares.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees included statutory reserves (Investment Allowance Reserve) or the Infrastructure Development Reserve in "free reserves" for the Resources Test, when only reserves freely available for distribution should be counted.

Company qualifies all tests for buy-back of shares and came to the conclusion that it can buy 80,000 equity shares @ ₹25.

topic_text: Topic 2: Prov. Sect. 70 Comp. Act, 2013
question_html:
Alpha Chemicals Ltd., a listed company, proposes a buy-back of 12% of its equity share capital from its free reserves under Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013. On scrutiny of its records, the following details were observed: 1. The company intends to route the buy-back through its wholly-owned subsidiary. 2. The company had defaulted on repayment of a term loan to a public sector bank, which was fully repaid 27 months ago. 3. The company has not filed its Annual Return and Financial Statements for the preceding financial year. 4. The company had declared a dividend in the last year, but the amount remains unpaid for 35 days from the date of declaration.

You are required to: Examine the compliance of Alpha Chemicals Ltd. with the requirements of Section 70 of the Companies Act, 2013 and state whether the company is eligible to proceed with the proposed buy-back. (5 Marks)
answer_html:
As per Section 70 of the Companies Act, 2013, the company cannot buy back its own shares under the following conditions, all of which apply to Alpha Chemicals Ltd.:

1. Buy-back through Subsidiary – Prohibited. Section 70(1)(a): A company shall not buy back shares through any subsidiary, including wholly owned subsidiaries.

2. Default in Term Loan – Three-Year Cooling Off Required. Section 70(1)(c): A company that has defaulted in repayment of a term loan can buy back shares only after 3 years from the cessation of default. Alpha repaid the loan only 27 months ago — still short of the required 36-month period. Hence, not eligible.

3. Non-Filing of Annual Return and Financial Statements. Section 70(2): Buy-back is prohibited if the company has not complied with Sections 92 (Annual Return) and 129 (Financial Statements). Alpha has failed to file both which disqualifies it from buy-back.

4. Unpaid Dividend for More Than 30 Days. Section 127 read with Section 70(2): Non-distribution of declared dividend within 30 days is a punishable offence. Dividend unpaid for 35 days, this is a default.

Alpha Chemicals Ltd. is not eligible to proceed with the buy-back under Section 70 due to multiple violations.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Many examinees identified only one or two of the four independent Section 70 violations, most often missing the wholly-owned-subsidiary prohibition since it is easy to assume a wholly-owned subsidiary is functionally the same entity as its parent.

topic_text: Topic 1: Introduction
question_html:
Balance Sheet of P Limited as at 31st March, 2025: Share Capital ₹1,500 lakh (150 lakh Equity Shares of ₹10 each); Reserves and Surplus ₹2,750 lakh (Capital Reserve 380, Securities Premium 300, Revaluation Reserve 120, General Reserve 1,800, Surplus 150); Long Term Borrowings ₹3,450 lakh (12% Debentures 2,250, Unsecured Loans 1,200); Short Term Borrowings (Current Maturities) ₹1,980 lakh; Trade Payables ₹1,500 lakh; Total ₹11,180 lakh. Assets: PPE ₹5,675 lakh; Inventories ₹1,005 lakh; Trade Receivables ₹1,500 lakh; Cash and Cash Equivalents ₹3,000 lakh; Total ₹11,180 lakh.

Considering the large surplus funds, the company decides to buy back 30 lakh Equity Shares on 1st April, 2025. Prevailing market value ₹16/share; to induce shareholders, offer price is 25% over market. Buy-back is duly authorized by Articles and necessary resolution passed.

Comment with your calculations, whether buy-back of shares by the company is within the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013. If yes, pass necessary journal entries towards buy-back of shares. (7 Marks)
answer_html:
Determination of Buy-back of maximum no. of shares as per the Companies Act, 2013:

1. Shares Outstanding Test: Number of shares outstanding 150 lakh; 25% of shares outstanding = 37.5 lakh.

2. Resources Test: Paid up capital ₹1,500 lakh; Free reserves (300+1,800+150) ₹2,250 lakh; Shareholders' funds ₹3,750 lakh; 25% of Shareholders' funds ₹937.5 lakh; Buy-back price per share ₹20 (₹16 × 1.25); Number of shares that can be bought back = 46.875 lakh.

3. Debt Equity Ratio Test (loans cannot exceed twice the equity funds post buy-back): Loan funds (3,450+1,980) = 5,430 lakh; Minimum equity to be maintained after buy-back (2:1 ratio, a/2) = 2,715 lakh; Present equity/shareholders' funds = 3,750 lakh. Using the simultaneous-equation method (amount transferred to CRR = x, maximum permitted buy-back of equity = y): (3,750−x) − 2,715 = y, and y/20×10 = x (i.e. y=2x); solving gives x=345 lakh, y=690 lakh. Maximum number of shares at ₹20/share = 34.50 lakh shares.

Summary: Shares Outstanding Test 37.5 lakh; Resources Test 46.875 lakh; Debt Equity Ratio Test 34.50 lakh. Maximum number of shares that can be bought back (least of the three) = 34.50 lakh. Company qualifies all tests; it can buy a maximum of 34.5 lakh shares, but wants to buy back only 30 lakh equity shares @₹20 – therefore, the buy-back of 30 lakh shares is within the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.

Note on CRR: if one share is bought back, ₹10 face value is reduced from share capital, ₹10 premium (20−10) is reduced from Securities Premium, and an amount equal to the face value (₹10) must be transferred from free reserves to CRR, since CRR itself is not a free reserve available for dividend distribution.
