topic_text: Topic 1: Introduction
question_html:
Aerodots Ltd. has the following capital structure as on 31.03.2024: Equity Share Capital (shares of ₹10 each) ₹6,00,000 [thousands]; Reserves: General Reserve ₹5,40,000; Securities Premium ₹2,00,000; Profit & Loss ₹1,00,000; Revaluation Reserve ₹30,000; Investment Allowance Reserve (Statutory Reserve) ₹75,000; Infrastructure Development Reserve ₹25,000; Loan Funds ₹20,00,000 (all figures ₹ in thousands, as printed).

On 1st April, 2024 the company wants to buy back 14,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹30 per Equity share.

You are required to calculate maximum permissible number of equity shares that can be bought back.

Buy Back of shares is duly authorized by its articles and necessary resolution has been passed by the company.
answer_html:
Statement determining the maximum number of shares to be bought back (in thousands):

ParticularsNumber of shares
Shares Outstanding Test (W.N.1)15
Resources Test (W.N.2)12
Debt Equity Ratio Test (W.N.3)11
Maximum number of shares that can be bought back [least of the above]11

Thus, the lowest being 11,000 shares, the company cannot buy back 14,000 shares.

Working Notes:

1. Shares Outstanding Test: Number of shares outstanding 60 (thousand); 25% of the shares outstanding = 15 (thousand).

2. Resources Test: Paid up capital ₹600 (thousand); Free reserves (540+200+100) ₹840 (thousand); Shareholders' funds ₹1,440 (thousand); 25% of Shareholders fund ₹360 (thousand); Buy-back price per share ₹30; Number of shares that can be bought back = 12,000 shares.

3. Debt Equity Ratio Test (loans cannot exceed twice the Equity Funds post Buy-Back): Loan funds ₹2,000 (thousand); Minimum equity to be maintained after buy-back in the ratio of 2:1 (a/2) ₹1,000 (thousand); Present equity shareholders fund ₹1,440 (thousand); Future equity shareholders fund (see W.N.4) (1,440−110) = ₹1,330 (thousand); Maximum permitted buy-back of Equity [(d)−(b)] ₹330 (thousand); Maximum number of shares that can be bought back @ ₹30/share = 11,000 shares.

4. Amount transferred to CRR and maximum equity to be bought back, by simultaneous equation method – let amount transferred to CRR = x, maximum permitted buy-back of equity = y. Equation 1: (Present Equity − Transfer to CRR) − Minimum Equity to be maintained = Maximum Permitted Buy-Back ⇒ (1,440−x)−1,000 = y ⇒ 440−x = y. Equation 2: y/30 × 10 = x, i.e. 3x = y. Solving: x = ₹110 (thousand), y = ₹330 (thousand).

Alternatively, Maximum number of shares from debt equity ratio test may be worked out as: Buy-back price + Face value of equity shares = ₹30+₹10 = ₹40. Excess of equity fund over the minimum equity to be maintained = 1,440−1,000 = 440 (thousand). Number of Shares that can be bought back = 440/40 (thousand) = 11 (thousand).
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: Many examinees failed to calculate the number of shares eligible for buyback under the Debt-Equity Ratio Test. Errors were also observed in the Resource Test and Shares Outstanding Test, resulting in incorrect calculations of the maximum permissible number of shares for buyback.

question_html: Summarized Balance Sheet of Vijay Ltd. as on 31st March, 2025: Equity Shares of ₹10 each 3,50,000; 8% Cumulative Preference Shares of ₹100 each 1,75,000; 6% Debentures of ₹100 each 1,40,000; Sundry Creditors 1,75,000; Provision for taxation 3,500; Total 8,43,500. Scheme of Internal Reconstruction approved and effective 31st March, 2025: (1) Investments brought to market value; (2) Taxation liability settled at ₹5,250 out of Current Assets; (3) balance of P&L written off; (4) equity shares reduced to ₹4 each; (5) preference shares reduced to ₹60 each; (6) debenture rate increased to 9%, debenture holders surrender ₹100 debentures and exchange 1-for-1 for fresh ₹80 debentures; (7) balance Current Assets revalued at ₹1,57,500; (8) PPE written down to 80%; (9) one creditor of ₹70,000 gives up 50% of claim, allotted 8,750 equity shares of ₹4 each in settlement. Pass Journal entries.
answer_html:
Journal entries (books of Vijay Ltd.):

  1. Capital Reduction A/c Dr. 1,750; To Investments A/c 1,750 (investments revalued to market value).
  2. (a) Provision for taxation A/c Dr. 3,500; Capital Reduction A/c Dr. 1,750; To Liability for taxation 5,250 (tax liability ascertained). (b) Liability for Taxation Dr. 5,250; To Current Assets (Bank) 5,250 (tax paid).

  5. 8% Cumulative Preference Share Capital A/c Dr. 1,75,000; To 8% Cumulative Preference Share Capital A/c 1,05,000; To Capital Reduction A/c 70,000 (conversion of preference capital to ₹60 each).
  6. 6% Debentures A/c Dr. 1,40,000; To 9% Debentures A/c 1,12,000; To Capital Reduction A/c 28,000 (fresh ₹80 debentures issued to existing holders).
  7. Capital Reduction A/c Dr. 1,87,250; To Current Assets A/c 1,87,250 (current assets revalued).
  8. Capital Reduction A/c Dr. 87,500; To Property, Plant & Equipment A/c 87,500 (PPE written down to 80%).
  9. Sundry Creditors A/c Dr. 70,000; To Equity Share Capital (₹4) A/c 35,000; To Capital Reduction A/c 35,000 (creditor's claim settled 50% cash-equivalent-in-shares, 50% given up).

mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees missed crediting Capital Reduction for the "gain" side of each conversion entry (e.g. the difference between old and new share/debenture face values), recording only the reduction without recognising the corresponding Capital Reduction credit.

  7. Loan A/c Dr. 2,50,000; To Bank A/c 2,50,000 (loan repaid from cash proceeds).
  8. Capital Reduction A/c Dr. 7,68,750; To Profit and Loss A/c 5,63,750; To Plant A/c 43,750; To Trademarks and Goodwill A/c (balancing figure) 1,61,250 (losses/assets written off).

(and reduced) as on 31.3.2025: Share Capital 15,12,500 (75,000 6% Pref. shares of ₹10 = 7,50,000 + 1,52,500 Equity shares of ₹5 = 7,62,500); Long-term borrowings 2,78,750 (7,16,250−1,87,500−2,50,000); Trade Payables 2,58,750; Other Liabilities 43,750; Total 20,93,750. topic_text: Topic 2.3/3: Full internal-reconstruction scheme: capital write-down, asset revaluation, creditor/debenture/loan settlement, notes to accounts
question_html:
Sky Limited has decided to reconstruct the Balance Sheet since it has accumulated huge losses. The following is the balance sheet of the company as on 31st March, 2025 before reconstruction (₹ in lakh): Share Capital 4,200; Reserves and Surplus (1,566); Long term Borrowings 2,100; Trade Payables 306; Other Liabilities 72; Total 5,112. Assets: PPE 2,250; Current Investments 600; Inventories 900; Trade Receivables 1,350; Cash and Cash Equivalents 12; Total 5,112.

Notes to Accounts: Share Capital — Authorised: 600 lakh shares of ₹10 each 6,000; 24 lakh, 8% Preference Shares of ₹100 each 2,400; Total 8,400. Issued, Subscribed and Paid up: 300 lakh Equity Shares of ₹10 each, fully paid up 3,000; 12 lakh 8% Preference Shares of ₹100 each, fully paid up 1,200; Total 4,200. Reserves and Surplus: Debit balance of Profit and Loss A/c (1,566). Long Term Borrowings: 6% Debentures (Secured by Freehold Property) 1,200; Director's Loan 900; Total 2,100. Trade Payables: Trade payables for Goods 306. Other Liabilities: Interest Accrued and Due on 6% Debentures 72. PPE: Freehold Property 1,650; Plant & Machinery 600; Total 2,250. Current Investment: Investment in Equity Instruments 600. Inventories: Finished Goods 900. Trade Receivables: Trade receivables for Goods 1,350. Cash and Cash Equivalents: Balance with Bank 12.

The Board of Directors of the company decided upon the following scheme of reconstruction: (1) Preference Shares are to be written down to ₹75 each and Equity Shares to ₹2 each. (2) Preference Shares Dividend in arrears for 3 years to be waived by 2/3rd and for balance 1/3rd, Equity Shares of ₹2 each to be allotted. (3) Debenture holders agreed to take one Freehold Property at its book value of ₹900 lakh in part payment of their holding. Balance Debentures to remain as liability of the company. topic_text: Topic 4: Methods Charging Goods Branches
question_html: Why goods are marked on invoice price by the head office while sending goods to the branch?
answer_html: Goods are marked on invoice price to achieve the following objectives: (i) To keep secret from the branch manager, the cost price of the goods and profit made, so that the branch manager may not start a rival and competitive business with the concern; and (ii) To have effective control on stock i.e. stock at any time must be equal to opening stock plus goods received from head office minus sales made at branch. (iii) To dictate pricing policy to its branches, as well as save work at branch because prices have already been decided.
mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is listing only the stock-control rationale for invoice pricing and omitting the equally important reason of concealing the cost/profit margin from the branch manager to prevent a rival business being set up.
chapter_label: Accounting for Branches Including Foreign Branches

topic_text: Topic 1.2: Branch account at invoice price with stock reserve for unrealised loading in closing stock
question_html: Care, a retail business, opened a branch Omega on 1st January, 2025; all branch sales on credit. Goods supplied from Head Office, invoiced at 10% above cost. Transactions (Jan/Feb/March 2025): Goods sent to Branch (purchase price) 60,000 / 75,000 / 90,000; Sales as per branch monthly report 57,000 / 63,000 / 82,500; Cash received from debtors and remitted to HO 30,000 / 76,500 / 52,500; Returns to HO (invoice price) 1,800 / 900 / 3,600. Branch closing stock at 31st March, 2025: ₹80,100 at invoice-to-branch price. Record in HO books, showing balances as on 31st March, 2025 and the branch gross profit for the three months.
answer_html:
Branch Account (books of Care, Head Office): To Goods sent to Branch A/c (2,25,000 total invoice value: 60,000+75,000+90,000, at 10% above cost) 2,47,500; To Goods sent to Branch A/c — returns loading (6,300 × 10/110) 573; To Stock Reserve (80,100 × 10/110) 7,283; To Net Profit (balancing figure, transferred to General P&L) 56,045. By Goods sent to Branch — Loading 22,500; By Goods sent to Branch — Returns 6,300; By Bank (cash remitted, 30,000+76,500+52,500) 1,59,000; By Balance c/d — Closing Branch Assets: Stock 80,100, Debtors (Sales 2,02,500 − Collections 1,59,000 = 43,500) 1,23,600. Total both sides ₹3,11,400.

Memorandum Branch Debtors Account confirms Debtors closing balance ₹43,500 (Sales 2,02,500 − Cash received 1,59,000).

Branch gross profit for the three months: ₹56,045 (the loading on goods sent, net of returns and closing stock reserve, represents the branch's realised gross margin for the period).
mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees forgot to create a stock reserve for the unrealised loading in the closing stock (still at invoice price, not yet sold), overstating the branch's reported profit.

topic_text: Topic 7: Adj & Recon of Branch & HO Accounts
question_html:
(i) Why goods are marked on invoice price by the head office while sending goods to the branch?

(ii) Rama Ltd. has a branch at Delhi, that closes its books of accounts every year on 31st March. This is an independent branch, which maintains comprehensive books of accounts for recording their transactions. You are required to show Journal Entries in the books of branch on 31st March, 2026 to rectify or adjust the following: (A) Head Office allocates ₹2,70,000 to the Branch as Head Office Expenses, not yet recorded by Branch. (B) Depreciation of Branch Fixed Assets, accounts kept by Head Office, not yet recorded in Branch Books ₹2,30,000. (C) Branch paid ₹2,80,000 as salary to a Head Office manager, debited by the branch to its Salaries A/c. (D) Head Office collected ₹2,60,000 directly from a Branch Customer on behalf of the Branch; intimation received by the branch only now, not recorded till now. (E) A remittance of ₹3,00,000 sent by the Branch has not yet been received by Head Office. (F) The Branch incurred Advertisement Expenses of ₹60,000 on behalf of another Branch. (G) Goods worth ₹1,50,000 dispatched by the head office, but the branch has received goods worth ₹1,10,000 till date of reconciliation; rest received subsequently. (H) Goods worth ₹25,000 returned by the branch to head office yet not received by the head office. (6 Marks)
answer_html:
(i) Goods are marked on invoice price to achieve the following objectives: (a) to keep secret from the branch manager the cost price of the goods and profit made, so that the branch manager may not start a rival and competitive business with the concern; (b) to have effective control on stock, i.e. stock at any time must equal opening stock plus goods received from head office minus sales made at branch; (c) to dictate pricing policy to its branches; (d) to save work at branch because prices have already been decided.

(ii) Books of Branch – Journal Entries:

#ParticularsDr. (₹)Cr. (₹)

topic_text: Topic 5.1: Goods invoiced at cost plus a fixed margin - Trading and Profit and Loss (Final Accounts) method with a Stock Reserve for unrealised profit in closing stock
question_html:
Following is the information of Kullu Branch of M/s Best Enterprises of Shimla for the year ending 31st March 2023: (1) Goods are invoiced to the branch at cost plus 20%. (2) Branch sold goods at invoice price plus 25%. (3) Other Information is as follows: (i) Stock (at cost price) as on 1st April, 2022 is ₹2,25,000. (ii) Goods sent by Head office to branch during the year (at cost price) are ₹14,85,000. (iii) Goods returned by Branch to Head office during the year (at Invoice price) are ₹75,000. (iv) Sales by the branch during the year ₹19,50,000. (v) Expenses incurred at Branch ₹56,000.

You are required to ascertain the following: (a) Profit earned by the Branch by Preparing Trading and profit and loss account for the year ended 31st March 2023. (b) Also find the stock reserve on Closing stock.
answer_html:
(i) In the books of Kullu Branch – Trading and Profit and Loss Account:

ParticularsAmount ₹ParticularsAmount ₹

To Goods received by Head office17,82,000By Goods returned by Branch75,000
To Expenses56,000By Closing stock (Refer W.N.)4,17,000
To Net profit (Bal fig)3,34,000
Total24,42,000Total24,42,000

(ii) Calculation of Closing Stock: Cost price 100; Invoice price 120 (100+20); Sales price 150 (120+25% of 120). Opening Stock (at invoice price) 2,70,000 [₹2,25,000 cost × 120/100]; Goods received (at invoice price) 17,82,000 [₹14,85,000 cost × 120/100]; Less: Goods Returned (at invoice price) 75,000; Subtotal 19,77,000; Less: Cost of Goods Sold (at invoice price) 15,60,000 [Sales ₹19,50,000 ÷ 150 × 120]; Closing Stock (at invoice price) 4,17,000.

Stock reserve in respect of unrealised profit = 4,17,000 × (20/120) = ₹69,500.
mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: Some examinees prepared the Trading and Profit and Loss Account by taking the cost price instead of the price at which goods were sent to the branch. This led to errors in determining the stock value and the branch's profit.

question_html: Shanti Limited (Chennai), incorporated 1st April 2024, opened branches at Madurai and Tiruchi. Goods invoiced to branches at Cost + 25%. All branch expenses paid by HO; each branch has its own Sales Ledger, sends weekly statements, remits cash collections daily. Prepare Branch Accounts as they would appear in HO's books, using the Debtors Method, for the year ended 31st March 2025.

Loading = 25% on cost = 1/5th on invoice price.

Memorandum Branch Debtors Account (both branches): To Sales (credit) 1,25,200/1,10,000; less Sales Returns 2,300/1,200, Bad Debts 6,000/—, Cash collected from debtors (balancing figure) 82,400/85,200 = Closing balance 34,500/23,600 (matches given closing Trade Receivable, confirming the collection figures).

An alternative full solution exists recording goods at cost price instead, giving the same net profit figures (82,200/92,800) through a differently structured account.

This resulted in an incorrect computation of net profit. Many examinees also arrived at an incorrect amount of cash collected from branch debtors.
